en: The *Yogacintāmaṇi* of Śivānandasarasvatī, typed from *Yogacintāmaṇi*, edited by Haridas Śarma. Calcutta: Calcutta Oriental Press (no date).
Transcribed by Ramya for the Hatha Yoga Project.
Not Proofread!!! Page 1:
Yogacintāmaṇiḥ
The First Chapter.
Salutations to the Gurus, to the Goddesses, to the Yogis, and salutations to Hari.
[I bow to that which is] eternally most subtle, consisting of the single essence of consciousness, liberated, pure, and auspicious.

We incessantly worship that light which is the self-luminous effulgence, dense with bliss, which yogis— whose minds have been brought under control— behold as the full abode, shorn of all conceptualization, accessible through the Upanishads, and established by the means of valid knowledge. 1.
He possesses the brilliance of ten million suns against the dense, great, and insurmountable darkness of illusion;
he is the full moon scorched by the rays of the sun at the end of the eon known as saṃsāra;
and he is the ground of compassion and beauty, acting as the fierce wind at the end of the eon for the ocean of suffering.
May the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who brings about the awakening to all meanings, be ever more abundant for me. || 2 ||
Resembling a fire that consumes the flood of obstacles, his beautiful form is like a wish-fulfilling gem for the fulfillment of all desires.
I bow to Lambodara of fierce valor, whose feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Acyuta, Īśa, and others. ||3||
Having bowed to the venerable Vyāsa, the ascetic Śaṅkara, the spiritual preceptor Bhava, the teacher Śrī Rāmacandra, and all those lords of yogis whose lotus feet are the state of intense bliss;
[I shall expound] the *Śrī Yogacintāmaṇi*, which has fallen into the midst of the ocean of various texts.
Yati Śivānanda clearly composes [this work] which accomplishes every purpose without exception. || 4 ||
Yoga, however, is precisely non-conceptual *samādhi*. Thus Patañjali said:

"Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ*). That state of the mind which, preceded by the cessation of mental fluctuations directed toward external objects, abides in the form of Brahman, is called non-conceptual *samādhi* known as cessation; this is what is termed Yoga. This is supported by the rule in grammar, "the suffix *yuC* is used in the sense of *samādhi*. It is also stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"O Rāghava, there are two methods for the dissolution of the mind: Yoga and Knowledge."
"Yoga is the cessation of its fluctuations; knowledge is thorough investigation.
Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* as the words of the Lord:
"Just as for one whose mind is unified, yoga arises from the cessation of other mental fluctuations..."
Wherein one's own nature is contemplated as entirely empty and free from appearance.
The yoga of non-existence has been proclaimed, by which one perceives the Self,
wherein one beholds the Self as eternal bliss and stainless.
"But for me alone, the Supreme Lord has taught the supreme yoga. Thus [it is said].
In the *Āditya Purāṇa* it is also said: "From yoga knowledge is born; yoga is the state of one-pointedness of mind.
In the *Yogabīja*, the Goddess said:
O God, what is called yoga? And of what nature is the practice of yoga?
Or what might be attained through yoga? Tell me all that, O Śaṅkara!
The Lord said:
"That which is the union of the apāna and prāṇa breaths, as well as of the mind together with the rajas quality;
that which is the union of the sun and the moon, and of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)."
"Thus, the union of the web of dualities is called yoga.
Here, the union of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), characterized as seedless absorption (nirbījasamādhi), is called yoga;
however, it should be understood that others [the various practices] are merely its constituent parts.
It will be explained in detail in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Having made the mind free from activity and having unified the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) with the Supreme Self, one is liberated; he is called one who is engaged in yoga."
Having turned all the external openings inward as well as the internal ones,
one should join the collection of senses with the mind alone, and the mind with the Self.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), liberated from all states of being, is merged into the Supreme Self;
this is both knowledge and yoga—everything else is merely the prolixity of other books.
The wise say that the conjunction of the self and the mind is called *yoga*;
some, however, maintain that the union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths is also *yoga*.
"The union of the sense objects with the senses is called *yoga* by the wise"—thus [it is said].

Since *prāṇāyāma* (breath control) is established as a limb of *yoga* (*yogāṅga*) in all *yoga* scriptures, it does not possess the status of *yoga* itself. For this very reason, the mention of "some" (*kaiś cana*) is merely an introduction of an alternative view for the purpose of revealing the secret [of this system]. By the "union of sense objects with the senses," the contemplation of the *nāda* (inner sound) and the gazing at the space between the eyebrows or the vital breath (*prāṇa*), etc., are intended. Since the possibility of attaining *samādhi* through these means has been stated by *yogins* such as Patañjali and others, it will be explained in detail [later].
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"O Khāṇḍikya, hear from me as I speak the true nature of yoga,
abiding in which the sage, having attained absorption in yoga, does not fall away."
The union of that distinguished movement of the mind, which depends upon one's own effort,
with Brahman is designated as yoga.
Thus, he whose yoga consists in the discernment of dharmas endowed with absolute distinction is indeed called a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu).

The meaning of the two [verses] is as follows: having turned away from sense-objects the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which by nature tends toward the external and is habituated to engaging with objects, and having directed it inward through an effort consisting of self-application; that specific movement—knowledge—which is distinguished by being produced by the mind acting as its cause and which has turned away from the state of the individual soul (*jīva*); the conjunction of that movement with Brahman as its object, arising from the contemplation of the non-difference of the individual soul from Brahman, is called *samprajñāta-samādhi*. This is the meaning of the two.

The meaning of the third case [suffix], however, is as follows: for one who possesses such practice, there is a quality characterized by the extreme distinction consisting of the dissolution of the mind into the supreme Brahman known as Viṣṇu;
and that yogin whose yoga occurs is designated in the scriptures as a "seeker of liberation" (*mumukṣu*) because he possesses the practice of yoga, which is the direct means to liberation.
By this, samādhi characterized by non-discernment (asamprajñāta) has been described.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"This root *yuj* in the sense of 'union' has reached its ultimate limit of stability."
Since that [practice] is appropriate for him, he is therefore called a yogin.

He has reached—that is, attained—the supreme state of the living being (*jīva*) and Brahman known as the direct realization of non-duality (*advaita-sākṣātkāra*), and not merely their conjunction. That state is appropriate for one who possesses the practice of non-duality; for that state is called *yoga* by way of the etymological derivation that "it is joined" (*yujyate*). By this, the *asamprajñāta-samādhi* (non-cognitive absorption) is indicated. Likewise, in that very same work:
"That which is the cessation of the mind is considered *yoga* by the practitioners of *yoga*.
By this, the *nirvikalpa* (thought-free) state is indicated. Yājñavalkya says:
"Know that knowledge consists of yoga, and yoga is endowed with eight limbs; the union of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (parātman) is declared to be yoga."

By this, the cognitive (*samprajñāta*) and non-cognitive (*asamprajñāta*) [samādhis], characterized respectively by the dissolution and non-dissolution of the mind, have been briefly described. It is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Prince, that which is oneness with the Supreme Brahman—that alone is celebrated as Yoga; what other definition of Yoga could there be?"
It brings about the complete exhaustion even of that karma which initiates the present body.
O Protector of the Earth, hear also the fruit of that yoga and its definition:
That which is declared to be the supreme Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, pure and imperishable—
the dissolution of the mind therein is designated as yoga.
Through that yoga and that awakening, when the mind has dissolved therein,
the Puruṣa does not perceive any distinction from its cause.
O Lord of Men, the distinction between self and other is imagined through ignorance;
upon the destruction of that [ignorance], there is indeed no longer any distinction between self and other.
O scorcher of foes, this non-differentiation between the Supreme Self and the individual self is indeed the supreme yoga; it has been described to you in brief.

Here, by the passage beginning with "by the higher Brahman," *asamprajñāta-samādhi* (non-cognitive absorption) is described. Now, one might object: since all yoga scriptures enumerate eight limbs of yoga—namely, restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*)—it appears that *yoga* is something entirely distinct from *samādhi*, which is merely counted as one of its limbs. This is true. For *samādhi* is of two kinds, distinguished as *samprajñāta* (cognitive) and *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive). Among these, *samprajñāta-samādhi* is a limb (*aṅga*) of *asamprajñāta-samādhi*. This determination of the relationship between the limb and the possessor of the limb (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is established in the *Pātañjala* [Yogasūtra].
It has been stated that the triad beginning with *dhāraṇā* (concentration) is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it directly assists [the practice].

On the other hand, the five beginning with *yama* (restraint) are stated to be "external" (*bahiraṅga*), because they assist *samādhi* (absorption) by means of uprooting the contrary thoughts such as violence (*hiṃsā*). [Regarding] *āsana* (posture)—P.

However, even among those [eight limbs], there is a progressively greater degree of utility. As stated in such passages as, "When mastery over posture is attained, there is steadiness of the vital breath," and so forth.

Likewise, although *dhāraṇā* (concentration) and *dhyāna* (meditation) are internal relative to the other limbs because they produce *samprajñāta-samādhi* (cognitive absorption), they are external relative to the seedless absorption known as *asamprajñāta*, since they assist it only indirectly. This is established by the two sūtras: "The triad [of concentration, meditation, and absorption] is internal relative to the preceding [limbs]" and "Even that is external to the seedless [absorption]. Vasiṣṭha and Yājñavalkya, however, maintain that all four beginning with *yama* (restraint) are internal.
Yājñavalkya says:
"In the beginning, four are external; those that follow are indeed internal.
These four have been declared as the limbs of yoga, O fair-faced one."
Vasiṣṭha says:

"Listen to the four internal [practices] beginning with pratyāhāra. Here it should be understood that the practices beginning with yama and ending with dhyāna are external limbs (bahiraṅga) because they assist each subsequent one and bring about *samprajñāta-samādhi*; for *nirbīja-samādhi*, *samprajñāta-samādhi* alone is the internal limb (*antaraṅga*).

That by which the true nature of an object is correctly and thoroughly known—being free from doubt, error, and indecision—is *samprajñāta-samādhi*, a specific form of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). It is called *samprajñāta-samādhi* because it possesses this specific cultivation. Furthermore, it is fourfold, distinguished by its components such as *vitarka* (gross thought) and so forth: namely, with *vitarka*, with *vicāra* (subtle thought), with *ānanda* (bliss), and with *asmitā* (I-am-ness). Thus, the venerable Patañjali stated:
"The *samprajñāta* [samādhi] follows the forms of *vitarka*, *vicāra*, *ānanda*, and *asmitā*."

Meditation (*bhāvanā*) consists in the repeated fixing of the object of meditation within the mind after the abandonment of other objects. The object of meditation is twofold: the Lord (*īśa*) and the principles (*tattva*). The principles, moreover, are twofold: insentient (*jaḍa*) and sentient (*ajaḍa*). The insentient ones are twenty-four in number, distinguished as *prakṛti*, *mahat*, *ahaṅkāra*, the eleven organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five gross elements (*bhūta*). In brief, however, they are simply *prakṛti*, which is designated as the power of the Lord (*īśvaraśakti*) or as *māyā*.

In such scriptural passages as, "The power of the Divine Self, hidden by its own qualities," and "Know Māyā to be Prakṛti and the Great Lord to be the wielder of Māyā," [the subject is established]. The non-inert is the Puruṣa. The inert is also of two kinds: subtle and gross. Among these, when first the gross elements and the sense organs are taken as objects and contemplation is performed through the intermingling of verbal expression and the synthesis of preceding and succeeding moments, that is designated as *savitarka* (with deliberation).

Likewise, when the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) has as its object a subtle internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as delimited by space, time, and qualities (*dharma*), it is designated as "with deliberation" (*savicāra*).

When that contemplation is not so delimited and has only the substratum (*dharmī*) as its object, this is called the "samādhi beyond deliberation" (*nirvicāra-samādhi*); it is also termed the "attainment of the graspable" (*grāhya-samāpatti*).

When the *sattva* of the internal organ is contemplated while permeated by traces of *rajas* and *tamas*, then, due to the absence of those [guṇas] and the predominance of the *sattva* consisting of bliss and light, there arises the samādhi called "with bliss" (*sānanda*). Those who possess stability in this alone are called "bodiless" (*videha*).

Beyond this, when meditation proceeds by taking as its object pure *sattva* which is not overwhelmed by even a trace of *rajas* or *tamas*, that *samādhi* is called "with self-sense" (*sāsmita*). This is because, in that state, the object of cognition—the *sattva*—is subordinated, while the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) predominates, such that only pure existence remains. Furthermore, one should not suspect there is no difference between egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and self-sense (*asmitā*); for where the internal organ perceives objects through the expression "I am," that is egoism.

But where, through inward-turning, in the process of inverse transformation, when the mind has dissolved into its own nature (prakṛti), pure existence alone shines forth—that is "I-am-ness" (asmitā). Those who delight in these [states] alone are designated by the term "merged in nature" (prakṛtilaya). However, for those who, having known the Supreme Puruṣa, proceed toward meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), this discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti) is called "absorption into the grasper" (grahītṛ-samāpatti).

This samādhi with cognitive awareness (saṃprajñāta-samādhi) has four stages; it is designated in the Yoga scriptures by such terms as "with conceptualization" (savikalpa), "with seed" (sabīja), and "contemplation" (nididhyāsana). Regarding the definition of the samādhi without cognitive awareness (asaṃprajñāta-samādhi), the venerable Patañjali says: "The other [samādhi] is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation and consists of residual latent impressions (saṃskāra)."

The meaning of this is as follows: "Cessation" (*virāma*) means that by which one ceases; it is the abandonment of thoughts such as *vitarka* and so forth. That which is both cessation and a mental modification (*pratyaya*) is "cessation-modification" (*virāma-pratyaya*). Its "practice" (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated fixing [of the mind] upon that in the consciousness. Whatever mental fluctuation arises therein, its continuous negation through the formula "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), preceded by which is the *samādhi* consisting of residual impressions (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*), is the other, namely, the "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*) *samādhi*; this is the meaning.

Because nothing whatsoever is cognized as an object there, it is called "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi. This is described as "seedless" (*nirbīja*), "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*), "unsupported" (*nirālamba*), and "royal yoga" (*rājayoga*). Regarding royal yoga, Vāmadeva said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, beautiful with supreme bliss!
By your grace, I have obtained the ancient Yoga in its full detail."
"Tell me of another suffering that has been described by you.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"The former is endowed with external mudrās and is absorbed in external yoga."
Indeed, that very same internal yoga is that which is endowed with the internal mudrā.
That very yoga has been described by the preeminent sages as Rājayoga;
because it shines among all yogas, it is remembered as Rājayoga.
"That which leads the embodied soul to that radiant king, the imperishable Supreme Brahman, is called Rājayoga."
Names common to the two types of samādhi,
as stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, and manonmanī."
That is immortal, like the lunar light; it is without support and free from stain.

"Amanaska, laya, śūnya-aśūnya, parāpara, jīvanmukti, sahaja, and turya are all synonymous terms. Thus, the two-fold nature of samādhi has indeed been shown and cited previously in such passages from the Purāṇas and other texts: "Mantrayoga, laya, Rājayoga, and likewise Haṭha..."

"Yoga is declared to be fourfold by the yogis who perceive reality. Since this fourfold nature of yoga is thus heard, and since the word "yoga" is observed to be used in various senses—such as *karmayoga*, *bhaktiyoga*, *vairāgyayoga*, and *sāṃkhyayoga*—in the Gītās attributed to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Śiva, and others, one might ask: how can it be determined that "this alone is yoga"? To this we reply: True; it is like the use of the word "life" (*jīvana*) for the means of sustaining life.
Because the application of the word "yoga" is appropriate for the direct and indirect means of attaining yoga, such as mantra-yoga and others. To explain:

in the repetition of mantras (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth, yoga and the attainment of yoga arise solely through the grace of the Lord when He is propitiated, and not otherwise. As stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa* in the words of Śiva:
"O slayer of Krauñca, by my grace alone, the yogi shall become omniscient, perfected, and free from old age and death; it cannot be otherwise. Thus it is said in the *Mānasollāsa*.
"Through the grace of the Guru, one obtains yoga characterized by its eight limbs;

through the grace of Śiva, one obtains eternal perfection in yoga. Thus it is said in the Śaiva [tradition]: "By those who are proficient in the recitation of mantras dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others..."
"The mantra-yoga is accomplished just as it was by the King of Vatsa and others.
Thus [it is said]. In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "One who seeks knowledge attains knowledge, and one who seeks liberation especially so."
"One should indeed remember Virūpākṣa, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Furthermore, it is clearly evident in all the Yoga scriptures that the recitation (japa), worship (pūjā), and other rites dedicated to Īśvara constitute limbs of yoga (yogāṅga). As will be stated:
"Rājayoga is indeed seedless absorption (nirbīja-samādhi); laya is cognitive absorption (samprajñāta); and haṭha is simply breath control (prāṇāyāma)."
And so it is said in the *Yogabīja*:
"Mantra, Haṭha, Layayoga, and Rājayoga—these are its stages in succession;
though one, this is designated as the fourfold Mahāyoga."
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva! Please explain to me, in due order and according to reality, this fourfold essence of yoga (yogatattva) in accordance with the divisions of the stages (bhūmikā)."
The Lord said:
"With the syllable *sa*, the vital air goes out; with the syllable *ha*, it enters.
The individual soul always mutters this mantra, 'Haṃsa, Haṃsa'."
Through the word of the Guru, the recitation within the suṣumnā becomes reversed;
that which is proclaimed as "I am He, I am He" is called mantra-yoga.
On the Western Path, realization arises through the yoga of mantra;
by the letter *ha* alone this sun is signified, and by the letter *ṭha*, the moon is said to be expressed.
The unification of the sun and the moon is called *haṭha*;
through *haṭha*, the dullness arising from all defects is attained.
When the knower of the field and the supreme self become one—
O Goddess, when that unity is accomplished, the mind attains dissolution.
When the yoga of absorption (layayoga) arises, the vital breath attains steadiness;
through absorption, perfection is attained—the state of supreme bliss.
"Having attained the state of *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis], one shines by means of *rājayoga*.
The fourfold yoga is to be known in connection with *prāṇāyāma*.

Previously, *mantrayoga* was described as external; however, the distinction here is that it is internal. *Haṭhayoga* is said to be characterized by the unification of the two vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) known as the sun and the moon."
In the Vāsiṣṭha:
"The moon, as the apāna, nourishes the body from the outside;
the sun, or else fire, as the prāṇa, digests this internal form."
But according to another opinion (matāntara):
The perceptions regarding these two are inverted.
As it is said in the *Amṛtasiddhi*:
"Prāṇa should be known as consisting of the moon, and apāna likewise as consisting of the sun."
Both leaders of the body perform the coming and going.

"The union of these two should always be practiced with effort by those seeking liberation; through their mastery, all perfections arise for the wise. Based on this statement from the *Gītā*, and from the declaration of Yājñavalkya, "The union of prāṇa and apāna is known as prāṇāyāma," the term *prāṇāyāma* is expressed here by the word *haṭha*.

That particular state of contemplation in which the manifestation of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) arises for the yogi who has dissolved into the Supreme Self is called *samprajñāta-lakṣaṇa-samādhi* or *layayoga*. Furthermore, even within *layayoga*, the dissolution of both the vital breath (*marut*) and the mind (*manas*) into the nine wheels (*cakras*) is called *layayoga*, by means of which the yogi, endowed with the supreme sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and others, shines throughout the three worlds. And that [state] which is of the nature of seedless meditation is called *rājayoga*. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
Under the influence of prāṇa and apāna, the individual soul (jīva) runs upward and downward;
flickering along the left and right paths, it finds no stability.
Just as a bird bound by its tether is drawn back even though it has flown away,
so too the individual soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), is drawn along by the out-breath and in-breath (prāṇa and apāna).
The downward-moving breath draws up the upward-moving breath, and the upward-moving breath draws up the downward-moving breath.
The knower of reality joins these two, which are situated above and below.
With the sound "ha" it goes out; with the sound "sa," it enters again.
The individual soul (jīva) constantly recites this mantra, "haṃsa, haṃsa."
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times—
this is the number of mantras that the individual soul recites constantly, day and night.
The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā bestows yoga upon yogins;
by the mere intention of this [mantra], one is liberated from all sins.
"There is no knowledge equal to this, no recitation equal to this,
and no wisdom equal to this— there has been none in the past, nor will there be in the future.
All three of these are indeed limbs of Rājayoga.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "The various postures (*pīṭha*), breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*), and divine techniques (*karaṇa*),
as well as all practices of dissolution (*laya*) and forceful yoga (*haṭha*), are for the sake of attaining *Rājayoga*."
"A person established in rājayoga is a deceiver of time.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the six rites (ṣatkarma) are included. The term "pīṭha" is also an indicator for restraint (yama) and observance (niyama), because those two are taught as limbs of yoga in all yoga treatises.

Therefore, although in this verse it appears that all the practices beginning with *yama* and *niyama* directly assist *rājayoga*, nevertheless, upon a thorough examination of the preceding and following texts, such is not the established conclusion. It has already been stated that the eightfold group beginning with *yama* is useful for *samādhi* both directly and indirectly. Among those, the six *karmas* and the *mudrās* will be explained later;
therein, the six *karmas* function by way of removing defects such as phlegm (*śleṣman*), and in the absence of such defects, they are simply not required.

Others, however— disinclined to perform the six duties because they are fraught with many misfortunes even when practiced correctly— assert that the accomplishment of all tasks occurs through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) alone;
therefore, they maintain that Haṭha has no fixed auxiliary limbs.
And thus says the Ātmārāma:
"Is [the breath] free from the six activities, causing heaviness, phlegm, disease, and so forth?
One should then perform *prāṇāyāma*; it is accomplished without effort."

"One should perform the six acts for the purpose of removing fat and phlegm; otherwise, one should not perform them, because it is necessary for the equilibrium of the *doṣas*. According to some noble ones, "impurities are dried up by *prāṇāyāmas* alone," and thus other practices are not approved by their view. Regarding the *mudrās*, however, *mūlabandha*, *jālandharabandha*, *uḍḍīyāna*, *mahāmudrā*, *mahāvedha*, *mahābandha*, and *śakticālana* are directly beneficial to *Haṭha*. As for *viparītakaraṇī* and *khecarī*, the distinction is that they serve as means for the perfection of the body.

In the *Vāsiṣṭha*, however, the direct utility of *khecarī* is also stated. For instance: "Having diligently pressed the uvula at the root of the palate with the tongue, when the vital breath has entered the upper aperture, the vibration of the breath is restrained. Thus it is said in the *Mānasollāsa*.
"The suppression of both the downward and upward breaths until they reach the palate,
and the placement of the tongue upon the uvula, is the means for accomplishing yoga."
In the *Nandikeśvara-tārāvalī*:
"When the female serpent has been awakened by the upward-flying *jālandhara-mūlabandha*..."
"Releasing [the breath] inwardly and entering the *suṣumnā*,
the bearer of fragrance abandons both going and coming."
In the Haṭhapradīpikā:
"By means of various postures and also through diverse breath-retentions (kumbhaka) and yogic exercises (karaṇa)..."
When the primordial power (ādi-śakti) has awakened, the vital breath (prāṇa) dissolves into the void (śūnya).
For the yogi who has awakened the power that has arisen and abandoned all drawing-in [of breath],
the state of the innate (sahaja) arises of its own accord.
"When the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the void within the Suṣumṇā channel,
the knower of yoga then eradicates all the sense organs," as stated in the Vāsiṣṭha.
Through the contraction of the regions beginning with the anus, through the sequential performance of postures and other practices,
through devotion, the purification of the seat (āsana), and through contemplation on the meaning of the scriptures of the virtuous;
O Rāma, through right conduct, by avoiding the company of people, by total renunciation, by sitting in a comfortable posture,
and indeed by the practice of breath control, [this is attained] after some time.
O observer of noble vows, through the abandonment of anger and greed, there is the renunciation of enjoyments;
and through that renunciation, they come completely under control in the cessation of both giving and taking.

"All the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of a person who knows that [Truth] are like servants because of his sovereignty. [Objection: But since many fruits are heard of for *mudrās*, *haṭhayoga*, and so forth, why should they not be considered primary? [Reply: No, because that would contradict the actual purpose. Thus it is stated in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā: "The mention of a fruit in relation to subsidiary parts is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); that which has no fruit when in proximity to something that possesses a fruit is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that. Furthermore, the practice of ritual action (*karma-yoga*) is simply the propitiation of the Lord (*Īśvara*). And that is enumerated among the observances (*niyama*) which constitute the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*) in all Yoga treatises. Accordingly, there are two *pātañjala-sūtras*: [The sūtras follow.]
"Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute the yoga of action.
"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances."

Penance (*tapas*) consists of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such observances; self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the recitation of the *praṇava* and other sacred texts; and devotion (*praṇidhāna*) is the dedication of all actions to the Supreme Lord without expectation of fruit. These are called the yogas of action (*kriyāyoga*). Through their practice, *samādhi* arises. Regarding the means by which the yoga of action serves as an aid to *samādhi*, Patañjali states: "It is for the purpose of cultivating *samādhi* and for the purpose of attenuating the afflictions (*kleśa*). The afflictions are ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to cling to life (*abhiniveśa*).

Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*)—which consists of the error of perceiving that which is not [as it is]—is the breeding ground for the four afflictions beginning with egoism (*asmitā*), taking the form of the "apprehension of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. Egoism (*asmitā*) is a specific modification of the mind whose object is the identity of the *sattva* (the intellect) and the *puruṣa* (the self), and which takes the form of the "I-maker" (*ahaṅkāra*).

Attachment (*rāga*) is the form of desire that always regards pleasure as existing; aversion (*dveṣa*) is the disparagement of the causes of suffering; and clinging (*abhiniveśa*) is stubborn persistence. Since these five are designated by the term "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because they produce suffering, and since they are subsidiary parts of the great misfortune called *saṃsāra* and are obstacles to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is through the eradication of the fundamental demerit (*pāpa*) that constitutes their root—by means of weakening them—that the practice of yoga (*kriyā-yoga*) becomes a cause for meditative absorption. Furthermore, those afflictions which are gross and have already begun to bear fruit are removed by meditation (*dhyāna*) in the form of one-pointedness of mind.

And thus there are two sūtras: "Their fluctuations are to be abandoned by meditation," and "The subtle ones are to be abandoned by re-absorption. These afflictions have ignorance as their root. Their fruit consists of the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics [of karma]. And the fruit of action, in its aforementioned form, is the experience of pleasure and pain. Furthermore, there is the attainment of a birth corresponding to that karma, as well as lifespan and objects of the senses. By way of these, [it is said]: "When the root exists, its fruition is birth, lifespan, and experience"; for here, birth and lifespan are also declared to be fruits of karma.
Wealth, although pleasant as a means for producing enjoyments, should be understood as suffering for the discerning person, because it is seen to result in a bitter taste upon its transformation.

These afflictions, rooted in ignorance, have as their ripened fruits—known as karmic latencies (*karmāśaya*) consisting of virtuous and non-virtuous actions—the results of birth, lifespan, and experience; therefore, they must certainly be abandoned by the discerning person.

The abandonment of that [bondage] is accomplished by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), which cuts off the obstacles that serve as its root. And right knowledge is accomplished through the scripture (*śāstra*). This scripture consists of four sections called "causes" (*hetu*) regarding what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and so forth; thus it has a fourfold arrangement (*caturvyūha*). Namely: "Suffering-filled transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is to be abandoned; the conjunction of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*) is the cause of what is to be abandoned; the cause of that [conjunction] is ignorance (*avidyā*); the absolute cessation of the conjunction of primordial matter and the spirit is abandonment"—that itself is isolation (*kaivalya*). In this regard, the cause is discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*).

And thus the Sūtras state: "Suffering yet to come is that which is to be abandoned; the cause of what is to be abandoned is the conjunction of the seer and the seen; its cause is ignorance; from the absence of that [ignorance] comes the absence of conjunction, which is abandonment; the isolation of the seer is the result; and unflinching discriminative discernment is the means of abandonment," and so forth.

The subsequent sūtras concerning the seer, the seen, and their conjunction are as follows: "The seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he observes the mental modifications"; "The seen consists of the elements and the senses, characterized by the natures of illumination, activity, and inertia, and exists for the purpose of experience and liberation"; "Conjunction is the cause of the perception of the essential natures of the powers of the self and the owner. The meaning of this is: the Puruṣa is the seer, whose nature is consciousness, who is unchanging, and who, by mere proximity, makes the object—though devoid of its own transformations—manifest.

The "visible" (dṛśya) consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—characterized by illumination, activity, and restraint—which take the form of the objects of perception such as earth and the rest, defined by the subtle elements (tanmātras) and so forth, and which undergo gross and subtle transformations. It comprises the threefold organs—the cognitive, the active, and the internal—and has enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga) as its purpose. The cause of conjunction (saṃyoga) is that which serves as the means for the perception of the essential nature of the two eternal and all-pervading entities known as the power of the object (svaśakti) and the power of the subject (svāmiśakti), which exist in a state of non-perception during the stage of dissolution.

"The nature of being an enjoyer from time immemorial is precisely this conjunction of the seer and the seen. Here, this must be considered: in the phrase "the seer is pure consciousness alone" (*draṣṭā dṛptimātra*), the word "alone" (*mātra*) is intended to exclude the relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) as maintained by the Naiyāyikas; it does not, however, preclude [the self's] having bliss and purity as its essential nature. This is just as Sarvajñātmamuni stated: "The supreme reality is one's own innate nature, which is pure consciousness alone. The word "alone" is based on the Vedic scripture: "This Self is dearer than a son... (*tadetat preyaḥ prattrāt*).

Because the nature of the Self as bliss is established either by the mark (*liṅga*) of being the object of unconditional love or by the experience "I slept happily," for this very reason the Śruti text, "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who is bodiless," is intended to negate only pleasure and pain derived from sense objects (*vaiṣayika*). Otherwise, there would be no sense in such statements as, "Other beings live on only a fraction of this very bliss," or "That which is the Infinite (*bhūman*) is bliss; there is no bliss in the finite."

"Who else could breathe, who else could live, if this bliss did not exist in space? "For he alone causes this [world] to rejoice. "Knowing the bliss of Brahman," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss"—there would be contradiction with such infinite scriptural passages. Nor can it be said that these texts are intended to teach that bliss belongs to Brahman and not to the individual soul (*jīva*); for through such scriptural statements as "That thou art," "This Self," "The Brahman which is immediate and direct," and "The Self which is within all," the identity of the *jīva* and Brahman is established. Therefore, the word "only" (*mātra*) does not exclude the nature of bliss.

However, it is more appropriate [to say] that it is precisely the delimiter of the relationship between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*). This is the meaning of the aphorism: "Uninterrupted discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the means of liberation. The meaning is as follows: that discernment—that is, the wisdom (*prajñā*)—regarding the distinction such that "the *guṇas* are one thing and the *puruṣa* is another," is the means for "liberation," which is the relinquishing of the visible world (*dṛśya*). It was stated that for a person who has attained discriminative discernment through scripture and inference, this [wisdom] is not yet the [final] means because of the persistence of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). [The word] "uninterrupted" (*aviplava*) [is used].

The meaning is "of one who is devoid of false knowledge. This is what is being said: "Having grasped discrimination through knowledge consisting of scripture (*śrutimaya-jñāna*), and having established it through knowledge consisting of reasoning (*yuktimaya-jñāna*), [one practices] cultivation (*bhāvanā*) served with long duration, uninterruptedness, and reverence. Discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which has reached the culmination of excellence and is accompanied by direct perception—being free from the disturbances of false knowledge along with its latent impressions (*savāsana*)—is the means for liberation," so say Vācaspati Miśra.

As for the commentary of Bhojarāja: "That in which there is no *viplava*—that is, no interruption in the form of emergence (*vyutthāna*)—is called discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). It is the transfer of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) into the inward-turned intellect (*buddhi*), which is unassailed by the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, and from which the conceit of being a knower and an agent has ceased due to the dissolution of ignorance through the force of cultivating the counter-thesis that 'the qualities (*guṇas*) are one thing and the Puruṣa is another.'"

"And when that [discriminative knowledge] has proceeded as a continuous stream, liberation (kaivalya) indeed occurs through the cessation of the object-of-sight's authority. Here, this must be considered: the mere cognition of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is not itself the nature of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) which serves as the means of liberation; rather, discriminative discernment is the first stage. Immediately following this, however, when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is purified and free from even a trace of *rajas* and *tamas*, there arises the state characterized by the identity of the form of the fluctuations [with the Seer]. This is established by the Sūtra: "Then the Seer abides in his own nature."

The supreme means for the attainment of *kaivalya*—characterized by the realization of the identity "I am Brahman," which has the nature of the manifestation of Brahman whose sole essence is full consciousness, and which is denoted by the term "cessation" (*hāna*)—is discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), defined as the knowledge that the qualities (*guṇas*) are one thing and the Spirit (*puruṣa*) is another. However, this explanation is useful solely for the purpose of distinguishing between the insentient and the sentient, because it serves as the specific cause for the cessation of the mental modification consisting of the egoistic identification with the inert body and so forth, which is the root of all misfortunes that have proceeded from time immemorial. For this very reason, even liberation is expressed in this system by terms such as "cessation" (*hāna*) and "aloneness" (*kaivalya*).

As for that which has been stated: the nature of one's own self as it manifests in the state of liberation, and the nature of the means to liberation as delimited by its unique object—both of these are directly revealed by the Śruti itself.

...this [Self] was not specifically explained as the primary subject by the venerable Patañjali. Thus, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman," and "He knew the Self alone as 'I am Brahman,'" and "Therefore, he became all that," knowledge is presented as the means and then concluded: "So now, he who knows thus, 'I am Brahman,' becomes this All."

Furthermore, that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition of things as otherwise than they are has also been demonstrated in that very *Avidyā-sūtra* by such passages as, "Now, he who thinks, 'He is one and I am another,' does not know," and so forth. Enough of this digression. What is meant is this: for one whose internal organ (*svānta*) is rendered utterly pure by all actions performed for the sake of the Lord—excluding those actions motivated by desire and those prohibited— [P.22]

For a person who has developed detachment through perceiving the defects of sense objects, and who—desiring the knowledge of the Self that eradicates all suffering along with its root, as understood from the Vedic statement, "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow"—has attained seedless *samādhi* by means of the practice of *nididhyāsana* reinforced by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) under the guidance of a true teacher, his ritual actions (*karmāṇi*), having fulfilled their purpose through the form of *samādhi*, cease of their own accord solely by way of the purification of the intellect (*buddhiśuddhi*).

And so it is said in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*: "Once the inclination of the intellect toward the Inner Self has been properly accomplished through purification, actions cease like clouds at the end of the rainy season. And in the *Rājayoga*:
"The yogi should not abandon actions;
rather, he is liberated by means of actions, through the destruction of the very volition that is the root of action."
To the extent that the dissolution of mental constructs occurs through constant practice,
to that same extent does the renunciation of action become more excellent for the yogi.
He who possesses the lofty innate bliss, who is himself ever-delighted in constant practice,
and who has abandoned all conceptual constructions— that wise one should renounce ritual action.

One should avoid like an outcaste that person who claims that even for a knower of Brahman there is worldly activity joined with ritual action— a person who has fallen away from both karma and Brahman.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Dharma must be practiced with effort, especially by a yogin;
those who know yoga understand that there is no yoga without dharma."
In the *Yājñavalkyagītā*, Gārgī said:
"O Master, how should a man engaged in yoga perform his prescribed duties during the two twilights or at night? And what is the expiation for one who does not perform them?"
Yājñavalkya said:
O lady of excellent hips, whatever ought to be performed by a man engaged in yoga during the two twilights or at night is indeed accomplished through that yoga.
And when the fire of one's own internal *agnihotra* has been intensified by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), for one who performs pure action with the oblation of a purified mind;
O young woman, what atonement can there be for him? For he has indeed accomplished his purpose when the separation between the individual soul and the Supreme Soul has been attained.
The action prescribed by the injunctions must be performed constantly by those who know Brahman;
however, at the time of separation, the yogi should not abandon it, thinking "it is suffering."
Karma is proclaimed to be his abode and his hell;
for it is not possible for a yogin to abandon karma entirely.
"Therefore, until death, the yogi must always perform action in a twofold manner.
As stated in the Bhagavadgītā: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means."
"For that very person who has ascended to yoga, tranquility (śama) is said to be the means.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Therefore, with every effort, remaining established in the ordinances of caste and stage of life..."
The wise one, having resorted to the final state, becomes the power of Māyā.
He whose mind is eternally dedicated to the Lord possesses that supreme dharma;
he attains the highest station described by the exponents of the Vedas.
O best of beings, for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and Śūdras,
their duty is that which is prescribed for their own respective caste, performed with joy and free from hatred.
"For that very thing is established as the cause of knowledge.
And in the *Yogabīja*: "O Goddess, without action, the perfection of yoga does not arise."
Neither knowledge nor the enjoyment of heaven is obtained by those devoid of merit.

"Therefore, that very effect which has a means of accomplishment must be achieved quickly; success is not attained otherwise—this is the speech of the Wise. Furthermore, the worship of Īśvara alone is the primary means of yoga. Thus, in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra], in the definition of the means of yoga: "Or through devotion to Īśvara" (*īśvara-praṇidhānād vā*). Here, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*). The meaning of the sūtra is that yoga and the fruit of yoga arise solely from the grace of Īśvara when He is worshipped with specific forms of physical, vocal, and mental devotion.

In Vedānta, there is the Vyāsa-sūtra: "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical. By this, since Patañjali has stated that even the path of devotion (bhakti-yoga) is a limb of Rāja-yoga, it is not the primary yoga.

To explain: the meaning of the statement "their cessation is achieved through practice and detachment" (*abhyāsavairāgyābhyāṃ tannirodhaḥ*) is as follows. Through the practice and detachment to be described hereafter, the mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*)—which consist of illumination, activity, and restriction, and which have ceased their outward attachment—come to abide within their own cause, the mind, in the form of latent power (*śakti*), by turning inward. In this process, detachment, born from perceiving the defects of sense objects, effects an aversion toward them; whereas practice, by demonstrating a peaceful flow that generates happiness, produces firm stability. Therefore, through these two, the mind [attains its goal]. (P.25)
Samādhi is called the cessation of mental fluctuations. He states the general and specific definitions of practice (*abhyāsa*) in two sūtras:
"In that regard, effort toward stability is practice."

"But that [practice], when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with reverence, becomes firm ground. "The modification of the mind established in its own nature when devoid of fluctuations is 'stability' (sthiti); the effort toward that, the enthusiasm, and the repeated fixing of the mind in that state is called 'practice' (abhyāsa). The meaning is that this very practice, when pursued over a long period, without interruption, and with excellence through yoga, becomes firm ground—that is, it becomes stable. In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Liberation comes through self-knowledge, and that indeed does not exist without yoga."
Furthermore, yoga is not accomplished merely through practice over a long period of time.
Yoga is not attained by resorting to the forest, nor by reflecting on various scriptures,
nor by gifts, nor by vows, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices.
Yoga is not attained by sitting in the lotus posture, nor by gazing at the tip of the nose;
it is not attained through ritual purity, nor through silence, nor even through the propitiation of mantras.
Through persistent application, constant practice, firm resolve in that very [object], and by not desisting again and again, yoga is accomplished; and not otherwise.
For one who constantly sports with the self, likewise for one who is united with the self,
and who is satisfied in the self alone, the perfection of yoga is not far off.
Then, he who does not perceive a second thing apart from the Self,
delighting in the Self— that lord of yogis becomes Brahman here in this very world.
For that Brahman is to be known by one's own self-experience, like the face of a young maiden;
indeed, one who is not a yogi does not know it, just as one blind from birth cannot perceive color.
"For one whose nature is constant practice, that [reality] becomes self-evident;
because of its subtlety, it is the supreme, eternal Brahman, which cannot be described. Thus [it is said].
In the *Āgama*, the *Pārameśvara-tantra*, it is said:
"Therefore, those who desire liberation must practice constantly;
from practice comes perfection, and through practice one attains liberation."
Through practice one attains consciousness; yoga proceeds from practice.
The perfection of the elements comes from practice, and the mastery of the vital breath comes from practice.

"Through practice, there shall be deception of time and likewise victory over death; through practice, the perfection of speech and the power to act at will will certainly come to pass. Thus it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
"Whether young, a child, or very old, or even diseased or weak,
one attains perfection through practice in all yogas, provided one is not bound by external constraints.
This is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi*, following the description of *mudrā* and *prāṇāyāma*.
Thus, the wise who desire liberation should always practice;
from practice yoga is born, and through yoga everything is accomplished.
By this yoga of practice, the vital air (vāyu) becomes mastered;
through the mastery of the vital air, the internal fire (vahni) increases greatly day by day.
For when the fire increases, food is indeed digested in the mouth;
through the complete digestion of the food, the increase of the vital essence (rasa) is produced.
When the rasa is constantly increased, the bodily constituents (dhātus) then increase;
indeed, through the nourishment of the constituent, the primary rasa itself increases.
When the primary essence is perfected, one becomes firm of body and possesses great strength;
through sheer power, great mastery and great practice arise.
P.27 Through the great binding and great practice, the digestion of the mercury occurs;
all defects, including the impurities of the root-urine decoction, are dried up.
All sins committed throughout ten million lifetimes are consumed right here through the yoga of practice, just as grasses are by fire.
Whatever divine austerities there may be, even by the tens of thousands and millions upon millions,
they become multiplied by millions of millions through the yoga of practice.
"Nature, its qualities, defects, and various diseases in the body perish through the yoga of practice, just as clouds in the sky are dispersed by the wind. Thus,
there are two sūtras concerning the general and specific characteristics of dispassion (*vairāgya*):

"Freedom from craving for objects perceived or heard"—the meaning of this is as follows: "A perceived object (*dṛṣṭa-viṣaya*) is one apprehended right here [in this world], such as sound and so forth. A heard object (*ānuśravika-viṣaya*) is one [found] in the world of the gods and so on. It is 'heard' (*anuśrūyate*) from the mouth of a teacher; thus it is 'hearing' (*anuśrava*), namely the Veda, and that which comes from that is 'heard' (*ānuśravika*)."

When one has become free from craving by seeing the insipidity of transformation (*pariṇāma*) in both of these objects, there arises the notion of mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*). This discernment—that "these [objects] are under my control, but I am not under their control"—is called the [second] detachment. The first detachment has objects as its domain; the second has the *guṇas* as its domain. Among these, the detachment whose object is the *guṇas* is called supreme. This detachment occurs only when the discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* has arisen.

"Because it is extremely conducive to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*). By this, it is stated that even Sāṃkhya-yoga, which has discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) as its primary object, possesses the status of yoga. Furthermore, in this way, one should see that *śravaṇa*—which consists in determining the purport of Vedāntic statements regarding the non-dual reality—and *manana*—which consists in reflecting upon the meaning heard through logical arguments—are included within the regulation [of the mind] by setting aside heterogeneous mental impressions and establishing a flow of homogeneous mental impressions; or rather, they are included within the cognitive (*samprajñāta*) meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by meditation (*dhyāna*).
And likewise, Yājñavalkya says in the *Niyamavivaraṇa*:
"The wise declare that hearing the Vedāntas is the hearing of the established truth (*siddhānta*);
while performing the hearing of the Vedāntas, one should practice yoga therein."

Therefore, it should be understood that there is nothing external to the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga) that is denoted by the word "yoga. Now, an objection may be raised: in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, it is said— "The method for crossing over the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is called by the word 'yoga';
likewise, it refers to the means of self-knowledge as well as the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇas)."
"Although both types are indeed declared by the word 'yoga,' nevertheless, this [latter] has attained its conventional usage primarily as that which is joined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

If it is asked how yoga can be the mere restraint of the mind given this statement, the answer is: it is true, for it was stated with the intention that the restraint of the mind consists essentially in the restraint of the vital breath. For this very reason, *prāṇāyāma* itself is, through the sequence of practice, designated by the terms withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*).
And so Dattātreya says:
"Prāṇāyāma is traditionally defined as the restraint of the vital breaths;
it is that by which the senses, which have been set in motion toward sound and other objects, are restrained by those of self-controlled mind."
They are withdrawn by means of yoga; therefore, it is known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal).
That which is held steady by the wise is called dhāraṇā (concentration).
The term *prāṇāyāma* and others are proclaimed as *dhāraṇā*;
these two *dhāraṇās* are known as *yoga* by the yogis who perceive reality.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is said to consist of twelve breath-controls (prāṇāyāma);
by twelve withdrawals, concentration (dhāraṇā) is proclaimed."
For the sake of union with Īśvara, there should be meditation consisting of twelve dhāraṇās;
by means of these twelve meditations alone, samādhi is designated.
"Beyond the state of samādhi is the infinite light, self-luminous;
when that is seen, the ritualistic section [of scripture] and the cycle of coming and going cease.
Likewise, in that very same work, the measure of dhāraṇā and so forth is stated:
"Dhāraṇā lasts for five nāḍīs, and dhyāna lasts for six;
through the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama), samādhi shall arise after twelve days.
Thus [it is said]. Vasiṣṭha states the measure of a ghaṭikā:
"Sixty breaths (śvāsa) constitute one prāṇa; six prāṇas constitute one ghaṭikā;

five ghaṭikās constitute one zodiacal sign (rāśi); and twelve signs constitute a day. Thus, since one-twelfth of a sign is two and a half prāṇas, twelve and a half breaths—that is, the air held for that duration—constitutes the first prāṇāyāma. The intermediate [prāṇāyāma] ends with twenty-four breaths, and the superior ends with thirty-six breaths; this is the established conclusion (rāddhānta). As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"A single breath constitutes a *mātrā* in *prāṇāyāma*.
This means that for a person who has fallen under the influence of sleep, the duration of time it takes for a single inhalation and exhalation to occur is called a *mātrā* of *prāṇāyāma*.
The definition of *mātrā* will be explained in detail later on. Furthermore, the vibration of the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is also one and the same.
In the Vāsiṣṭha: "That which is the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the vibration of the mind (citta).
Therefore, the wise person should exert great effort to conquer the vibration of the vital breath. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, it is well known in all the Yoga scriptures that samādhi consists precisely of the dissolution of both [the mind and its objects].
As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa (P.30):
"When the vital breath is completely exhausted and the mind dissolves,
that state of equanimity which arises is here called samādhi. For this very reason, it is the word of Śiva that knowledge and liberation occur only when both have perished.
"O Goddess, as long as the vital breath lives, how can knowledge arise in the mind?
As long as the mind does not die, the vital breath also lives.
He who brings these two—the vital breath and the mind—to dissolution [attains liberation]."
"That man attains liberation, and no other in any way. In the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"Likewise, for those whose vital breaths have dissolved through the intense practice of a single reality,"

"And the restraint of the mind—this is the summary of the meaning of the word 'liberation'. Now, for this disease of transmigratory existence, which causes all manner of afflictions, there is only one remedy: the restraint of one's own mind.
"The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra, joined with desire, anger, and the rest"—thus the passage continues in full. In the Vāsiṣṭha:
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings."

"Attached to sense-objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense-objects, it is held to lead to liberation," and so forth. Since other scriptures also declare that transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is rooted in the mind, and since they likewise declare that both the knowledge of reality and liberation are dependent upon the conquest of the mind, one might ask: "Since the human goal consisting of liberation—which involves the uprooting of the entire universe along with its playful manifestations and which is the cause of all evils—is possible through the restraint of the mind alone, what is the use of the conquest of the vital breath (prāṇa), which is difficult to achieve and causes the suffering of many diseases and ailments? If this is argued, we say no; for without the conquest of the vital breath, the conquest of the mind is impossible.
Thus, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
When the wind moves, the mind moves; likewise, when it is still, the mind is still. The yogi attains the state of a pillar; therefore, he should restrain the vital air.
Just as a drop of water does not remain still for even a single moment when struck by the wind, so too is the mind; therefore, one should not place trust in it.
Therefore, one should restrain the breath for the sake of stability of the mind;
for the purpose of restraining the breath, one should practice the six-limbed yoga.
As long as the breath remains within the body, the mind is free from affliction;
as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, whence can there be fear of death?
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Thus has it been told to you, O King! Now understand from me this Yoga as well:
having attained it, a Brahmin becomes a yogi and shall not go to any other state than the eternal."
When the self is difficult to conquer, the yogi should first conquer the self by means of the self;
he should exert effort toward that conquest—listen to me regarding its method.
Just as the impurities within mountain ores are consumed when they are smelted,
so too are the defects produced by the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath.
"One should burn away the defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sins by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). Thus it is said in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
When the wheel of the channels has been purified by various breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas),
let the vital air enter easily, piercing the opening of the Suṣumṇā.
"When the vital breath moves through the middle channel, stability of the mind arises;
that state of being which is the mind's perfect steadiness is itself the state of *manonmanī*. (P.
In the Vāsiṣṭha:
"Yogins practice the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇa) for the sake of purifying the mind,
through breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma), meditations, and applications devised by skillful means."
The wise know that breath-restraint (prāṇasaṃrodhana) bestows the fruit of tranquility, is the supreme cause of peace, brings auspiciousness, and is the well-being of consciousness.
There are two seeds for the tree of mental fluctuations for one who observes the vow of worldly activity:
one is the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), and the second is firm latent impression (vāsanā).
The mind is adorned with the limbs of the movement of the vital breath as its cosmetic ointment.
When that [mind] is restrained, the mind will surely become tranquil;
through the cessation of the mind's vibration, this cycle of worldly existence dissolves.
Just as worldly activity ceases when the movement of sunlight has subsided, so too,
through practice, when the movement of the vital breaths has come to an end.
"The mind attains tranquility, and Nirvana remains as the only residue. In another treatise:
"The dull-witted person who would seek to accomplish Yoga without breath-control (prāṇāyāma)..."
"He does not attain the state of the perfected ones, just as a lame man cannot attain the gait of a horse."
In the *Yogabīja*: "The mind is bound by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that [breath] resides within living beings;
just as a bull is tied with a rope, so too is this mind."
The mind cannot be mastered through various kinds of mental deliberations;
therefore, the means for its conquest is indeed the conquest of the vital breath (prāṇa).
O beloved! Without the perfected means, the vital breath cannot be brought under control by means of logic, disputations, networks of scriptures, reasonings, mantras, or medicinal herbs.
Having disregarded the means, one proceeds upon the path of sacrifice.
By that very fragmented cognition, a person becomes a partaker of afflictions.
The practitioner of yoga who, out of delusion, desires to achieve yoga by merely restraining the breath is like one who wishes to cross the ocean while mounted upon an unbaked clay pot.
If one's vital breaths have dissolved while the practitioner is still alive and his body has not yet fallen,
his mind is liberated from defects.
When the mind is purified, the knowledge of one's own true self shines forth.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, through yoga, knowledge may arise in a single lifetime;
for this reason, the practitioner should always practice yoga until its completion.
"Those desiring liberation must practice the conquest of the vital breaths for the sake of liberation."
And the *Patañjali-sūtra* states:

"Or, by means of exhalation and retention, [there is] of the vital breath"—the meaning is that there would be the cessation of the mind (*cittanirodha*). Thus, only when there is mastery over the mind does mastery over the vital breath (*prāṇajaya*) occur, because the two depend upon each other in their respective functions.
Likewise, in the *Viśiṣṭa*:
It is eternally inseparable from the life-force and consciousness of living beings,
existing like the fragrance inherent in a flower or oil within a sesame seed.
"Like the container and the contained, these two perish if even one is absent;
yet, through their non-destruction, they accomplish the supreme task known as liberation. — Thus, in the *Rājayoga*.
The mind and the vital breath are always merged like milk and water, performing identical functions;
as far as the activity of the mind extends, so far extends the activity of the breath, and as far as the activity of the breath extends, so far extends the activity of the mind.
In that regard, from the destruction of one follows the destruction of the other; from the activity of one follows the activity of the other.
"In the two [periods] that are not destroyed, there is an increase by zero and the group of faculties; in the two that are destroyed, there is the attainment of the state of a seer."
In that regard as well, the destruction of the vital breath (pavana) is to be accomplished by practicing the six-limbed yoga and other such methods;
however, the dissolution of the mind is achieved through the grace of the Guru.
It is indeed easily accomplished in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Just as stability of mind arises through constant practice,
so too does stability of breath, speech, body, and vision arise.
Therefore, one should strive in the method for the dissolution of the mind,
by which even the fierce wind is destroyed within a month;
therefore, through the dissolution of one's own body, senses, and intellect—
"The non-dual consciousness remains innate and established," says Sureśvarācārya:
"When the mind attains stillness, the vital breath becomes still."
"One should practice the eightfold yoga for the sake of the immovability of the mind. Thus it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"From the steadiness of the mind, the breath becomes steady; from that, the seminal essence (*bindu*) becomes steady."
"Just as from the stability of the *bindu* (the seminal point), the stability of the *piṇḍa* (the physical body) arises through effort."
In the *Amṛtasiddhi*:
"Death occurs through the falling of the *bindu*; life comes from the retention of the *bindu*.
When the *bindu* is perfected as the great essence (*mahārasa*), all accomplishments (*siddhi*) arise."
The Bindu is Brahmā, the Bindu is Viṣṇu, and the Bindu is the Lord Sadāśiva;
the Bindu is the all-pervading God, the Bindu is the mirror of the three worlds.
The Bindu is the all-pervading God, the form of existence, and the stainless one.
And this dwells in the form of a drop within all living beings.

The seed with its drop (bindu) is known to be of two kinds: that which originates from the male and that which originates from the female. The seed is declared to be of the male, while the menstrual flow (rajas) is of the female origin.
Through the external application of these two, the creation of men arises;
when the yoga is internal, then one is called a yogin.
The *bindu* is said to consist of the sun, and the *rajas* likewise consists of the moon;
from the union of these two alone, the supreme state is born.
The drop (bindu) bestows heaven, bestows liberation, and likewise bestows dharma and adharma;
within it, all the deities abide in a subtle form.
This is the reality, this is the seed; this is said to be the essence of all.
By means of the vital breath (vāyu), the drop (bindu) falls, and there is no other means for the realization of the drop.
The wind reaches whatever state the bindu attains;
for just as the wind is mastered, so too is the purification of the bindu accomplished.
When swooning, it removes disease; when bound, it leads to the power of moving through the sky (khecaratā);
when absorbed, it grants all siddhis; and when motionless, it bestows liberation.
In whatever state the drop (bindu) may be, such is the state of the mind;
when this vital air (vāyu) moves, then the drop is said to be moving.
In whose body the *bindu* moves, his mind is likewise unsteady;
when the *bindu*, the mind, and the vital air are all constantly in motion.
The world is born and dies; this word is the truth, this is the truth.
That which is indeed the sound (nāda) along with all its drops (bindu) is proclaimed as the mind (citta).
Nāda, bindu, and citta— the practice of the unification of these three,
though they are situated separately in the external body, [is the means to liberation].
Nevertheless, once the wind has been established, all [other elements] are certainly established by everyone.
When the wind is restrained through the middle yoga, it dies away in the middle channel.
Then the drop (bindu) and the mind (citta) die together with the vital air (vāyu);
all the principles (tattvas) of the drop likewise reside within the body.
"They move within the movement of the vital air (vāyu), and they die from the destruction of that air.
In the Vāsiṣṭha, Śrī Rāma said:
"Of those that move incessantly within the body, like those dwelling in a cave within a house..."
"How is the movement of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the other winds restrained?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, dispassion, practice, and yoga..."
When one has formed a firm resolve toward detachment from the activities of former saṃsāric existence.
From meditating upon that which is desired as being one with oneself for a long time,
and through the practice of the density of the single reality, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained.
Through firm practice of breath-restraint such as inhalation (pūraka) and the rest, performed without fatigue,
and through union with solitary meditation, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is suppressed.
Through the experience of the reality of sound as it is woven into the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*,
and through meditation with a mind free of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained.
At the tip of the nose, twelve finger-breadths away in the stainless sky,
as the two eyes become tranquil, the movement of the breath is restrained.
Through firm practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the Guru,
and through the application of posture and diet, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained.
Through practice, these methods of yoga become free from obstacles and serve as the means for a fortunate person to shatter the cycle of existence.
Having attained firmness through practice and being adorned with dispassion, [the mind becomes one-pointed].
The movement of the vital breaths (prāṇas) according to their latent impressions (vāsanā) is considered fruitful.

"From which words, accompanied by conceptual constructions and mental fabrications, turn back; that state remains for a person once conceptual construction has been completely destroyed. Thus it is said. Although there are other means for the conquest of the vital breaths (prāṇa), they are not written here for fear of prolixity.
Therefore, Haṭhayoga and Rājayoga must both be practiced with great diligence.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Without Haṭha there is no Rājayoga, and without Rājayoga there is no Haṭha;
therefore, this pair does not succeed, so one should practice them both."
"Those who practice Rājayoga without Haṭha, or Haṭha without Rājayoga,
I consider them to be devoid of the fruit of their efforts.
Thus it is said in the Viśiṣṭa as well.
As long as the ego-sense has not dissolved, so long is there no destruction of latent impressions;
and as long as the latent impressions are not destroyed, so long does the mind not become stilled.
As long as there is no realization of reality through the method, there is no destruction of the mind;
and as long as there is no pacification of the mind, there is no knowledge of reality.
As long as there is no attainment of reality, so long is there no destruction of latent impressions.
Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—
having become mutual causes for one another, these remain difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, O Rāghava! with diligence, through human effort and discernment, having cast far away attachment to enjoyments, one should take refuge in these three.
As long as these three have not been thoroughly practiced again and again,
the attainment of reality will not occur, even in hundreds of aeons.
O Mahāmati! There is the exhaustion of speech, the imperishability of consciousness, and the destruction of the mind.

O noble one! When these [mantras] are practiced simultaneously and equally, they yield their fruit for the practitioner. However, even if each one is practiced individually for a long time, those mantras do not bestow accomplishment merely by being recited.
By these three, long-established and firmly knotted in the heart,
they rise up without hesitation, like the fibers of a lotus stalk.
The persistence of the cycle of worldly existence, practiced through hundreds of previous births,
is never extinguished anywhere except through yoga practiced for a long time.
The complete abandonment of latent impressions and the simultaneous restraint of the vital breaths—this is the bindu;
therefore, one who knows that should practice it, free from those [obstacles].
Through the complete abandonment of latent impressions, the mind attains the state of non-mind;
through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, it becomes tranquil—do as you wish.
Because one acts without attachment, because one has abandoned the contemplation of worldly existence,
and because one perceives the destruction of the body, latent impressions do not arise.
When latent impressions have perished in the absence of objective existence, the mind no longer functions.
"O Rāma, there are two seeds of the mind: the vibration of the vital breath and mental impressions. When one of these two is destroyed, both are quickly destroyed. Thus [it is said].

Now follows the exposition of the means to yoga (*yogopāya*). Among these, some have already been mentioned previously in connection with other topics. Here, however, is the sequence of the means: first, through the comprehension of reality (*tattva*) attained via scripture (*āgama*), inference (*anumāna*), and the instruction of a teacher (*ācāryopadeśa*), there arises a withdrawal of the mind from its objects, which engenders faith (*śraddhā*) in yoga as the means to that [realization]. Immediately thereafter—

P.39 Enthusiasm; for one who possesses enthusiasm, there is mindfulness regarding the subsequent stages. Through that mindfulness, the mind becomes favorable and, being established in the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth, it comes to possess the meditative absorption (samādhi) which is a limb of yoga. Then, for one endowed with all the limbs of yoga, through the excellence of wisdom (prajñā), there arises cognitive absorption (samprajñāta-samādhi). From the practice of that and from its object, supreme dispassion (paravairāgya) arises, which is non-cognitive absorption (asamprajñāta-samādhi).

And that cause of isolation (*kaivalya*) is indeed cessation (*nirodha*) preceded by the discriminative discernment (*anyathākhyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa; for the mind, having accomplished its entire purpose through the performance of all its functions, is withdrawn from its office. In this regard, the yogi must first purify the mind through friendliness (*maitrī*) and the other [virtues], because a mind possessed of envy and the like cannot be conquered. Thus it is said in the *Gītā*:
"Yoga is difficult to attain by one whose self is uncontrolled;
but by one whose self is controlled and who strives, it can be attained through the proper means."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:

"As long as there is even a trace of effort, as long as there is the conceptualization of mental constructs, and as long as there is no attainment by the mind—what talk can there be of reality? Thus it is said.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"As long as the movement of the vital breath does not enter the central path,
and as long as the bindu is not firmly bound by the vital wind..."
"As long as that reality which is co-emergent with the sky is not known,
everything that is said is merely a deceptive and false prattle. Thus it is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi*.
As long as this lord of mercury,
whose nature is Brahman, remains within the body, that man is considered bound, unliberated, and subject to worldly existence.
One should know that body to be unaccomplished, belonging to those who do not lead the holy life;
it is mired in old age and death, and is the locus of all afflictions.
In the same way: "As long as the breath has not become motionless, having left the side paths and entered the center..."
One should know that to be unestablished which is accompanied by the qualities of wind and action.
"As long as the mind flickers toward internal and external objects,
one should know that the mind has not attained perfection, for it remains subject to the power of karma."
And thus says the *Patañjali Sūtra*:

"The clarification of the mind arises from the cultivation of friendliness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward those who possess happiness, suffering, virtue, and vice. Here, the words "happiness" and so forth refer to those [states] which defile a person with attachment and aversion. When one sees a happy person, envy arises; toward a virtuous person, hatred; toward a suffering person, indifference; and toward a sinful person, approval. But the yogi, by cultivating friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, joy toward the virtuous, and equanimity toward the sinful, uproots both attachment and aversion, which are the root of all affliction.

Thereupon the mind becomes serene; for one whose mind is serene, yoga is easily attained. It has been stated that the mind also becomes steady through meditation on whatever is desired, by means of the aphorism: "Or [by meditation] on whatever is desired. Furthermore, it is not unestablished that: "The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist."
When that is destroyed, the world is destroyed; therefore, it must be treated with great effort.

O son! Grinding hand against hand, crushing teeth against teeth, and pressing limb against limb, one should first conquer one's own mind; for, O son, one must always conquer all sense-objects in that very manner.
