Indeed, this lack of attachment is the supreme means for the conquest of the mind;
this alone is the highest method,
for by it the intoxicated elephant of one's own mind is swiftly brought under control and freed from its madness.
Of the wealth accumulated, two parts should be used for enjoyment, and one part should be filled with weapons.
For one who is unlearned, service to the guru is the portion that is honored.
One should satisfy with enjoyments the portion of one who is proficient in the sacred sciences,
and the portion of one who is unlearned, being honored, with service to the teacher.
For one who is engaged in productive work, he should fill one part with enjoyments;
two parts with service to the teacher; and one part with reflection on the meaning of the scriptures.
One who has attained proficiency should daily fulfill the mind's two parts with scriptural study and detachment,
and its other two parts with meditation and worship of the Guru.
O son, though the mind is always as if restrained by the power of wisdom and discernment, it cannot be conquered without blameless method.
Just as a rutting, wicked elephant cannot be controlled without a goad,
so too [the mind cannot be tamed] without the acquisition of the science of the self (adhyātmavidyā) and association with the virtuous.
The complete abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the simultaneous restraint of the vital breaths—
these, indeed, are the most excellent methods for the conquest of the vital breaths.
Those who, despite these existing methods, forcibly restrain their minds,
are like those who discard a lamp and seek to destroy darkness with the help of blind men—
fools who attempt to achieve victory over the mind through force.
"Therefore, they bind the lord of serpents with threads of venom that have been cast off."
Now, the method of yoga for following the path that is easy to traverse is described.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"The mind is the master of the senses, and the vital air (māruta) is the master of the mind."
O Lord, the dissolution of the vital breath (māruta) is that dissolution which is based upon sound (nāda).

O Sky of Thought! Let this alone be what is called liberation; for there is no distinction whatsoever between the dissolution of the mind, the dissolution of the vital breath, the resonance (nāda), or anything else.
This sound, acting as a sharp goad, is capable of restraining the mind, which is like a lordly elephant roaming through the garden of the sense-objects.
Just as a female bee drinking the nectar does not heed the fragrance, so too—
Likewise, the mind that is not attached to sound does not indeed long for sense objects.
Fire kindled in wood is extinguished along with the vessel;
the mind kindled by the *nāda* dissolves along with the *nāda*.
Having forgotten all that is external, like milk and water mixed in a sound,
the person then suddenly becomes one and dissolves into the space of consciousness.
The illustrious Ādinātha has taught seventy million methods of absorption (*laya*);
we consider that the practice of following the resonance (*nādānusandhāna*) alone is the task, and none other among the absorptions.
Having transcended indifference through constant practice, the self-controlled one [attains the goal].
"One should immediately focus on the resonance (*nāda*) for the purpose of attaining the state beyond mind (*unmanīkaraṇa*).
What kind of indifference is this?—
"Whether it be a coarse woolen blanket or a fine cotton cloth in the cold season..."
For wholesome food, cow’s milk or [human] breast-milk;
for edible items, alms or forest-grown produce; for a drinking vessel, a wooden trough or another person’s water-cup.
For the swift attainment of the state beyond mind (unmanī), two methods are approved by me:
either the practice of the supreme reality or bliss, or the worship of the inner sound (nāda).
For those whose minds have entered into subtlety, even for the dull-witted,
the victory born of *nāda* arises quickly, bestowing a continuous flow of bliss.
Seated in the Muktāsana posture, the yogi, maintaining the Śāmbhavī Mudrā,
should constantly listen to the internal sound within his right ear.
Having abandoned all thought with an attentive mind,
one who desires the sovereignty of yoga should pursue the sound alone.
Covering his ears with his hands, the sage should listen to the internal sound;
he should make the mind steady until it attains the state of stability.
This sound, when practiced, causes the external resonance to revolve;
thereafter, having conquered all distraction, the yogi becomes happy.
It is heard that during the initial practice, various kinds of great sounds arise;
as the practice continues, however, sounds increasingly subtle are heard.
At the beginning there is the loud and tumultuous sound of clouds, thunder, and kettledrums;
in the middle, there is the sound of mṛdaṅga drums, conchs, bells, and kāhala trumpets.
Others, however, have the sounds of clusters of small bells, lutes, and bees;
thus various kinds of sounds are heard arising from within the body.
Even when great noises such as those of clouds or kettledrums are being heard, [these internal sounds continue].
Then one should perceive the sound itself, which is subtler than the subtle.
Having abandoned the gross for the subtle, or having abandoned the subtle for the gross,
one should fix the mind right there upon the Supreme and not cause it to wander elsewhere.
Wherever the mind first enters into a sound, one should make it very steady right there; by that means, it dissolves together with it.
Sound is the seed, Haṭha is the field, and equanimity is known as the water;
the wish-fulfilling creeper of the Transmental state will come into being immediately.
In the *Rājayoga*:
"Wherever the vision is, there is the dissolution of the elements and the senses;
the power of all beings becomes united with the vision through the target."
With the gaze directed upward, the piercing is downward; with the face turned downward, the piercing is upward.
Having established [the mind] here according to this rule, one shall become liberated while living.
With his vision expanded in every direction and then gradually withdrawn,
he beholds the supreme reality, which is beyond the reach of the eye, by means of the self through the self.
The first view that has emerged adheres to whatever it encounters;
having become fixed right there, it perishes gradually.
By forcibly suppressing the supreme conceptualization, those who remain constantly vigilant during its destruction find that their vision,
diminishing through the disappearance of its objective support, gradually attains peace.
The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are like common courtesans;
the Śāmbhavī Mudrā alone is like a protected woman of noble family.
With the inner object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from blinking or opening of the eyes—this is it.
"But this Śāmbhavī mudrā is concealed in all the scriptures."
In the Haṭhapradīpikā:
"When the yogi dwells in the forest of austerity with his mind dissolved in the internal object,
though he looks outward with a gaze of motionless pupils, he does not see."
O Guru, by your grace, this indeed becomes the Śāmbhavī Mudrā;
that reality which is the state of Śambhu, free from both void and non-void, vibrates forth,
having taken root in the hearts of the lords of yogis who possess the samādhi of continuous contemplation upon the Nāda.
Only one who has bowed at the feet of the Guru knows that single bliss which is beyond the reach of words;
with eyes half-open, mind steady, and gaze fixed on the tip of the nose,
he may bring even the sun and moon to dissolution within the state of utter motionlessness.
What more need be said? That supreme reality, which is of the nature of light, devoid of all external things, and intensely radiant, attains that highest state, the ultimate object beyond words.
Having joined the Śrī-Śāmbhavī, Khecarī, and Śrava-sthāñcala through their distinctions,
one should unite them with the Tārā and the Light, and slightly raise the eyebrows.
This is the path of the former yoga, which brings about the state of *unmanī* in an instant;
some [seek it] through a web of scriptures, while others are burdened by a multitude of restrictive observances.
Some are deluded by logic and do not know the Savior at all.
Regarding the fourfold states of yoga, various distinctions are heard; and these states will now be described.
The Brahma-knot becomes pierced, giving rise to bliss and emptiness;
the body becomes variegated and momentary, and the unstruck sound (anāhata) is heard.
When the Viṣṇugranthi is pierced, which indicates supreme bliss,
and there is the penetration of the Great Void (atiśūnya), then the sound of the kettledrum (bherī-śabda) arises.
Then, on the third [day], having pierced through, the auspicious sound of Vimala proceeds to the Great Void (mahāśūnya),
which is the refuge of all accomplishments.
Then, having pierced the bliss of consciousness, there arises the innate bliss;
then, having pierced the Rudra-knot, the vital breath reaches all the seats.
Just as the sound of one who is spitting becomes like the resonance of a lute,
so too does the mind become unified, signifying royal yoga (rājayoga).
Sureśvarācārya says: "When the breath enters the Suṣumnā at its seven tips, it is heard as eightfold,
like the sounds of a bell, a drum, a conch, a lute, a flute, and so forth."
O Tanūnapāt, O Savior, O Lord of the Star, you who are like the sun:
when the vital breath has entered the channel of Brahman, what form indeed would it illuminate?

In the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*, the procedure for the arising of the *nāda*: Now, with the heel pressed against the *kambu* [the base of the throat]... having placed the heel of the left foot at the root of the banner of *nāda*, with the body and neck held straight, the self-restrained one should withdraw the senses from their objects.
Having repeatedly filled the ocean with winds drawn in by the beak of a female crow,

one who possesses steady and pure intelligence should block the opening of the *nararipu* (the perineum) with both thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, and the nostrils with the two middle fingers as they fit.
One should not fix one's own mind too intensely upon other abodes than the lotus-born Brahmā.
By performing this every single day according to one's capacity, even as it is broken [by obstacles],
this vital breath of the body gradually enters within the Suṣumnā.
Then the sound born of effort becomes the producer of innate resonance;
gradually, in the playing of the lute, it becomes equal to the sound of a well-struck, sweet-toned vīṇā.
At first, it was like the sound of a hall of intoxicated bees, a tumultuous mass of "Hūṃ" cries;
then that roar became equal to the resonance of a flute-player’s bamboo pipe shimmering with a full breath of wind;
and following that, it resembled the ringing of bells, deep and profound like the thundering of the ocean.
In this hollow of the Brahma-nāḍī, there exists a city with the thundering roar of a rumbling rain-cloud.
The wind that arises naturally from his life-force becomes completely conquered by him;
for that one of immeasurable merit, who is the abode of great qualities, the powers such as *aṇimā* come to be.
Having blocked the opening of the enemy of the son of the king of gods with two of his own fingers,
the mortal suddenly hears a sound spreading forth from there like the deep roar of the ocean.
Even for one who merely contemplates this sound— the progeny of the enemy of the Lord of the Thirty-three—
there arises here a constant attainment of virtues, as that person becomes free from all impurity.
The wise one, having properly restrained the tips [of the bow] with his fingers,
and having restrained Rudra, the vital breath (marut), the excellent bull, and the sixth sense within the two bows,
beholds at that very moment the Supreme, which is sung within the subtle flow.
"Endowed with the light of Tripurā, marked by the digit [of the moon], and possessing a splendor that is both manifest and unmanifest.
Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Such, O fair-faced one, is the means for conquering the wind, namely the vital breath (prāṇa)."
Likewise, it is possible for one who, having taken his seat, possesses a concentrated mind.
Having brought the organs under control by force from their objects, the wise man,
being composed, draws the *apāna* upward with the syllable *praṇava*.
One should properly bind the sensory organs, beginning with the ears, using the two hands:
both ears with the two thumbs and the two eyes with the two index fingers.
Having covered the two nostrils as well as the navel with the hands,
one should maintain the concentration upon the head for as long as the experience of bliss lasts.
By this very [path], the vital breath departs;
therefore, it is the destroyer of life, passing through the Brahma-randhra in the Suṣumṇā like a thread within the interior of a lotus stalk.

The arising of the sound (nāda), however, is by means of this very [channel] alone; it is pure, resembling a crystal, and the sound proceeds from the crown of the head, established like the resonance of a lute.
At first it resembles the sound of a conch shell; in the middle, it is like the roar of clouds;
and when the resonance has reached the path of the sky, it is like a mountain torrent.

"When the vital air has entered the aperture of space (the *brahmarandhra*), and the mind is established in the Self, the practitioner becomes eternally blissful; by him, the vital air has been conquered. Thus it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
One should perform the closing of the pair of ears, the eyes, and the nostrils;
then, within the path of the illustrious, pure Suṣumnā, the stainless sound is clearly heard.
Through the discourse on wood and the hollow, listen to the internal sound;
this is the speech formerly uttered by Ādinātha for the awakening of Matsyendra.
The mind attains maturation through the practice known as "the unsupported" (nirālamba);
therefore, the yogin must constantly attend to the resonance of the inner sound (nāda).
Upon hearing the *nāda*, the mind— the inner horse—
becomes entirely one-pointed in the state of voidness and no longer runs away anywhere.
The inner sound acts as a tether for the deer of the internal mind,
and it even merges into the binding of that internal steed.
For one who is intent on the resonance of the bell and the production of sound,
there is the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*); and of that sound, there is the vibration (*dhvani*).
The light is contained within sound, and the mind is contained within the light;
when that mind reaches dissolution, that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
One should contemplate up to the point where the wood is reached as long as sound persists;
that which is beyond sound is the supreme Brahman, which is proclaimed as the Supreme Self.
Whatever is heard as name and form is indeed power;
he who hears it is formless—he alone is the Supreme Lord.
"Tens of millions of *nādas* and hundreds of millions of *bindus*—
all of them dissolve there where the stainless God resides. Thus it is said regarding *rājayoga*.
"When the mind moves, saṃsāra arises; when it is unmoving, dissolution occurs.
Therefore, one who is devoted to equanimity should make the mind steady."
When one becomes indifferent [to all objects], then reality shines forth;
when reality has been self-revealed, one's own bliss arises at that very moment.
Satisfied by bliss, one should always be intent upon practice;
for one who is constantly devoted to practice, there is neither rule nor sequence.
The yogi should not think of anything, for he should be intent on equanimity;
by the cessation of all thought, reality itself is revealed to him.
When reality is self-revealed, one becomes absorbed in it through its defining characteristic:
that all this which is visible—the mind and everything moving and unmoving—is nothing but that.
The state of the mind's becoming unmanī (unstruck) is declared to be the absence of duality;
it arises for one who is without mental activity, remaining indifferent and composed.
Both the state of being lowly and the state of being superior arise even for the body;
when the mindless axe has been applied, they are uprooted from their very foundation.
But when the thorn of the internal organ has been extracted, the sage becomes truly happy;
[he is one] who, though still possessed of the cords of breath and crowded with the abodes of the senses, [is liberated].
Having torn asunder the net of the mind, one becomes happy like a fish [escaping from a net];
with the group of senses fully stilled, such a person is endowed with the power of wisdom.
Having conquered the enemy that is the mind through the discipline of weaving, one shall become happy;
for the rope composed of the three qualities is very firm in binding the self to the Self.
Having cast [all things] away with the very razor of mindlessness, one shall attain liberation;
just as everything dissolves and goes to its setting when the sun has departed.
In that same way, the entire universe, along with its web of karma, dissolves into the state of mindlessness—
the stainless nectar that is free from the grasp of the senses and devoid of agitation.
One who has bathed in the lake of the mindless attains the supreme nectar.
With his inhalation and exhalation ceased, his perception of sensory objects was utterly destroyed.
Devoid of activity and free from all undertakings, it indeed brings joy to the yogi;
with all mental constructs destroyed and every impulse departed.

May that certain dissolution, which is self-realized and beyond the reach of words— just as the single staff, the triple staff, and so forth, or likewise the smearing with ashes and such— be victorious.
The plucking out of hair, the state of nakedness,
and the wearing of red garments [are practiced] by one who has awakened to his own true nature and remains forever indifferent.
For one who is constantly devoted to practice, this [text] is of no use anywhere;
at that time, through the excellence of vision, various postures [are mastered].
And because of the state of the internal organ, the yogi is not affected [by external objects];
he who remains as if asleep even while constantly in the waking state.
Devoid of inhalation and exhalation, he is certainly liberated.
That state which arises at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking— [that is liberation].
Cultivating that state, the yogi is certainly liberated indeed.
Just as someone who has risen from sleep perceives sense objects,
so too does the yogi remain awake because of the exhaustion of the sleep of yoga.
By the yogi who increases through the surging flood of the nectar of glorious detachment,
the tree of the world will fall, its roots in the mind having been uprooted.
When and where the mind becomes steady, and from whatever cause it arises,
then one should not deliberate further as to where the mind goes;
for when the mind is unrestrained by external objects, it dissolves of its own accord.
Though restrained with great effort, it cannot be prevented from acting;
by the power of the wind, this [body] rises up in an instant.
The mind is indeed difficult to restrain as long as one has not realized the ultimate reality; but once the supreme reality is known, the mind becomes like a crow perched upon a pillar.
Just as a skilled weigher makes a swaying scale steady,
so too, through constant practice, does the movement of the mind become steady within the Self when happiness arises.

Just as when gold is cast [into fire], whatever impurity it leaves behind becomes pure, so too, when the state of *amanaska* has arisen, that very reality is certainly the stainless, innate nature. Therefore, having abandoned all sense objects through the yoga of the partless inner self (*adhyātma-yoga*), [one attains that state].
The destruction of the wind, and with it the destruction of the mind following its [the wind's] dissolution, is liberation.
This is the innate, stainless, partless, and changeless Being-Consciousness;
O skillful ones, strive for its attainment by first practicing the state beyond the mind (amanaska).
The wise person should understand that there are four states of the mind.
And it is distinguished by its coming and going, well-knit and well-restrained.

That which is disjointed is said to be tāmasa; that which involves coming and going is rājasa. That which is well-connected is said to be sāttvika, while that which is perfectly absorbed is devoid of the guṇas.
That which is disjoined and characterized by coming and going grasps the objects of conceptual construction;
that which is well-integrated and firmly settled removes the objects of conceptual construction.
Then, through the application of practice, if it becomes supportless,
at that time it has become one with the flavor of equanimity (samarasībhūta) and is indeed supreme bliss itself.
The mind that is motionless due to bliss is therefore called "well-joined" (suśliṣṭa);
when it has become exceedingly motionless and full of bliss, it is called "well-absorbed" (sulīna).
For one who practices with the mind as the precursor, the state is called "dissociated and moving.
Thence follows the state that is "slightly moving and unmoving," accompanied by joy and characterized by coming and going.
"Thus, for one who has become such, meritorious deeds and even those performed with doubt do not cling to him while they are being done by the virtuous.

By thus describing the nature of one who has ascended to yoga, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva declares that for that very person, the manifestation of the bliss of Brahman occurs during the stage of practice through meditative absorption (samādhi).

For instance: beginning with "When one is free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be disciplined," it continues: "The self united in yoga perceives the same everywhere, possessing equal vision."
By this, and also by the Śruti:
"The bliss that arises when the mind, its impurities shaken off by samādhi, is established in the Self..."
"At that time, it cannot be described by speech;
rather, it is apprehended by one's own inner organ (antahkarana) itself.
The venerable Vidyāraṇya says:
"To the extent that the ego is forgotten through the yoga of practice,
to that same extent is one's own bliss inferred by the subtle vision."
Although this meditative absorption is difficult for humans to attain over a long period of time,
nevertheless, it is non-momentary and leads one to the certainty of the bliss of Brahman.
In the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra] as well,

four states of the mind (citta) are described according to the differentiation of the guṇas: outward distraction (vyutthāna), the commencement of samādhi, one-pointedness (ekāgratā), and cessation (nirodha).

This, however, is the process therein: because it is an effect of *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*, the mind (*citta*) is also composed of the three *guṇas*. *Prakṛti* has already been described previously during the exposition of the principles (*tattva*); as for the *guṇas*, they are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Among these, *sattva* is characterized by the qualities of clarity and illumination; *rajas* is characterized by the qualities of activity, feverishness, sorrow, and so forth; while *tamas* is characterized by the quality of inertia known as resistance to activity, and is further characterized by the qualities of heaviness, obscuration, dejection, and so on.

And thus, because the mind possesses these three qualities (*guṇa*), and because of the various transformations of those three qualities—which consist of mutual suppression and subduing—there arise five states designated by the term "stages" (*bhūmi*): the distracted (*kṣipta*), the deluded (*mūḍha*), the occasionally distracted (*vikṣipta*), the one-pointed (*ekāgra*), and the restrained (*nirodha*). Among these, the *kṣipta* (distracted) is that which is impelled toward objects such as pleasure and the like by *rajas*, and is therefore extremely unstable. The *mūḍha* (deluded) is that which is possessed of the state of sleep through *tamas*, as well as intoxication, fainting, and so forth; it is devoid of discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done due to anger and other passions, and is intent upon harming others. The *vikṣipta* (occasionally distracted) is distinguished from the *kṣipta*.

And its specific characteristic is this: it is predominantly unstable, though stability occurs occasionally; for even though there is an increase of *sattva* here, it is nonetheless slightly deficient in *sattva* because it is touched by *rajas* and *tamas*. Regarding sovereignty and the objects of sense such as sound and so forth, it feels affection. And due to the predominance of *sattva*, although it desires to be intent upon reality (*tattva*), because reality is obscured by *tamas*, it considers only the powers such as *aṇimā* to be sovereignty and becomes intent upon them.

The wise person applies their mind for a moment. Then, when [the mind] is being tossed by a particle of *rajas*, it finds no stability and remains merely in a state of movement. Regarding sound and the other objects, there is an established state of attachment due to their natural flow. When [the mind] is tossed, because occasional concentration (*samādhi*) is subordinate to distraction (*vikṣepa*), it is of no use for yoga. Even though there is a cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-nirodha*) here, because it lacks the quality of being a means to liberation even indirectly, it is to be abandoned. All three of these stages are indeed to be abandoned.

When one-pointedness has been suppressed, due to the excellence of the stage and the being, there is a sequential cessation of outward activity through the dissolution of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); thus, these two are to be cultivated as they are conducive to meditative absorption (*samādhi*). In that state, one-pointedness is a continuous flow; for here the mind, having become manifest as consisting of *sattva* and having its veil of darkness (*tamas*) removed, yet still being touched by a trace of *rajas*, becomes possessed of righteousness, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.

Just as for the medium-level yogi who has attained concentration with discernment (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) on the stage of "honeyed" wisdom (*madhumatī*), the mental essence (*citta-sattva*) has its fluctuations ceased and consists of the awareness of mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); so too, for the yogi who has transcended what is to be cultivated, the mental essence—its stains of even the slightest passion having departed—is established in its own nature, being like refined gold (*tapanīya*) purified by the continuous process of smelting through practice and dispassion, once the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas* have been shaken off.

For one who has withdrawn the senses from their objects, because his remaining duties have been completed, there remains only the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) as the final object of action.

Here, the term "object of cultivation" (*bhāvanīyapada*) refers to that reality which is distinct from the self; thus, through one-pointedness, there is the cessation of external mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*). And when all fluctuations, along with their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), have been restrained, there occurs their dissolution. It is within these two stages that the possibility of yoga exists.

In that regard, the stage of emergence belongs to the distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-bhūmi*), which arises from the *kṣipta* (distracted) and *mūḍha* (deluded) stages. The commencement of concentration (*samādhi*) occurs due to the predominance of the quality of goodness (*sattva*). One-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) and cessation (*nirodha*) constitute the final stages. Furthermore, there are formative forces (*saṃskāras*) corresponding to each transformation. Among these, the formative forces produced by emergence are destroyed by the formative forces born of the commencement of concentration. Those born of that [commencement] are destroyed by those born of one-pointedness. Those born of one-pointedness are destroyed by those born of cessation. Even the formative forces born of cessation are destroyed by those very same [formative forces].

Just as lead mixed with gold, when being smelted, consumes both itself and the impurities of the gold; so too do the impressions (*saṃskāra*) born of cessation, produced by one-pointedness, consume themselves and [the residual traces].
Now, for the yogin whose mind has become steady through the aforementioned means, the various types of *savikalpaka* (conceptual) *samādhi* gradually manifest.
Following that, the seedless *samādhi* known as *asamprajñāta* manifests. To demonstrate this, the *sūtras* of Patañjali, together with their commentary (*vyākhyā*), are presented below.

"For one whose fluctuations have ceased, like a noble gem, there is a meditative absorption (samāpatti) consisting of being established in and colored by that [object], with respect to the grasper, the instrument of grasping, and the graspable. This refers to the absorption in the ungraspable form, which follows the state of being absorbed in the graspable—whether gross or subtle, consisting of the great elements or their subtle counterparts—preceded by one-pointedness toward those objects; this occurs for the mind that has attained stability through the aforementioned means and is, like a crystal gem, naturally composed of its own essence when it is not overwhelmed by rajas and tamas.

Then there arises the attainment of the object (*grahaṇa-samāpatti*), which consists of identification (*tanmayatā*) preceded by one-pointedness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) permeated by slight traces of *rajas* and *tamas*. Following that, there occurs the attainment of the subject (*agrahītṛ-samāpatti*), which consists of identification preceded by one-pointedness on the luminosity of *sattva* within the pure internal organ known as "stability" (*sthiti*). Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "One-pointedness is its being colored by that; when the mind has become submerged in that [object], there is the excellence of the object being meditated upon. This refers to the state of being colored by that object and the resulting transformation into its nature.

The meaning is that such an attainment (*samāpatti*) is a transformation into that very form. Furthermore, that attainment is fourfold, distinguished as *savitarka* (with deliberation), *nirvitarka* (without deliberation), *savicāra* (with reflection), and *nirvicāra* (without reflection). Among these, "the attainment mixed with the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, object, and knowledge is *savitarka*"; that is, the attainment characterized by conceptualization is one in which the appearance is gross (*sthūla*), being intermingled with the conceptual construction of word and object.

"When memory is purified, [the samādhi] is 'without vitarka' (nirvitarkā), appearing as mere nobility while being empty of its own form. When, through the practice of that [samādhi], the memory of linguistic conventions—which follows as an inseparable consequence—has been abandoned along with the objects of that convention, and when both the conceptualizations following from what has been heard and followed are also abandoned, then the object, remaining in the wisdom of samādhi which is empty of those [conceptualizations], exists by its own nature alone.

That [cognition] is a *nirvitarka* (non-discursive) attainment when it consists of the object's own nature alone and does not conceptualize it even by way of that form; being thus directed toward a gross object, it is non-discursive. By this very [attainment], the *savicārā* (discursive) and *nirvicārā* (non-discursive) attainments having subtle objects are explained. A subtle object—such as the *tanmātras*, the sense organs, and so forth—is what appears when it is delimited by space, time, qualities (*dharma*), and so on, along with the conceptualization of the meaning of words. That attainment in which such an object appears is the *savicārā* attainment.

An object that is subtle, appearing as the mere substratum devoid of place, time, qualities, and so forth, manifests [in consciousness]. That in which this occurs is the "nirvicārā" (non-discursive) meditative attainment; it is the supreme perception of yogis alone, because it is entirely free from even a trace of the superimposition of what is unreal.

Among these attainments (*samāpattis*), the state free from discursive thought (*nirvitarka*) is superior in comparison to that which possesses discursive thought (*savitarka*) and has a gross object; beyond that is the state with subtle objects (*savicāra*); superior to that is the state free from conceptual construction (*nirvicāra*), which has as its object a subtle reality reaching up to *pradhāna*; and finally, through the power of intense practice, even that *nirvicāra* state becomes pure (*nirmala*), the mind being freed from the latent impressions of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) and becoming fit for a continuous flow of stability.

"In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing. At that time, a wisdom known as truth-bearing arises, untouched even by the scent of error. "It has a different object from the wisdoms of scripture and inference, because its object is the unparticularized [reality]. This truth-bearing wisdom is distinct from knowledge derived from verbal testimony and inference; it illuminates subtle and concealed objects in their very form with perfect clarity. Thus, two verses have been cited by the authors of the Commentary:
"Having ascended the clarity of wisdom, the wise man, free from grief, looks upon all grieving people as one standing on a mountain peak looks down upon those on the ground."
"By means of scripture, inference, and the savor of the practice of meditation— cultivating wisdom in these three ways— one attains the supreme yoga. Thus [it is said].

"The impression produced by that [state] obstructs other impressions. And by means of the impressions generated by this [state], the impressions born of distraction become incapable of producing their effects. "These indeed are the seeded concentration (*sabīja-samādhi*). Thus, the four attainments (*samāpatti*) have been described. It is called "seeded concentration" because, according to its etymology, it exists together with a seed, which is the objective support (*ālambana*).

That which is with conceptualization was previously stated to be *samprajñāta-samādhi*. When even that, though it has a seed, undergoes dissolution—due to the dissolution of all mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) back into their own cause—whatever fluctuation arises from mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra* alone), [that is *asamprajñāta-samādhi*].

Through the mere process of negation—"not this, not this"—there arises the non-conceptual, seedless *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*. When this exists, the person becomes pure, established in the light of his own essential nature alone. This very yoga, known as seedless samādhi, is the cause of the supreme goal of human life; apart from this, there is no possibility of liberation even in theory. In this regard, the authority consists of the statements of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth.
In the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]: "The world-process is a garden difficult to endure, like the spreading of a poison-plant's venom."
"It is pacified by the purifying Yoga-Gāruḍa mantra.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
"The wise man should strive in such a way that supreme liberation may be attained."
That, however, is attained through yoga and not by any other means whatsoever.
For yoga is indeed the supreme medicine for those scorched by the heat of worldly existence,
whose minds are intent upon the higher and the lower, and in whom world-weariness has arisen.
And that [person], whose entire mass of afflictions has been consumed by the fire of yoga,
attains the supreme, all-encompassing nirvāṇa; of this there is no doubt.

Having attained the perfection of yoga through the realization of one's own self, nothing further remains to be seen; by that very realization, everything has been accomplished. Delighting in the Self, eternally fulfilled, he has attained a happiness that is my very likeness.
Therefore, there should be detachment even from that which consists of bliss;
therefore, there should be detachment even from that which consists of bliss.
"Yogis whose selves are purified by austerity and whose senses are restrained—
those great-souled ones cross the great ocean by means of yoga alone.
(From the Yājñavalkya-smṛti)

"Sacrifice, conduct, compassion, non-violence, charity, and the study of one's own scriptures—these are indeed the duties of actions; however, the supreme dharma among them is the realization of the Self through yoga.
Thus said the great sage Mātaṅga.
Abandoning sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and other rites, the best of the twice-born,
devoted to the practice of yoga and tranquil, attains the supreme Brahman.
For Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, women, and Shudras, Yoga is the purifier;
there is no other means for the peace of actions or for liberation than Yoga.
In the Ruru Purāṇa, the words of Śiva are: "Henceforth I shall proclaim the yoga that is most difficult to attain,
by which they behold the Self, the Lord, like the radiant sun."
"The fire of yoga quickly burns away the entire cage of sin;
clear knowledge arises, which directly bestows the attainment of nirvāṇa.
[This applies] to the forest-dweller, the householder, the forest-recluse, and the student.
For those who are constantly engaged in this, the principle of Māyā arises.
Having attained unsurpassed yoga and shaken off the turbidity of delusion, I shall, without delay, destroy all darkness by means of the lamp of knowledge.
"A householder is liberated from bondage; no deliberation is required in this matter.
And likewise, in the section on the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*):
"He should be devoted to the practice of yoga and should constantly be a reciter of the *Rudra-hymns*."
"Having established the internal fire within himself, the twice-born should become a wandering mendicant,
constantly devoted to the practice of yoga and dedicated to the knowledge of the Self. Thus says Manu in the section on the duties of the ascetic (yati-dharma):
"One should perceive through the yoga of the Supreme Self the manifestation of beings as such,
and their arising within bodies, both high and low.
— *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*
In this world, the sin of a man who delights in the practice of yoga perishes;
for that person who is accomplished in practice and devoted to yoga is able to destroy all obstacles.
"Having quickly abandoned the two bodies, one becomes liberated from bondage. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Just as even a very small lamp can destroy a vast darkness,"
"Even a small practice of yoga may destroy great sin.
In the Viṣṇudharma:
"That which is for the welfare of all beings and beneficial even to women..."
Tell us what is even superior to that which is for worms and insects; speak of that supreme good for us.
Thus addressed previously by the gods and the celestial rishis, Kapila replied to them that yoga alone is the supreme good.
Regarding the path of yoga, Vyāsa says in the Mahābhārata:
Even one of inferior caste, like a woman, if desiring righteousness,
may both of them attain the supreme goal by this path.
Whether he be a knower of all dharmas, or even a man devoid of skill;
whether he be the most excellent of the righteous, or the greatest of evildoers;
whether he be a tiger among men, or one who bears impotence.

"He indeed crosses over the great suffering of the ocean of old age and death; even one who merely desires to know it transcends the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman). Thus says Dattātreya in the *Yogatattvaprakāśa*.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or a Śramaṇa, a Buddhist or even one who has fallen from his status,
a Kāpālika or a Cārvāka— provided he is wise and endowed with faith.
"One who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga shall attain all perfections.
And in the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā:
"The state which is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the practitioners of Yoga."
He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, he truly sees.
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the self and conquered the senses,
whose self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, he is not tainted.
For one who is not disciplined, there is no wisdom; for one who is not disciplined, there is no meditative cultivation.
For one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; and for one who is not at peace, how can there be happiness?
Constantly disciplining the self, the yogi of restrained mind attains the supreme peace of Nirvana, which abides in Me.
In this, there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear.
Whatever fruit of merit is declared in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities,
and in acts of charity— the yogi, having known this, transcends it all and attains the supreme, primeval state.
"Therefore, apply yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in actions.
And in the *Yogaśāstra*:
"This is the ladder to liberation; this is the deception of Time:
that the mind, having turned away from habitual practice, becomes attached to the Supreme Self.
— *Yogabīja*
Salutations to you, the primordial Lord; salutations to you, the Lord of the universe.
Salutations to you whose form is the universe; salutations to you who transcend the universe.
Salutations again and again to You, the agent of creation, sustenance, and dissolution;
salutations to You, O Lord of the gods of gods; I bow to the Supreme Self.
Salutations to you, the perfectly complete one, the cause of joy for the world;
O Sadāśiva, Lord of the universe, ocean of the nectar of compassion!
All living beings are enveloped by the net of illusion through pleasures and pains;
O Lord Śaṅkara, tell me out of compassion how their liberation may be achieved.
This path brings about all accomplishments, cuts through the net of illusion,
destroys birth, death, old age, and disease, and bestows happiness.

The supreme state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) is difficult to attain through various paths;
it is obtained only by the path of the perfected ones (siddha-mārga) and not from any other, as spoken by Śiva.

They have fallen into the snares of the scriptures, their wisdom being utterly deluded.
That state which is inexpressible cannot be described even by the gods;
since it is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, how could it be illuminated by a scripture?
"It is partless, stainless, tranquil, transcending all, and free from affliction;
yet this very same [reality], in the form of the individual soul (jīva), is enveloped by the fruits of merit and demerit.

"How did that eternal state of the Supreme Self come to belong to living beings?

Beyond the state of all existing things, the stainless form of gnosis vibrates within itself like water; from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arises.

The aggregate of the five elements, consisting of the three realms and the qualities (guṇas), is always joined with pleasure and pain; it is the family of the living being throughout its various states of existence.

yet desire, anger, fear, anxiety, greed, delusion, pride, and so forth [belong to the ego].
Old age and death, wretchedness, grief, lassitude,
hunger, thirst, hatred, shame, pleasure, pain, despondency, and even joy;
waking, dreaming, deep sleep, as well as doubt and pride.

Therefore, for the sake of destroying these defects, I shall tell you the means;
some say that here knowledge alone is sufficient for your success.
O Goddess, how can liberation be possible through knowledge devoid of yoga?
And yoga devoid of knowledge is indeed useless for the task of liberation.
The Goddess said:
"From ignorance alone comes transmigratory existence; from knowledge alone one is liberated.
"Tell me with gracious words what further task I must perform through yoga.
The Lord said: "O Goddess of the Suras, I shall tell you that which you have spoken as the truth!"
In the beginning, that which is to be known is of the very nature of knowledge; it is realized through knowledge as the means.

"How is this soul, which is free from defects such as lust, anger, and fear, yet enveloped by all faults, liberated through knowledge? The Goddess said:

"What rule could there be for him afterwards, or how could even a prohibition apply?
He is the man of discernment, ever-yoked, and free from the delusion of worldly existence.
Lord Ishvara said:

Through the process of purification, it has attained the state of wandering in saṃsāra in the form of intense suffering;

Devoid of the knowledge of creation, maintenance, destruction, and manifestation—

Likewise, when the knower abides in whatever is perfumed by latent impressions, there is no distinction here between the two; their perception of worldly existence is the same.

By humans through diseases arising from cold and heat, pleasure and pain;

Īśvara said: "Liberation is attained through knowledge alone; it is not otherwise according to those [scriptural] statements.
Everyone says that victory comes by means of a sword; what then?"

otherwise, birth and death will continue again and again.
Through the yoga of the union of prāṇa and apāna, the oneness of the moon and the sun occurs;
the wise one should then digest the body composed of the seven dhātus by means of the fire.
His diseases, as well as injuries such as cutting and striking, perish;
thus he remains as an embodied being whose very nature is the supreme ether.
What more need be said? For him indeed there is no fear of death;
he appears in this world like a living body, yet is himself like a burnt rag.
"P.67 There is no merit greater than yoga; there is no state higher than yoga;
there is nothing subtler than yoga; indeed, there is nothing superior to the path of yoga. Thus it is said.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Just as fire carried by the wind may burn even the entire earth,
so too the yogi, having attained power, blazing with splendor, and possessed of great strength [can do the same]."
O Pārtha! The Sun, with his infinite rays, dries up the entire world;
[so too do] twenty... endowed with the power of yoga.
Neither the Lords of Creatures, nor the sages, nor the gods, nor the great elements have power over them;
neither Yama, nor the Ender, nor even Death with his terrifying stride can prevail when they are enraged.
O King! You have mastery over yoga and over the immortal splendor of yoga;
and you possess many thousands of selves, O bull among the Bharatas!
Having acquired strength, the yogi should travel across the earth with all of them;
he may enjoy certain sense-objects and then again practice fierce austerity.
"And then, O dear one, he should withdraw it again, like the sun its qualities of radiance. Thus [it is said].
In the *Mānasollāsa*:
"By the grace of the Vedas and the teacher, and by the power of the practice of yoga..."
When the awakening to one's own self occurs even through the grace of the Lord, [then liberation is attained].
"Just as one perceives food eaten and residing within the belly as being one's own self,
so too does the Lord of Yogis perceive the entire universe swallowed by the Fullness.
This is a statement of Śiva to Bāmadeva regarding Rājayoga.
Who indeed knows the true greatness of Rājayoga?
Wherever a knower of that resides, that place becomes a vessel of merit.
By seeing or touching this [image], even the ignorant, together with twenty-one generations of their kin, attain the state of liberation; how much more so those who are devoted to it!
"He who knows specifically the internal yoga and the external yoga—
he is to be saluted by you and by me as well; he is to be saluted even by Śeṣa, so what need is there to mention others?"
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Those who constantly practice the great yoga once, twice, or thrice a day— these should be known as Maheśvaras."
In the Gītā:
"The yogi is superior to the ascetics, and even superior to those possessed of knowledge;
the yogi is also superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi. Thus it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
"A yogi indeed excels over a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), and a thousand celibate students (brahmacārins). — *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*.
By that act, both parents have their purpose fulfilled; blessed is that country and that lineage in which one who has attained yoga becomes a consumer of what has been given.
Seen, spoken to, or questioned,
he who possesses discernment regarding the duties of men purifies the sins of people accumulated over hundreds of millions of births.
"But the supreme dharma is that which consists in the vision of the Self through yoga. Viśiṣṭa says: "He whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it reaches direct experience [is liberated]."
"All those who come within the range of his vision are liberated from all sins.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "By means of the āsana one destroys the dust [of the senses], and by means of prāṇāyāma one destroys sin."
The yogi releases mental modification through withdrawal of the senses.

"Through concentrations (dhāraṇās), one attains steadiness of mind; through meditation (dhyāna), the vision of the Lord; and through absorption (samādhi), one attains liberation, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma. Thus it is said.

[Objection: But since yoga, defined as the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, falls outside the scope of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can ignorance be removed by the knowledge produced thereby? Moreover, there is not even the possibility of liberation without the removal of ignorance.

Thus says the Śruti: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey [to liberation]. [If this is argued, we reply: True, that [liberation] is to be attained by the mind alone.

On the strength of scriptural passages such as, "But it is seen by the keenest intellect, by the subtle mind of those who perceive the subtle," the mind is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When the position is adopted that statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) produce only indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), then the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) and so forth would occur through a mind whose every defect has been eliminated by the practice of yoga. However, when [the following is considered]:
"From which words turn back, along with the mind, not having reached it."

On the strength of such scriptural passages as "This [body] is certainly composed of clouds," and because it requires the assistance of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the mind—like its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—is not an independent instrument of valid cognition. Even if one accepts the position that immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises from sentences such as "That thou art" alone, even then, for a person whose mental defects have been eliminated through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) is possible through the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) alone.
Thus say the venerable feet of Vidyāraṇya:
"Having abandoned the meditator and the meditation, [the mind] gradually becomes focused solely on the object of meditation."
The mind is called samādhi when it is like a lamp in nirvāṇa.
When this web of latent impressions has been completely dissolved,
and the accumulation of karma known as merit and demerit has been uprooted from its very foundation;
"When a statement is free from obstruction and expresses that which is immediate, it produces an immediate realization, like [the perception of] a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand.

Furthermore, the threefold possibility consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*) is established because the practice of Sāṅkhya-Yoga—which serves as the remover of that [possibility]—is enjoined by the Śruti itself for the purpose of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
For instance, the Śruti says: "The Self, indeed, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
And there is also Smṛti:
"It should be heard from the words of the scriptures, reflected upon through reasonings, and, having reflected, constantly meditated upon; these are the causes for [right] vision. Thus [it is said].

It has been stated that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are indeed restrictive disciplines (*niyama*). However, meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*)—whether in the form of meditation (*dhyāna*) consisting of the worship of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*), or in the form of cognitive absorption (*samprajñāta-samādhi*)—when fully matured, becomes seedless absorption (*nirbīja-samādhi*).
Thus, the venerable Vidyāraṇya says:
"The worship of the attributeless, when matured, gradually becomes absorption (*samādhi*)."
That which is called the cessation of concentration is obtained without effort.
Upon the attainment of cessation, only that object which is free from internal attachment remains for the person;
when this has been repeatedly cultivated, the knowledge of reality arises through the [instructional] statement.
The practice of yoga is for this very purpose, as heard in the *Amṛtabindu* and other scriptures;
those most skilled in yoga call this "dharmamegha" (cloud of dharma) samādhi.
"Since he rains down thousands of streams of the nectar of Dharma,
the millions of karmas accumulated here in this beginningless saṃsāra go to destruction by him, and pure Dharma increases. Thus it is said.

In this regard, although the eligibility for yoga is obtained for all living beings in the scriptural passages from the Purāṇas and other sources cited here, nevertheless, in the case of yoga which has liberation as its fruit, it is appropriate that only those who possess dispassion are eligible.
Thus, it is stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā:
"He whose mind is detached from objects, both those perceived through direct experience and those heard of in tradition, is qualified for this yoga; no one else. — Sureśvarācārya.

"For one who is dispassionate toward this world and the next, who desires to abandon worldly existence, and who indeed seeks to know [the Self] for the sake of one-pointed concentration— it is such a person who is praised as being qualified."

In this matter, the established rule is as follows: among the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), only a Brāhmaṇa [is eligible]; even among them, only one who has renounced the world (*saṃnyāsī*); and even among those, only one who possesses knowledge that—through yoga practiced over many previous births—sublates the notion of the body being the self (*dehātma-jñāna*). Liberation occurs only for such a person who has attained the direct realization (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*) of reality which sublates the notion of the body being the self. For others, however—Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and women—even if they are devoted to the truth through the practice of yoga, liberation occurs only after they have gradually attained birth as Brāhmaṇas.
Thus it is said in the *Gītā*: "Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection."
"Even among those who have attained perfection through effort, only some know me in truth.
Likewise, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"For those men for whom there is no practice of yoga from a previous birth..."
For the attainment of yoga, there is this sequence beginning with the Śūdra and Vaiśya.
He becomes a woman, then a Śūdra, and thereafter he attains the state of a Vaiśya;
from there he becomes a Kṣatriya, and then a Brāhmaṇa who is free from the taint of buying and selling.
"Then he becomes a learned reciter (anūcāna), then a sacrificer (yajvā), and after that, one who has renounced action (karmayāsin).
Thereafter, the yogi attains the state of knowledge and shall gradually obtain liberation. Thus it is said.

For those women, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas who lack the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of yoga practiced in previous births, there are now [the following] limbs of yoga for the attainment of yoga and the acquisition of liberation:

Whether by the performance of one's own duties as prescribed for one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), or by another superior and subtle dharma, those who have attained birth as Brahmins, have taken up renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), and have practiced yoga for a long time, attain liberation; such is this sequence. However, for those in whom the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of yoga practiced in previous births persist, they regain yoga through that very prior impression, and by means of attaining birth as Brahmins in due course, they attain liberation. [As it is said: "In the *Dānadharma*, Śakra performed penance for the sake of attaining Brahminhood!"
For this matter was indeed described in detail to Mataṅga.
When will our liberation come about through the Son of Dharma?

"O Keśava, Mukunda has requested the goal of liberation here;

were likewise devoted to the practice of yoga, tranquil, and established in the knowledge of Brahman.
"It is heard that having attained birth as Brahmins, they were liberated;

This being the case, it is determined that Janaka and others who were Kṣatriyas, Sūta, Lāṅgala, and others who were Vaiśyas, Gārgī, Sulabhā, and others who were women, and Vidura, Pailavaka, and others who were Śūdras, were liberated only after attaining birth as Brahmins.

If it is objected that even for those who have attained the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of Brahman and the Self—thereby dispelling every doubt—it appears as if a new birth occurs, which is inconsistent; we say no, because we hear of Vasiṣṭha and others, who are the crest-jewels of all those born of Brahman, being born once or many times. Sometimes you are born from the sky, sometimes you are born from water;
sometimes you are born from a mountain, and sometimes you are born from fire.
For the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas, as Viṣṇu is about to descend to the earth,
this will now be his eleventh birth under the name of Rāma.
O Lord of Sages! For the sake of relieving the burden of the earth, this will now be the sixteenth birth of Viṣṇu in the house of Vasudeva.
"Reṇukā was born as a human being; this Hari [appeared] for the sixth time.

This is to be connected with the following word "saṃsmarāmi" (I remember).
In the Gītā:
