If it is argued that their birth is for the purpose of maintaining the cosmic order (*niyati*) consisting of the protection of the world, then in this case as well, only a Brāhmaṇa is entitled to liberation, because the supreme Lord’s cosmic order remains in force. If it is further objected that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) would be useless since it does not bring about the cessation of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), we say no; for liberation is inevitable once the obstacles of *prārabdha* karma—which can only be destroyed through experience—are removed, and because such knowledge produces the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukti*) even during the time of that experience.
Thus says the Śruti:
"For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall attain [the goal]," and so forth. This meaning is well-known in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other texts.
Furthermore, it has already been shown previously by citing the "Yogabīja" passages that liberation belongs to the yogin alone.

If it be objected: "Is it not heard that liberation for every living being results from death in Kāśī? How then can it be said that only a Brāhmaṇa has the qualification for liberation?"—the answer is: True; even there, it is heard that only one who has experienced his own auspicious and inauspicious karma, who has thereby attained a divine body, and who is qualified for the instruction of Viśvanātha, [attains liberation]. Furthermore, because a divine body possesses the same characteristics as a Brāhmaṇa body, this meaning is clearly established in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.

However, others maintain that because it is heard in scripture that all castes have the right to practice yoga, everyone is liberated through the knowledge of reality arising from yoga. They say, moreover, that for those such as Kṣatriyas who are devoid of yoga, there is gradual liberation.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, the sages said:
"O Blessed One, O destroyer of the god Hiraṇyākṣa and of obstacles!"
Indeed, four stages of life have been proclaimed; among them, the single-mindedness of yogis is said to be the foremost.
The tortoise said:
"Having renounced all actions and having resorted to unwavering meditative absorption,
that yogi who remains motionless is a true renunciant, not one of the five other types."
"Therefore, this fourfold order of stages for the twice-born is established;
a fifth is not found in any of the Vedic scriptures.

One who has attained seedless samādhi (nirvīja-samādhi) alone should be known as a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), because he has abandoned all actions without remainder and possesses the direct qualification for liberation.
Therefore, in the absence of yoga, renunciation is difficult to accomplish and obstacles arise at every step. As stated in the Bhagavad Gītā:
"O Pāṇḍava, know that what they call renunciation is itself yoga;
for no one becomes a yogi without having renounced their worldly intentions."
"But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
the sage disciplined in yoga, O Brahmin, attains it before long."

If it be objected: "Surely, for a person who has engaged in a yoga that requires a long time to accomplish, if he dies prematurely by fate, or abandons the yoga out of fear of wasted effort, or due to fierce obstacles, or through the fault of attachment to sense-objects, how can any wise person's engagement in this [path] be justified from the outset? [The answer is: The destiny of a yogi who dies in the midst of practicing yoga has been described in detail by Viśiṣṭha in the *Yogasaptabhūmikāvivaraṇa*, and the stages (*bhūmikās*) will be explained hereafter. Rāma said: "For one who is fallen or one whose faults have not yet ascended [to be overcome], there is indeed the expansion of worldly association."
This first stage here has not been awakened even throughout hundreds of other births.
Alternatively, through association with the virtuous or by chance,
detachment indeed arises from a profound reflection upon the nature of worldly existence.
When dispassion has arisen in a person, the emergence of the stages [of yoga] necessarily follows;
consequently, transmigratory existence is destroyed—this is the summary of the meaning of the scriptures.
For the embodied being whose life has transcended through the stages of yoga,
former misdeeds are exhausted in accordance with the portions of those stages;
thereafter, [he dwells] in celestial palaces and in the cities of the world-protectors.
He delights in the groves of Mount Meru, accompanied by his beloved.
Then, when the accumulation of merit and previously committed demerit are both exhausted through the depletion of their fruits, the yogin is born again.
Having been born in the house of the pure, the prosperous, the virtuous, and the wise,
and being perfumed by yoga, he practices yoga alone.
"In that regard, the wise person, having practiced the sequence of the stages of yoga previously cultivated,
falls from what has been seen and rises high to the subsequent sequence of stages.
Thus, in the *Yogabīja*, the Goddess said:
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall now declare what was previously spoken by me at Agnyātha:
the Great Path of Ādinātha is indeed one alone, and not otherwise.
It would indeed appear as if twofold due to the distinction between different births;
that which is to be attained is reached only through gradual practice, and not otherwise.
The practice of yoga with a single body alone may attain perfection only after a long time, proceeding very gradually, like the movement of a monkey.
If the body perishes through negligence before the attainment of yogic perfection,
one endowed with the latent impressions (vāsanās) of previous lives shall obtain another body.
Then, by the power of merit, an association with a Guru will be accomplished;
through the path of the western gate, the fruit arises swiftly.
Through practice performed in previous lives, one quickly attains the fruit;
this indeed should be understood as that supreme "crow-like" method.
"Therefore, there is no state higher than practice; this is the 'crow's view' (the view of the ignorant).
Thus [it is said]. In the Bhagavad Gītā, Arjuna said, beginning with "One who lacks self-restraint but is endowed with faith... and continuing until "...thereafter he goes to the supreme goal."

Up to this point [P.77], the dialogue has taken the form of questions and answers regarding the nature of yoga that I too should understand. Even a person who merely desires to know yoga through its constituent limbs (*aṅga*) is a knower of the *Śabdabrahman*, which is the Veda; by transcending that, he obtains a fruit superior to all the Vedas—namely, residence for a long duration in the worlds of Brahmā and others.

Since such a fruit is obtained merely by the desire to know yoga, what need is there to mention the even greater abundance of fruit resulting from the actual practice of yoga? He states this principle of *kaimutika* (the "how much more so" argument) with the words beginning "for one who desires to know" (*jijñāsu-pare*).
Regarding the *rājayoga*:
"In former times, this Umā, the primordial power (*ādi-śakti*), obtained [realization] from me;
now, you alone have obtained the purification of birth."

"Through practice performed in other births, the reality manifests of its own accord; like one who has just awakened from sleep, it is indeed perceived directly even without instruction and the like. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"Even one who practices yoga by an improper path, if he practices with diligence,
will surely attain yoga in the course of much time—
just as the brahmin Jaigīṣavya did, and as Āsita and others did."
Janaka and others were Kṣatriyas, while Tulādhāra and others were Vaiśyas.
The seven— the Dharma-fowler and others, as well as the Śūdra Pailavaka and others— having practiced their respective duties in former lives, attained supreme perfection.
Maitreyī, Sulabhā Gārgī, and the ascetic Śāṇḍilī—
these and many others, though born of low wombs, [attained perfection].
They have attained the supreme steadfastness in knowledge due to their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in previous births.
Furthermore, some who have practiced yoga in previous births [attain it] according to the degree of merit from their own practice.

Having attained the state of Brahmā, some the status of divine sages (*devarṣi*), some the status of sons of Brahmā, some the status of *muni*s, and others the status of *bhagavat*s, they became directly realized of the Self even without instruction therein.
As it is heard in the Purāṇas and other texts that Hiraṇyagarbha, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Sanatkumāra, Vāmadeva, Śuka, and others were "perfected by birth" (*janmasiddha*).
"There is no suffering equal to passion; there is no happiness equal to renunciation."
"There is no god equal to Śumbha; there is no goal equal to Yoga.

Regarding the stages (*bhūmikās*), the venerable Patañjali, while defining the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—which serves as the means for attaining *kaivalya*, characterized by the absolute cessation of the suffering to be abandoned—in the seventh form of discriminative wisdom (*prajñā*), stated that there are seven [stages] by the aphorism: "His discriminative wisdom has seven stages culminating in the limit."

When discriminative discernment has arisen for the person, there occurs a sevenfold wisdom at the final stage, which culminates in all samādhis that have an objective support (*sālambana*). Among these, four are of the nature of liberation from the task (*kāryavimukti*): [1] "I have known what was to be known; there is nothing further to be known"; [2] "The afflictions are exhausted; there is nothing further to be exhausted"; [3] "Cessation has been attained by me"; [4] "Discriminative discernment has been reached by me. These exist in that state through the exclusion of other cognitive impressions (*pratyaya*).

In such a state, wisdom (prajñā) arises in this very manner. This meditative concentration (adhīḥ), because it consists of stainless knowledge regarding the object of action, is called "liberation from action" (kāryavimukti).

Liberation of the mind is threefold: [1] My intellect has accomplished its purpose; my qualities, having performed their functions, will not return to their source again, like stones fallen from a mountain peak—since these [qualities] are heading toward dissolution, and because there is no root cause for delusion and they serve no further purpose, how can there be a continuous flow? [2] And my meditative absorption (samādhi) has become second nature; when that exists, what else remains here for one who realizes the true nature, namely: "All this has that as its essence; That is the Truth; That is the Self; That art thou"? [3] What else is there here?
"He will say: 'He saw that very person. 'This is your Self, the immortal... there is nothing else... I am That; You are I. P.79

Since the non-difference from Brahman is established by such scriptural texts as "I am He," the form "I am Brahman" indeed arises within the discriminative knowledge (*vivekakhyāti*). However, even this does not directly constitute the means to liberation; rather, it is only through the non-conceptual state (*nirvikalpaka*) that follows immediately after it that liberation is attained. This is because, among the previously cited statements from the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*, it is specifically that primary yoga—which consists of the cessation of all mental modifications—that is designated as the means to liberation.

And it will be stated that for the arising of this discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which serves as the means for liberation, the very practice of the limbs beginning with restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is the cause, by way of purifying the mind. These have been explained in detail in the *Vāsiṣṭha*.
Thus Vasiṣṭha said:
"O sinless one, comprehend this sevenfold ground of knowledge!"
By means of this stage, one sinks further into the mire of delusion;
thus do the proponents of various classifications of the stages of yoga speak in many different ways.
Those who are free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of pride alone bestow happiness.
This very realization, which consists of knowledge of the rules, is sevenfold in its stages.
The state of being known as "the knowable" (sukti) exists within one stage as it transitions to another stage.
The first stage of knowledge is declared to be called "the desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā);
the second is "investigation" (vicāraṇā), and the third is "the thinned mind" (tanumānasā).
The fourth downfall would be that called "attachment."
The sixth state is known as that which arises from the categories of existence, and the seventh is remembered as the fourth (turya).
Liberation resides within these, from which one does not fall back again.
Now hear this etymological explanation of these stages:
why do I remain as if bewildered? I shall explain it to you according to the teachings of the virtuous.

The desire preceded by dispassion is called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious) by the wise. That engagement in right conduct which follows from the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, and the practice of dispassion is called *vicāraṇā* (investigation).
Non-attachment toward the objects of the senses arising from investigation and virtuous desire—
where that exists due to the absence of grossness, it is called *tanumānasā*.
Through the practice of the three stages, by virtue of the mind's withdrawal from objects,
when the pure self of sattva is established, that is declared to be the attainment of sattva.

The state called *saṃsakti* is said to be that in which the practice of the four stages has been intensely cultivated, resulting in the fruit of non-attachment, and in which the wonder of the "inner bark" has taken firm root.
Through the firm practice of the five stages, by delighting in one's own self,
and through the contemplation of both internal and external objects, [the state of the yogi is established].
Through prolonged effort induced by another,
there arises the sixth stage of comprehension, known as "the realization of the meaning of the words."
Through long practice over six stages, because no differentiation is perceived,
that state of abiding solely in one's own nature is to be known as the path leading to the Fourth State (turyagā).
For this fourth state (turya) exists here among those liberated while living;
beyond that, in the realm of liberation after death (videhamukti), lies that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
Rāma said:
"How is the practice of the seven stages of yoga performed? And what are the signs for each stage as one practices?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Man is of two kinds: the one who is engaged in worldly activity (pravṛtta) and the one who has withdrawn from it (nivṛtta).
Listen now to the characteristics of these two, who are oriented toward heaven and liberation respectively."
He who makes the determination, "How much is that Nirvana? To me, it is merely an excellent cycle of rebirth," is described as one who has entered into active worldly engagement (pravṛtta).
Like the entry of a tortoise's neck into the opening between a pair of moving bars,
at the end of many births, a man of discernment is born.
P.81 Alas, this saṃsāra is indeed essence-less; let us attain stability through equanimity.
What is the use of lingering over past actions? The day is spent by that very [equanimity].
"What could be the supreme rest, free from the excellence of action?"—
one who possesses such internal certainty is known as "Nivṛtti."
"How may I, having become free from passion, cross the ocean of saṃsāra?"—
when one is thus intent on warding off [defilements], then equanimity arises.
Day by day he attains detachment within his latent impressions,
and he proceeds with noble actions while rejoicing daily.
He constantly doubts those things that are grasped through much effort;
he does not undertake actions, yet he pursues meritorious deeds.
He is constantly afraid of evil and does not look toward worldly enjoyment;
his words are gentle, appropriate, and filled with affection and intimacy.
When one speaks words that are appropriate to the place and time,
then one has attained the first stage.
He serves virtuous people through mind, deed, and speech;
he studies the treatises on knowledge, having brought them from wherever they may be found.
Thus, having reached the stage of yoga known as *vicāraṇā*,

he resorts to the most eminent scholars who are renowned for their primary exegesis through the study of the Vedas (*śruti*), the law-books (*smṛti*), the conduct of the virtuous (*sadācāra*), and the practices of retention and meditation (*dhāraṇā-dhyāna*).

One who knows the distinctions between categories of things and has mastered what is to be heard understands the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, just as a master of the house knows his own home.
O Lord, he casts off even that which dwells on the outside— excessive pride, envy, hypocrisy, and delusion—
just as a snake sheds its skin.
One whose mind is thus disposed attains, through service to the teacher and the virtuous, the entirety of the scripture along with its secret doctrines, exactly as it is.
Then he falls upon that third stage of yoga, which is designated as non-attachment,
like a bodiless being falling onto a pure bed of flowers;
having established an unwavering mind upon the meaning of the words of the scripture exactly as they are.
By means of sequences of discourse on the supreme self, resting in the hermitages of ascetics.
In that same way, by censuring worldly existence and following the sequence of discourses on the inner self,
he who sits upon a bed or seat of stone wears away his former body.
The disciplined one passes his time wandering through forests and groves, graced by the tranquility of mind and the happiness of the state of non-attachment.
Through the study of excellent scriptures and the performance of meritorious deeds,
this vision of reality becomes clear for a living being exactly as it is;
having reached the third stage, the awakened one experiences it for himself.
There are two kinds of non-attachment; hear this distinction between them.
This non-attachment is twofold: the ordinary and the superior.
"I am neither the agent nor the enjoyer, neither the oppressed nor the oppressor"—
this non-attachment toward objects is what is called "commonality" (sāmānya), as opposed to attachment (saṅga).
Everything is fashioned by past karma, or else it is simply dependent upon the Lord;
whether it be happiness or suffering, what agency of my own could there possibly be in this?
Prosperity and enjoyment are great diseases; gains are supreme calamities;
unions lead only to separations; and mental anxieties are but maladies of the intellect.
The universal reflection that "He remains," while destroying all phenomena engaged in being swallowed by Time— that is non-attachment.
By this sequential yoga, through union with the great-souled ones and separation from the wicked, one attains the internal realization of the self through spiritual practice.
Through human effort and by means of continuous practice,
when the object has attained firm clarity like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, [the goal is achieved].
Neither the ego-sense nor the Lord is my agent, nor is past karma mine;
having cast far away the conceptualization of words and their meanings as being deficient, [one should remain].
On the shore beyond the ocean of saṃsāra, in that which is essence-less and the supreme cause,
there is neither a state of sitting nor speaking, neither silence nor speech, and neither mental cultivation nor its absence— by means of any insentient or sentient entity, nor by word or object.
That which is without beginning or end, unborn, and beautiful—that is called attachment to its activity.
Sweet with the fragrance of contentment, possessing pure sprouts upon its body,
and nestled at the tip of the stalk of the mind, it [the mind] navigates the thicket of obstacles and thorns.
Rooted in the mud of discernment and blossomed by the sun of internal discrimination,
this third stage bears fruit known as non-attachment.
Through the conjunction of pure associations and the accumulation of meritorious deeds,
the first stage arises by a chance occurrence, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
Like a sprout that has just emerged from the earth,
she must be protected with great effort by the sprinkling of the water of discernment.
One should daily and with effort cultivate that very portion which shines forth through inquiry and brings about its arising, just as a farmer tends to a sprout.
through effort, one may then attain the second stage;
for this third stage here is indeed the most excellent and free from attachment.
O Rāma! This triad of stages, which arises from the process of abandoning all mental constructions and volitions, is known as the waking state.
P.84 Just as if one were awake, because the perception of difference continues here quite clearly;
for those engaged in yoga, [the consciousness] arises here as being solely offered [to the Self].
Seeing which, a desire for liberation arises even in those of deluded intellect,
as they perform what ought to be done and refrain from doing what ought not to be done.
He who abides in natural conduct is considered noble;
first it sprouts from the ground, and thereafter it blossoms.
On the second or the third [attempt], the highest state of nobility bears fruit;
having died while in that state of longing, the pure yogi [attains] those worlds produced by his resolve.
Having enjoyed worldly pleasures for a long time, the practitioner of yoga is born again; yet,
through the practice of the three stages, when ignorance has reached its end and perfect knowledge arises in the mind, it is like the rising of the full moon.
Having reached the fourth stage, yogins with disciplined minds perceive everything as equal, undifferentiated, and without beginning or end.
When non-duality has attained stability and duality has come to rest,
those who have reached the fourth stage perceive the world as if it were a dream.
The first three stages are called waking, and the fourth is said to be dreaming;
the mind, however, dissolves like the vanishing of an autumn cloud.
Only a residue of beings remains once one has entered the fifth stage,
because here the mind is dissolved through the cessation of the world's conceptual constructions.
Having reached the fifth stage, which is well-suited for the seven steps,
he remains in non-duality alone, with all particular aspects completely stilled.
With the extinction of duality dissolved and awakened within, he remains joyful,
like one who has truly attained the sevenfold wealth upon reaching the fifth stage.
Though you remain inward-turned and intent upon outward activity,
you appear constantly as if asleep due to your state of total detachment.
Practicing this and dwelling within these stages,
one gradually descends to another stage, the sixth, known as Turiya.
Wherein there is neither the form of being nor non-being, neither "I" nor even the absence of egoism;
there one remains alone, with conceptualization exhausted, having emerged from both duality and unity.
Free from knots, with doubts stilled, he is one who contemplates liberation while yet living.
Even while thus appearing, it is extinguished; the mind remains like a lamp.
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky;
full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean.
This [yogi] has attained something, yet likewise he has nothing at all.
Having established himself on the sixth stage, he shall attain the seventh stage.
The seventh stage of yoga is called liberation while in the body (videhamukti).
By some she was called Śivā, and by others she was proclaimed as Brahmā.
By some she is called Viṣṇu, by others she is remembered as Śūnya;
by some she is declared to be Artha, and by others she is said to be Kāla.
By some, the state of being a possessor is defined as the distinction between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa);
by others, it is conceived in various other ways through diverse distinctions imagined for the self.
Though eternally indefinable, it is nevertheless defined in some way.
These seven stages have been described by me to you, O descendant of Radha.
"By means of the practice of these [meditations], suffering is no longer experienced.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Yogacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śivānanda, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Rāmajanmasadānandasarasvatī. ||1||
Chapter Two:
Therein, the determination of what is to be done and what is not to be done by the yogi.

A person who has attained yoga along with its secret and constituent parts through the grace of a true guru properly propitiated, and who is habituated to uninterrupted practice, certainly attains the aforementioned fruit.
As stated in the *Skandha*: "Having personally obtained the entire essence of yoga from a teacher, one of steady intellect..."
"As it has been said: 'By that [means] one obtains [the goal] and also attains liberation.
Thus says Sureśvarācārya:
"Through the grace of the Guru, one obtains yoga endowed with its eight limbs."
"And by the grace of Śiva, one attains eternal perfection in yoga.
And the Śruti says:
"He who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and as for the Lord, so for the Guru..."
"For these truths revealed shine forth for that high-souled one.
And as it is said: "A person who has a teacher knows.
From the *Yogabīja*:
"One should always serve that Guru by whom mastery over the winds is achieved;
through the grace of the Guru’s mouth, the wise man should effect mastery over the vital breaths.
— Yājñavalkya.
For all four [classes], five elders are enjoined by the Śruti:
the mother, the father, the preceptor, the maternal uncle, and likewise the father-in-law.
Among these, three are declared to be primary: the teacher, as well as the parents.
Among these, the most eminent one is the single teacher who knows the supreme truth.
Therefore, at all times, by all those seeking the supreme good,
teachers endowed with the memory of tradition should be honored through speech, mind, and other means.
In the *Rājayoga*: "He is not accessible through the declarations of Vedānta and Tarka, nor through various collections of scriptures and Āgamas,
nor through noble practices such as meditation."
Having abandoned the wish-fulfilling gem, which is the sole teacher.
He whose vision is steady even without an object of sight,
whose breath is steady without effort,
and whose mind is steady without a support—
He alone is the yogi, he is the guru, and he is the one to be served.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
there is nothing higher than the Guru, therefore one should always worship him.
When the reality has been shown by the Guru, one becomes identical with it at that very moment;
considering oneself liberated, one is released—of this there is no doubt.

"Just as copper becomes gold through contact with the elixir of accomplishment (*siddhirasa*), so too does a disciple become composed of reality (*tattvamaya*) upon hearing the instruction of the Guru.
Success does not come from the mere instruction of the Guru alone; rather, everyone attains everything only through their own exertion.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā: "Understanding through scripture, understanding one's own guru, and understanding one's own self— this is the restraint of the mind."
"These causes, when combined, are considered by the wise here [to be the means].
In the Vāsiṣṭha: 'O Rāma, the sequence of instruction is merely for the sake of maintaining order.'"
The sole cause for the recitation of mantras is the pure wisdom of the disciple alone—
[wisdom] from which all objects have been warded off and whose bonds have been cast aside.
No one can rescue another from distress except through their own fortitude—
whether by means of dispassion, scriptural wisdom, or qualities such as greatness.
One should personally uplift the mind with effort for the sake of warding off calamities;
this cannot be achieved through sovereignty over the three worlds, nor from the treasury of one who possesses wealth.
"The fruit is obtained from the mind when it is augmented by greatness.
Regarding *rājayoga*:
"Therefore, having obtained the innate [state] from a true guru, one should practice correctly."
It will come about effortlessly and constantly for one who practices with the self.
For one who is habituated to constant practice, that [reality] becomes self-evident;
it cannot be pointed out as "this is it," nor can it be described even by a teacher.
"One should diligently avoid the conjunction of speech, mind, and body;
one should always maintain the self very firmly with the thought, 'I am Brahman. — From the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
One should avoid intimacy with the wicked, traveling by carriage or on foot,
and likewise physical austerities such as bathing at dawn and fasting.
Excessive eating, over-exertion, excessive talk, adherence to rigid rules,
attachment to people, and idleness— by these six, yoga is destroyed.
Through enthusiasm, daring, fortitude, certainty regarding the knowledge of reality,
and the abandonment of association with worldly people— by these six, yoga is perfected.
"One should practice the entire procedure for the vital air (māruta) with a focused mind; otherwise, the wise person must not allow the mental faculty to function in any other way. (Ja.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "A woman is like glowing coals; a man is like a jar of ghee.
Therefore, one should diligently avoid association with women."
Just as one avoids association with women, one should diligently avoid the company of rogues, which constitutes a great obstacle.
As for the true nature of a rogue, it was stated by Dattātreya in the *Yogatattvaprakāśa*:
"Whether shaven-headed or carrying a staff, or even clad in ochre robes..."
The matted-haired ascetic, smeared with ashes, spoke these words of Nārāyaṇa.
Or, uttering "Namas Shivaya," one who is devoted to the worship of his own conduct,
purified by the twelve places, and adorned with many rosaries;
How can one who is devoid of action but brave in speech attain success? Neither the wearing of [ascetic] dress nor talk about it is the cause of success;
action alone is the cause of success—this is indeed the truth, O Sāṅkṛti.
For the sake of their genitals and bellies, those wearing the garb of practitioners speak of yoga.
But those hypocritical men, devoid of actual practice, deceive all people with their various kinds of empty talk; they are experts in such deception.
"‘We are yogis,’ say those fools who are devoted to worldly enjoyment;
likewise, the wise man [should treat] those who are devoid of the practice of yoga, step by step."
One who has accomplished his purpose should avoid those who merely wear the outward garb by means of words alone,
for they are always obstacles to the practice of yoga.
"Such wise men avoid them with great effort. Thus it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one who is without a wife, where is there any ground for enjoyment?"
Having abandoned a woman, one abandons the world; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the objects of the senses are the terrible poison.
Poison destroys but a single lifetime, whereas the objects of the senses destroy one across many births.
"While you dwell according to the scriptures, you must not be intent upon supernatural powers;
for after a long time, when they have fully matured, power will become abundant.
Thus [it is said] in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa regarding Alarka.
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear in truth concerning the yogin who, following the path of Brahman, does not falter. Dattātreya said:
Suffering arises from the fault of attachment for those whose minds are clung to the sense of "mine";
therefore, a man seeking liberation should diligently abandon attachment.
Through the dissolution of attachment, the coming together [of the elements] ceases, and the loss of this manifestation occurs;
freedom from possessiveness leads to happiness, and through dispassion, one perceives the defects [of worldly existence].
Detachment arises from knowledge alone, and knowledge is preceded by detachment;
that is a true home where one dwells, and that is true sustenance by which one lives.
That alone which leads to liberation is called knowledge; otherwise, it is ignorance.
O King, [this occurs] through the exhaustion of merits and demerits by means of experience.
Furthermore, because one performs the obligatory duties that ought to be done and not those performed for specific desires,
there is no accumulation of new *apūrva* and the exhaustion of what was previously acquired.

Through action a man incurs bondage to the body, yet not [to liberation]. These two— honor and dishonor— which cause pleasure and agitation in men, become the very causes of success for the yogin when their effects are reversed.
Honor and dishonor, when abandoned, are themselves said to be poison and nectar.
In that regard, dishonor is nectar, while honor is a most virulent poison.
One should set down one's foot purified by sight, and drink water purified by a cloth.
One should speak words purified by truth and reflect upon that which is purified by the intellect,
especially during the reception of guests, at ancestral rites, at sacrifices, and during festivals dedicated to the gods.
For the sake of attaining success among the great multitude, the knower of yoga should never make a request,
lest people should despise him and treat him with contempt.
Thus, the yogi should practice with diligence, not defiling the dharma of the virtuous;
he should cultivate that essence of knowledge which accomplishes what is to be done.
This multiplicity of knowledges is indeed an obstacle to yoga;
for one who should wander about thirsting with the thought, "this is to be known, this is to be known," [is hindered].
Even in thousands of eons, one would never attain knowledge [of this].
The three are the restraint of speech, the restraint of action, and the restraint of mind.
He for whom those three staffs are ever-restrained is a great ascetic possessing the triple-staff;
he for whom this entire world, both existent and non-existent, is composed of the Self alone.
For him who consists of both virtue and vice, who is dear and who is not?
With purified intellect, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, he dwells composedly among all beings.
That supreme, eternal, and imperishable state—
having gone there, one is indeed not born again.
Concentrated in mind, devoted to Brahman, free from worldly delight, pure, delighting in solitude, and having conquered the senses—
the great-souled one shall attain this yoga.
And from that, through yoga, he attains liberation.
O King of kings, a yogi intent on attaining perfection should practice yoga when he is neither bloated, nor hungry, nor fatigued, and when his mind is not distracted.
Having covered the activity of *tamas* with *rajas*, and likewise that of *rajas* with *sattva*,
the knower of yoga, established in the stainless reality (*tattva*), should practice yoga.
All this has been fully explained to you, O Ālarka, as it truly is;
now learn from me in brief that Brahman by which [all this] is attained.
Just as the moonstone releases water through contact with the rays of the moon,
yet does not do so when unjoined [to them], this is remembered as the simile for the yogin.
Just as the sun-gem produces fire when joined with the rays of the sun,
though it is not [fire] by itself— that too is a simile for the yogin.

O King of kings, where ants, rats, mongooses, house-lizards, and *kapiṅgalā* creatures dwell in a house as if it were their own master's home, there is no harm to them when that house collapses; this, O Lord of men, is the analogy for the attainment of yoga.
That house is one where one dwells; that is food by which one lives;
that is one's own by which one accomplishes one's purpose—what self-interest or sense of "mine" can there be in this?
Just as the body performs its functions through the organs even when they are fully surrendered to it,
so too the yogi should accomplish the supreme goal by means of the intellect and other faculties, which belong to another.
Even an ant, though possessing a tiny body and an extremely minute mouth, can lift a heap of earth;
this very ant serves as a metaphor for the yogi.
As the yogin ascends from the earth upon a vessel filled with substance,
beholding the lofty path, his higher discernment is thereby elevated.
Having beheld the supreme form of the blue crow, which is like that of a young ruru deer,
the yogi who grows together with it shall attain perfection.

"Having truly understood that exertion which a man makes toward his entire wealth when it is buried for the sake of survival, the yogi achieves the state of having accomplished all that was to be done. (P.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One who is not excessively satiated, nor afflicted by hunger, nor oppressed by the urge to void excrement or urine [should perform the rite]."
One who knows yoga should practice yoga neither when exhausted by travel nor when afflicted by anxiety.
"The yogi who is disciplined in diet and conduct, disciplined in his activities, and disciplined in sleep and wakefulness, attains the Reality. — *Bhagavadgītā* (6.17).
"Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all;
it is not for him who is habitually addicted to excessive sleep, nor for him who is ever awake, O Arjuna!"
For one who is moderate in diet and recreation, disciplined in actions,
and regulated in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
O Arjuna, he who, by means of self-mastery, sees equality everywhere—
whether it be pleasure or pain— that yogi is considered supreme.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Well-composed during the final watch of the night and the first watch of the day,
as well as during the forenoon and midday, one who is moderate in diet and has conquered the senses [should practice]."
The connection is that one should practice yoga.
Yājñavalkya says:
"A man who has indigestion, nor one who is belching, nor one oppressed by the urge to void excrement or urine [should not practice]."
One who has not vomited, nor suffered from diarrhea, nor overeaten, nor is overcome by fatigue [should take it].

"One should not practice when intent on excessive work, when the senses are agitated by anxiety, when engaged in important duties, when excessively hungry or thirsty, nor when there is bodily affliction or the onset of dejection and the like. Thus it is said.
In the Vāyupurāṇa,
immediately after the prohibitions beginning with "never when afflicted by a new disease," it is stated:
Having ascertained these faults, he who indeed yokes himself to them through negligence—
His bodily humors, which cause obstacles, become aggravated;
and dullness, deafness, and even muteness arise.
Blindness, loss of memory, and likewise fever and disease—
these defects indeed flare up for one who employs [the senses] out of ignorance.
Therefore, a yogi who is disciplined, concentrated, and ever vigilant through pure knowledge shall never incur any faults whatsoever.
In the Mahābhārata: "O lord of men, a yogi should never apply himself to yoga at the three times [of day] during the voiding of urine, the voiding of feces, or while eating."
Just as a vigilant archer, being fully concentrated, hits the target,
so too a yogi who is properly disciplined attains liberation without doubt.

Likewise, when disciplined, this self, being disciplined and motionless like the earth,
makes the self stainless, appearing like the sun.
And just as a focused helmsman, O son of Kuntī, best of kings,
would swiftly lead a ship upon the great ocean,
even so the knower of reality, disciplined in yoga, is intent on the concentration of the self.
O King, having abandoned this body, he attains a state that is difficult to reach.
Vyāsa says:
"The wise know that there are five faults of yoga which must be completely eradicated.
Lust, anger, greed, fear, and fifthly, sleep.
One conquers anger through tranquility and desire by abandoning volitional thought;
by cultivating purity, the wise man ought to eradicate sleep.
One should guard the genitals and the belly with fortitude, and the hands and feet with the eyes;
one should guard the eyes and ears with the mind, and the mind and speech with action. One should abandon fear through heedfulness, and pride by attending upon the wise.
Thus, one should daily recite these defects of yoga, remaining unattached to them.
Having made the mind and the senses one-pointed and composed,
he should fix the mind upon the Self during the first and last watches of the night.
Restraining the collection of his senses as one would guard a treasury from impurities, the sage, being self-controlled, should practice yoga at the three periods of the day.
One should constantly contemplate with one-pointed focus and not cause the mind to recoil from yoga;
by whatever means possible, one should strive to restrain the flickering mind.
One should practice that with diligence and never deviate from it;
one should not engage with others through speech, action, or even thought.
Equanimous and moderate in diet, he should remain the same whether obtaining or not obtaining [alms];
he should neither rejoice in praise nor feel aversion toward blame;
and regarding both of these, he should not dwell upon their auspicious or inauspicious nature.
One should not rejoice in gains, nor should one dwell upon losses.
Thus, for the virtuous man who is self-abiding, who perceives equality everywhere,
and who is constantly disciplined for six months, he transcends the Brahman of sound.
"In this interval on the path, one should not cease, nor be deluded.
Thus, since yoga does not succeed in the absence of the proper place and time, those two are first defined.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"Only after having secured a suitable place should one perform the limbs of yoga according to the Vaikrama method; for the realization of yoga does not occur in an improper place or time."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"When the existence [of an object] is not established, and when it is devoid of space and time, the perception of that which is non-existent occurs in yoga; therefore, one should avoid that."
A yogi devoted to meditation should not practice during these times: when it is excessively cold, nor when it is excessively hot, nor during the dualities consisting of fire and wind.
In a place where there is noise, upon the superimposition of fire or water, in a dilapidated cow-pen, in a temple of Śiva, on a heap of dry leaves,
by a river, in a cremation ground, or where reptiles dwell;
"One who knows the truth should avoid the practice of yoga in these places: in a dangerous spot, on the bank of a well, at a shrine, or on an anthill."— *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Not near water or fire, not in a dilapidated forest or a cow-pen,
not in a place swarming with gadflies and mosquitoes, nor at a shrine or a crossroads.

"One should not practice in a place defiled by hair, ashes, husks, charcoal, bones, and the like; nor in a place with a foul odor, nor in a place crowded with people. Thus it is stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* and other texts.
Immediately following the prohibition beginning with, "Not on ground that is impure, infested by flies, or swarming with mosquitoes," etc., it is said in that same [text]:
"I shall declare the defects that arise as obstacles for that fool who, out of delusion, performs [the rite] while disregarding these aforementioned faults."
Deafness, dullness, loss of memory, muteness, blindness, and cough arise instantly; likewise, these same afflictions arise for one who is joined with ignorance.
"Therefore, the knower of yoga must always protect [the body] with every means,
since the body is the instrument for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Thus [it is said].
Dattātreya—
after stating the prohibitions regarding place and time, and having described the defects such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and so forth that arise from negligence, he speaks of their remedy:
"If these defects should occur to yogins due to negligence, [then] the remedy is as follows..."
Listen to me as I explain what must be done by the yogi for their destruction.
Having consumed very warm, unctuous gruel, one should retain it right there;
such is the procedure for the pacification of vāta-gulma and likewise for udāvarta.
One should likewise cast a gruel toward the wind to counteract a wind-knot;
similarly, during a tremor, one should fix the mind upon a great, immovable mountain.

In the case of a failure of speech, one should meditate on the organ of speech; in the case of deafness, on the faculty of hearing; and likewise, one afflicted by thirst should meditate on a sour fruit in the case of the faculty of taste.
In whichever part of the body there is pain, one should apply a concentration (dhāraṇā) that is counteractive to it:
cooling concentration upon heat, and heating concentration upon cold.
Having placed a kīla upon the head, one should strike wood with wood;
by that means, memory is immediately restored to the yogin whose memory has been lost.
One should offer oblations to Heaven and Earth, and to Vāyu and Agni, who are all-pervading;
these are the remedies for non-human beings, species of creatures, and afflictions.
If a non-human being or an inner yogin should enter [the body],
these two— retention of breath and retention of fire— will utterly consume it while it remains within the body.

"Thus, O King, the knower of yoga must protect his body with all his soul, since the body is the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Now, those [duties] prescribed for him are being set forth; therein, time has been mentioned previously and will be discussed further.
In the Ādipurāṇa:
"In solitary mountain fastnesses, in the caves of temples of the gods..."
Those who know the truth understand that the practice of yoga must be performed.
Yājñavalkya says:
"Having reached a penance grove well-provided with fruits, roots, and water, there,
in a delightful and pure place resounding with the chanting of the Veda— "
It was filled with those who were devoted to their own duties, peaceful, and knowers of Brahman;
it was well-provided with water and endowed with various kinds of flowers.
In a place abundant with fruits and roots, which grants the fulfillment of all desires—
whether it be a temple, a riverbank, a village, or even a city.
One should construct a very beautiful hut with a narrow door and lacking external splendor,
well-smeared with cow dung or completely plastered with lime.
"One should construct a very beautiful hermitage that bestows the fruits of all desires.
The connection with the following clause is: "In that [hermitage], one should practice yoga. As stated in the *Yogatattvaprakāśa*:
One should construct a very beautiful hermitage with a narrow door and devoid of glare,
carefully plastered with either mud or lime.
It was always free from flies, mosquitoes, and gadflies;
it was diligently swept with a broom day after day,
perfumed with fragrant scents, and incensed with guggulu and other aromatics.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā:
"In a kingdom with a good king, in a righteous land, where food is plentiful and free from calamities,
the practitioner of Haṭha Yoga should reside in the midst of a solitary hut."
It should have a small door, a narrow opening, and a deep pit; it should not be too high or too low,
well-smeared with thick cow dung, spotless, and free from all living creatures.
"On the exterior, it is constructed with a pavilion, a well, and an altar, and is surrounded by a wall;
this is described as the characteristic of a yoga-maṭha by the Siddhas who practice Haṭha."— Thus in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"In that place which is free from all affliction, which brings pleasure to all the senses,
which generates serenity of mind, and which is made fragrant by the scent of garlands and incense"—
thus it is said in the Nandipurāṇa.
The temple was beautifully arranged, charming, and scented with perfumes;
it was adorned with fragrant flowers and the sweet aroma of incense.

The wise man should construct a beautiful yoga-hall by an auspicious path, adorned with sacred fords, rivers, trees, lotus ponds, and mountains, decorated with various types of paintings resembling the work of a master artist.

Likewise: "Having seen the peaceful sages depicted in a painting, and having seen the perfected ones (siddhas) depicted in a painting, the mind becomes inclined toward tranquility; having seen the perfected ones depicted in a painting, the intellect shall be directed toward spiritual exertion."
Then, in the center of the yoga-chamber, one should draw the maṇḍala of cyclic existence (saṃsāra);
and in some place, one should also draw a most terrible cremation ground and the hells.
Having seen those terrifying forms and that saṃsāra devoid of essence,
the yogi who desires accomplishment becomes free from despondency.

"And beholding living beings afflicted by disease, and those who have died from various causes—remaining thus with a pure soul in an auspicious yoga-hall"—the connection is "one should practice the limbs of yoga. This very definition of a yoga-maṭha is also stated in the *Liṅga Purāṇa* and other texts. Because the regulation of diet is extremely conducive to yoga by way of purifying the channels (*nāḍī*), and because the practice of yoga is forbidden for one whose mental essence (*sattva*) is unpurified due to impurity of diet, [this is prescribed] always.

We understand from the injunction regarding the practice of conduct (*cārābhyāsa*) that whenever there is hunger, one must eat at that very time. It is not proper to neglect knowledge—which is the primary element in comparison to everything else—merely out of regard for eating at a single fixed time, which is merely an auxiliary to knowledge. This is according to the maxim: "In a conflict between the primary and the secondary, the primary is stronger. For this very reason, in all other Upanishads, no restriction on the timing of meals is prescribed for practitioners of yoga. Thus it is said: "A Paramahaṃsa may eat once a day or twice a day."
"In whatever manner possible, the ascetic (*yati*) should be devoted to the practice of knowledge.

Here, the word *yati* is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all three stages of life (*āśrama*). Now, that which must necessarily be known by the yogi within the body is being described; for without the knowledge of that, there is no accomplishment of yoga. And so says Gorakṣa:
"The six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), the sixteen supports (*ṣoḍaśādhāra*), the two lakhs [of channels], and the five voids (*vyomapañcaka*)."

"How can those who do not know [this] within their own bodies become perfected yogins? Thus, the six cakras and sixteen ādhāras will be described. There are two hundred thousand [channels], both external and internal. These include the earth, the nose, and so forth, as well as the mūlādhāra and the others. As for the five voids (*vyomapañcaka*), they extend from the heart, the throat, the palate, the brow, to the aperture [of the crown]. This body is supported by the "well-supported single pillar" and the nine chambers through the mind; therefore, the mind itself is of the nature of the pillar. In the mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, and viśuddha [cakras], there reside, in order, the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
"By what means can the channels (nāḍīs) of all embodied beings be purified? What is the origin of the channels, and how is their retention performed according to rule?
Of what nature is the aggregate (skandha) said to be, and how many vital airs (vāyus) abide?"
And also the locations of the winds, and their respective functions individually.
O foremost among those who bear bodies, you ought to explain all those things that are to be known within this body;
for there exists no knower superior to you.
Having been addressed thus by his wife, Gārgī, with his mind fully absorbed in that matter,
looked at her and spoke all of this.
O beloved, know that the body of all living beings consists of exactly ninety-six finger-breadths measured by their own fingers.
The vital breath (prāṇa) extends twelve finger-breadths beyond the body;
some of the best of sages say it is fourteen finger-breadths.
Wise men say that it is exactly twelve finger-breadths in length;
[therein reside] prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
Nāga, Karma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
these forceful winds move through all the channels.
"Among these, five principal winds beginning with prāṇa are traditionally taught.
Among those, O best of men, these two—prāṇa and apāna—are the most important;
yet of these two, prāṇa alone is always the primary one for all living beings. Thus it is said.
The purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*) will be explained later. In the *Nakulīśayogapāra*, it is said:
"The tortoise-breath (*kaurma-vāyu*), through the differentiation of functions such as inhalation (*prāṇana*) and so forth, [proceeds] in due order."
"He has attained other names such as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and so forth. Thus it is said.
And in the *Amṛtasiddhi*:
"Although it is stated that there are innumerable winds in the body,"
Nevertheless, both Prāṇa and Apāna have been made the supreme performers.
Yājñavalkya says:
"In the middle of the mouth and nose, in the middle of the heart, and in the middle of the navel..."
Some say that the abode of the vital breaths is in the big toe of the foot.
Below and above the Kuṇḍalī, the one known as Prāṇa stands on all sides;
within these four, it illuminates like a lamp.
Some indeed say that the abode of the apāna wind is in the anus, the penis, the thighs,
the knees, the belly, the eyes, the hips, the shanks, and the navel.
Vyāna resides in the ears, the middle of the eyes, the hump [of the back], and also in the two ankles;
it stays in the throat, the pharynx, and the region of the buttocks—of this there is no doubt.
The *udāna* resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet and hands;
the *samāna* is established as all-pervasive throughout all the limbs.
Having consumed all flavors during the night,
it circulates through the seventy-two thousand channels of the body along with the fire.
The single samāna-vāyu alone, having pervaded its own fire,
is situated everywhere throughout the body along with its limbs and sub-limbs, together with the flames.
The five winds, beginning with the naga-wind, reside within the skin, bones, and other parts;
they equalize the water and food located in the stomach, as well as the chyle and other bodily constituents.
The vital breath, situated within the tandaka, should perform those [actions] individually:
one should place water above the fire, and food and other items upon the water.
Having reached the downward-moving breath (apāna), the vital air (māruta) blows together with it;
then the prāṇa, situated in the middle, again moves toward the fire.
Then, O best of brahmins, by means of the apāna wind,
the fire gradually blazes up throughout the entire interior of the body.
Then, ignited by that flame and impelled by the vital breath (prāṇa),
it made the water extremely hot while it was situated within the interior of the stomach.
The food, combined with condiments and placed upon the water,
was then thoroughly cooked by the fire through the heated water.
In the water of sweat and urine, there would be form and potency; taste would also be present.
O Gārgī! Food becomes feces; the prāṇa distributes it separately, along with the samāna wind, throughout all the channels.
And through the nine apertures of the void, there is the discharge of feces, urine, and so forth.
All the winds act continuously within the bodies, producing inhalation, exhalation, and coughing; this is celebrated as the function of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The function of the apāna-vāyu is the discharge of feces, urine, and so forth;
the activity of the vyāna-vāyu is also held to include the efforts of relinquishing and grasping.
That which is called udāna-karma is said to exist in the body like the eyes and other organs;
the function of samāna is proclaimed to be drying and so forth within the body.
That which possesses qualities such as belching is declared to be the function of Nāga;
the closing of the eyes and so forth belongs to Kūrma, and sneezing to Kṛkara.
"O best of Brahmins! The act of yawning is proclaimed as the function of Devadatta;
the functions of Dhananjaya, such as beauty and so forth, are fully proclaimed.
Likewise, for all five [vāyus], beginning with Prāṇa... there are no seed-syllables for the castes in the *Nakulīśagaparāyaṇa*."
The prāṇa is situated from the tip of the nose to the heart, the navel, and the big toe;
it is applied by means of the seed-syllables beginning with *nīla*, *...*, *kāra*, and *repha*.
Kṛṣṇa is the apāna wind, situated in the throat (kṛkaṭi), extending to the back, the end of the spine, and the heels;
he is joined with the seed-syllable ending in the letter 'na', namely Tāraka (nam).
Resembling Indra’s bow, it is the abode of the sense of touch;
endowed with stars and resplendent with the brilliance of its seed-syllable.

The udāna breath, possessing the luster of the rising sun and endowed with the beauty of the edge of a star, resides at the crown of the head, the middle of the palate, the tips of the fingers, and the soles of the feet.
White, pervasive, residing in the heart, the navel, and all the joints,
it is exceedingly radiant by means of the seed-syllable ending in the letter *la* (va) preceded by the *praṇava*.

The letter *ya* is the beginning of the syllable *repha*; that *ya*, together with the syllable *oṃ*, is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of *prāṇa*. This means that the letter *va*, which is the end of the syllable *la* and is preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, is the seed-syllable of *samāna*. In all these instances, it should be understood that the specific colors such as blue and so forth are mentioned for the purpose of meditation on the forms of the vital airs (*vāyu*). Yājñavalkya says:
"In the center of the body is the seat of fire, shining like molten gold."
The triangle belongs to humans, while the square belongs to quadrupeds.
This is the truth I tell you regarding the circle of moths:
in its center, the slender flame of fire always remains.
If you wish to hear where the center of the body is, listen:
two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis—
this is declared to be the center of the body.
The location of the bulb (kanda) for human beings is nine finger-breadths from the middle of the body;
it is four finger-breadths in width and likewise in length.
Having a form shaped like an egg and adorned with skin and so forth,
it resides in the middle of the belly of quadrupeds, animals, and birds.
In the midst of that is what is called the navel; from the navel arises the wheel, which possesses twelve spokes, and upon it the body is established.
Driven by merit and demerit, the living being revolves upon this wheel.
Just as a spider moves about within the midst of its web of threads.
In this mūlādhāra-cakra, this vital breath (prāṇa) moves below;
mounted upon the prāṇa, the individual soul (jīva) exists at all times within all bodies.
Above that, at the level of the navel, is the seat of Kuṇḍalinī, situated obliquely and extending downward;
she consists of the eightfold primordial nature and is coiled eight times.
The movement of the vital airs (vāyu) as it truly is, as well as water, food, and so forth—
all these remain constantly obstructed on all sides around the roots of the bulb (kanda).
Having likewise enveloped the opening of the *brahmarandhra* with the mouth itself,
at the time of yoga, it attains awakening through the downward breath (*apāna*) and the fire (*vahni*).
Vibrating in the space of the heart, brilliant as a serpent,
the vital breath (vāyu) then proceeds through the suṣumṇā channel by means of its friend, the wind.
The channel situated in the middle of the bulb is celebrated as Suṣumnā;
all those known as channels stand surrounding this wheel.
Of all the channels as well, O Gārgī, fourteen are principal:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, and Sarasvatī.
Vāruṇī, Puṣā, Hastijihvā,
Payasvinī, Viśvodarī, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and Yaśasvinī.
Alambuṣā and Gāndhārī—these are the fourteen principal ones.
Among them, three are the most principal; of these three, one is considered the supreme.
That is called Suṣumnā, the sustainer of the universe, which is said to be the path to liberation.
In the central path of the body, the Suṣumṇā is well-established;
it stands upright together with the bone situated along the spinal column.
She is called the path to liberation (muktimārga) and is celebrated as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
She alone is to be known as the unmanifest (avyaktā), subtle (sūkṣmā), and remembered as belonging to Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇavī).
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:

"Suṣumnā, the path of the void (*śūnyapadavī*), the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the great path (*mahāpatha*), the cremation ground (*śmaśānī*), the state of Śambhu (*śāmbhavī*), and the path of Brahman (*brahmamārga*)—these are synonymous terms. Here, the status of Suṣumnā as the path of liberation is established by the *Chāndogya* Śruti cited below: "Going upwards through those two, one attains immortality. Because it is the support for the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) that serves as the gateway to liberation, it is therefore designated by the name "Avimukta" (the Unreleased), just like Kāśī.

And so it has been said in the *Kāśīmīmāṃsā*: "There are three kinds of non-liberation (*avimukta*)," as stated in the Sūtra—"namely, the internal (*ādhyātmika*), the divine (*adhidaivika*), and the elemental (*ādhibhautika*)"; and this is also shown in the *Skanda Purāṇa* regarding the internal non-liberation: "Jābāli said: 'O Āruṇi, you are the *Ṛiḍā*; the *Piṅgalā* is considered Varuṇā; the *Naḍī* is within that, and it is the Avimuktaka. Likewise: 'That supreme *Suṣumnā* is the *Naḍī*, while this [city] is Vārāṇasī.'"
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa* as well, because this very [place] bestows liberation by virtue of being delimited by various specific locations, those locations are declared to be *Avimukta*:
"It is designated as *Vimukta* in the middle of the eyebrows, in the middle of the navel, in the heart, and in the head; likewise, it is proclaimed in the Sun and in Vārāṇasī."
"Likewise, between the Varaṇā and this [Asi], there is the city named Vārāṇasī.

And here, the word *avimukta* is synonymous with the word *vimukta*. Thus, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: just as the word *vimukta* is established in the *ādhidaivika* sense in the form of the junction of heaven and earth belonging to the son of Aditi (the Sun); and just as it is established in the *ādhibhautika* sense in the city known as Vārāṇasī situated in the middle of Vārāṇasī; so too, in the *ādhyātmika* sense, it is established in the region of the Suṣumnā, delimited by specific *cakras* at the center of the eyebrows, the heart, and the head. — Yājñavalkya, p. 107.
The Iḍā and the Piṅgalā are on its left and right sides respectively;

[This is achieved] at the base of the penis by the contraction of the staff-like body.

That which is the *lamvikā*, made long by means of shaking and milking from the reverse path,

This is the khecarīmudrā; its essential nature and its power will be described in the section on mudrās. If one places the tongue beneath the support of the palate and makes it touch the vault of the sky, the taste of nectar is attained therein and poetic skill becomes manifest.
The twelfth [sign] is the support for the ten [vital breaths], and its summit is the royal staff;

There, at the root of the nose, the gaze is made steady;

The wise one should move that sixteen-fold support of the eyes upward;

Now, regarding the six chakras in Sāṃkhya-yoga:

Viśuddhi is located in the region of the throat, and Ājñā is situated between the eyebrows.

Having avoided his own path, that moon, the jewel of the sky,

The fourfold refinement that proceeds within this womb,

By the mere binding of it, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish.
Those mantras which have been severed, obstructed, shaken, or paralyzed;

Meditators, those joined with Brahman, the cursed, the fainted, and the slain;

When joined with this procedure and applied by the Guru, all of them will, without long delay, become bestowers of both supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mokṣa).

There, having meditated upon Śakti at the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Pūrṇagiri,

"Through the awakening of the central power (*madhyaśakti*), supreme bliss arises.
This fruit has been explained in detail in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
"Now, I shall describe here the lotuses of the foundations (*ādhāra*)."

I shall briefly describe those situated within the Suṣumṇā, as well as the deities residing upon the petals of that lotus, the color of that lotus, and the Goddess who is its support. Regarding the "Lotus without Knot" (Ajagranthi-padma) which was previously mentioned by me, they say here that it is the primordial support.
