Upon these four petals, one should place the goddesses Niruddhā, Dajalā, and Virṇā, either individually or all together.

By the constant practice of meditation on the *mūlādhāra* upon the *hākinī* deities—the blazing drops (*bindu*) of power with flickering light—these excellent qualities arise for men in due order: paralysis, agitation, leaping like a frog, leaving the earth, and the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*). Furthermore, there is the excellence of luster in the body, the manifestation of sound, the kindling of the digestive fire, lightness of limb, acuity of one's own senses, health, and freedom from wretchedness.

By making the mind motionless within the center of the root-cakra through mere devotion, men speak of the past, the present, and the future, as well as scriptures they have never heard. Immediately abandoning the lotus-mouth of Brahmā, which is filled with waves of affection, Sarasvatī, assuming a divine form, dances within the interior of that [practitioner’s] own lotus-mouth. Having attained mastery over the mantra of the Lord of Tastes (Rasendra) and having conquered even time, which is so difficult to restrain, they reach the state of agelessness and immortality, and finally rejoice with delight in the station of supreme bliss.

In the beginning, the entire world was submerged in the waters of a single ocean; then there appeared the primordial form of Light, whose majesty was exalted within itself, existing in the form of a *liṅga*. The Great Lord (*Maheśa*), the swan that destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence (*bhava*), is the soul presided over by the six Siddhas, praised by all the gods, endowed with six faces and six sheaths (*kośas*). From the Blessed One, who bore the body of the primordial *liṅga*, the god Brahmā (*Dvirada*) arose. Vāṇī (Sarasvatī) became the eastern face of Śiva, and Mahākāla became his upper face.
The god Piṇākī, the consumer of oblations, became his southern mouth;
the blessed Lord Chagalaṇḍa became his western mouth; and he became his northern mouth.
At the base of the banner, there is a water-born lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna,
consisting of six petals; upon it is the orb of the rising sun, marked by the letters from *ṭa* to *kṣa* starting from the back,
their heads illuminated by the *bindu*, belonging to the Blessed Lord who is the trident-bearing Liṅga.
This place is the sphere of the best of yogis, and its presiding deity is Rākiṇī.
Here, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, by the power of his own innate *catura* (skill/awareness),
the excellent practitioner, his heart stilled by a flood of gentle bliss,
becomes like a ball of clay upon the surface of the earth for the gazelle-eyed women.
He whose side-glances are smiling with passion delights the hosts, his form suffused with splendor; here, having fixed his own mind upon the various and lofty web of scriptures he has heard,
the Avadhūta— having cast off old age and disease, capable and free from the fear of death— lives for a very long time.

The cool-rayed moon, firmly established within the body—which is a vessel of perpetual impurity—brings about the supreme purification for men; and from the lotus of the sky, the great mercury (mahārasendra) suddenly moves toward the lotus-eyed one (Viṣṇu). Those virtuous ones who hold this secret here are indeed the steadfast and supreme among men. Just as a great lordly elephant, its temples washed with rut, comes under control through gradual means, so too that powerful and futile force here, when restrained by stages, inevitably becomes subject to one’s own will.
In this yoga of the Vajra-axe, dissolution first arises for those devoted to it;
from passion, for those who wield the staff of the senses, consciousness is acquired through the power of dissolution.
And for men who partake of the flowing great essence of the internal blue, [consciousness arises] from the dissolution of the mind.
The rising moon of innate bliss, appearing under the guise of a gentle smile, has manifested.
Men who constantly meditate upon that which resides at the navel in the ten-petalled Maṇipūra lotus— resembling blue collyrium,
endowed with the ten syllables beginning with *ṭa* and *ḍa* located on the petals and topped by radiant *bindus*,
and perpetually presided over by Lākinī— attain liberation alone.
They perform subjugation, summoning, neutralizing poison, causing earthquakes, and so forth.

In this place, the minds of the virtuous are fixed; it grants supreme success in the netherworld (pātāla), serves as a means for attaining the incomparable heaven, and fulfills whatever is desired on earth.
It bestows beauty, the power to leave the earth, and the ability to enter the bodies of others, while overcoming old age—
It is the alleviation of all suffering and disease, or the deception of Time itself.
In the heart,
the wise describe that which is called the "unstruck" (anāhata) as being like a cluster of golden sindūra and indragopa insects at twilight, beautified by sixteen petals.
It is endowed with twelve Bhairavas beginning with Krodhīśa, along with the Staff (daṇḍa) and Maṇḍicandavīrya;
it is presided over by Kākinī through divine power, and eternally by the Goddess, the Haṃsa, and the Lord.
With their minds constantly absorbed in this state, the yogis remain stationed in that celestial palace; yet divine women, endowed with most wondrous forms and beauty, disturb them.
Their incomparable knowledge, which has the three times as its object, is shaken by the report of the city.
From afar indeed there is a vision, and the meeting with the Yoginī shall occur after a long journey.
Then, at the throat, there is a pure, unchanging lotus with sixteen petals, joined by the intensely smoky [syllables] encircled by the lords beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha.
In this place resides the Goddess Bhagavatī, the Śākinī, whose innate power is incomparable; she is eternally present as the one who pacifies the distress of those who seek refuge.
For the preeminent man who is ever-peaceful and established here through the yoga of practice, [she remains].
There would be competence on this earth even in the absence of the existence of studied scriptures.
A person whose mind is fixed on this place becomes a seer of the three times, free from disease,
and having conquered old age with hair as black as collyrium, he wanders upon the earth living beyond death.
In this state, having constantly fixed the mind and restrained the vital breath, even if the yogi becomes angry, he can shake the entire three worlds;
yet neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Hari, nor Hara, nor even the Sun-god [can do so].
Even Gaṇeśa is not capable of quelling this power of his:
his command is a pair of sandals, shining like the rays of the autumnal moon, which fell between the two eyebrows from the pair of his dancing feet.
Having uttered "Hākinī," one should also remember the two final letters, illuminated by a bindu, within the pair of petals here, O Goddess;
for one devoted to the yoga of meditation, there arises the recollection of the actions performed in previous births.
In the field of the abode of the *bindu*, there is the capacity for seeing and hearing from afar.
Here, with the fluctuations of his own mind focused upon it, he engages in a dialogue with the image;
furthermore, he causes men to go to other cities and even brings back to life those who have died.
Having learned the supportless mudrā solely from the mouth of one's own guru,
the excellent practitioner, with his intellect firmly fixed, remains bound right here.
Through constant practice, one beholds the entire multitude of stars within the abode of the immortals,
as well as the station of Viṣṇu and the Lord of the stars.
To Brahmā, whose pair of feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods; likewise to Mukunda;
to Śambhu, the leader of the divine assemblies; also to the Lord of the Pretas and the Lord of the Waters;
to Agni, the lord of day; to Pavana and Tārkṣya, and to the Lord of the Yakṣas.
Even the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, and the renowned Siddhas who are honored by the Guru.

The yogi constantly beholds that very mountain of gold, with its waters perpetually filled with waves high with various colors and its sands strewn with golden sand; and he also sees the lovely-limbed woman,
who bends under the weight of her lofty, full breasts, whose passion is aroused by love, and who is slow with child.
With a pair of shimmering eyes like those of a startled young doe, and with tremulous glances, she likewise surpassed the celestial nymphs.
Yakṣas, the foremost of Rākṣasas, and Mūrdhānas, as well as those of eternally auspicious form;
Vidyādharas adorned with the beauty of the crescent moon and the skull, and the Mothers— all these were present upon the lofty peaks that shrouded the expanse of the sky and all directions.
He beheld excellent mountains adorned with shining ornaments of various jewels and bracelets.
The surface of the sky was made delightful even by the *sāraṅga* deer,
while the earth was likewise heavy with its various fields;
[the ocean] was filled with high waves and multitudes of serpents, *makaras*, and elephants.
Even by means of terrifying clouds, the best of mountains,
and likewise the oceans, rivers, and streams filled with masses of water, [the world was not equal to it].
He saw the Sahasrālī river, as well as the lake filled with water and frequented by cranes.
The new mass of clouds— moving like swans, bordered by ospreys, dark as water near the trunks of elephants,
possessing a network of peacock feathers, favorable to the beautiful earth, and bringing an end to the traveler’s exile.
In this supreme, most wonderful, immutable, and great place— the sole source of bliss— one should fix the mind steadily upon the Supreme by means of the mudrā.
The yogin gradually attains identity with that through a mind free of support;
thereafter, by the power of absorption into his own great bliss, it manifests within.
When the mind has become dissolved there in that abode of the universe, first sparks like those of fire are seen; and immediately thereafter, a splendor appears that rivals the shimmering moonlight—
the Eternal Bliss, the Lord of Śrī, the Blessed Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person.
He whose greatness is inconceivable, who is meditated upon by yogis as the "Self"—
in this place, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ruler, the imperishable, becomes manifest.
The witness, who has entered within the innermost core of the worlds, is that very station, that supreme state;
having placed the vital breath there, those wise men, through the departure of their life-breath,
sport in that supreme, ancient Person, the Seer who is to be known through the Vedanta.
They constantly enter the all-encompassing Lord, the sole root of great bliss,
within the thousand-petaled lotus situated below the organ of emission, facing downward with its mass of filaments reddened.
Within that [lotus] is the moon, possessing three peaks like those of Mount Triśṛṅga, shimmering with a network of jewels and nectar.
Within that is the extremely subtle Brahmarandhra, which serves as the support for the nāḍī called Suṣumṇā;
this state is divine, exceedingly secret, inaccessible even to the gods, and must be guarded with great effort.
This is the supreme abode of the Kula known as Kailāsa, whose very form is the Bindu and whose nature is the Self;

there dwells the God of gods, Maheśa, who destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence. He is the primordial source of all beings, his head is a continuous stream of rays radiating with the essence of nectar, and he is the most exalted.
Is he not the one who pours forth a stream of nectar, bestowing desired fruits upon yogis and being attainable through yoga?
By the mere knowledge of this place, for men there shall be no further birth in this cycle of existence;
through the yoga of constant practice upon the assembly of elements, [one attains liberation].
And there shall be complete power to create and to destroy.
With his mind fixed here upon Kailāsa, which is the supreme abode and the dwelling place of Haṃsa;
The disease that has entered the yogi—caused by sin—is a mental affliction; he lives for a long time, liberated from death.
In this place dwells that sixteenth digit of the moon, free from the states of waning and waxing, eternally risen, facing downwards, possessing the luster of the rising sun,
yet subtler than even a single part of a hair-tip split a hundredfold.
And because it possesses subtlety and the vision of the Self, this internal Liṭ is a bearer of streams of nectar.
Beyond this stands the Blessed Lady, the sovereign goddess of the elements and so forth; she is known as Nirvāṇa, curved like a half-moon digit, and situated within the sixteenth [digit].
She is that which is formed by a single portion of a thousandfold-split morning sun.
Because of its subtlety, she who is the mother of the three worlds is like the radiance of twelve suns.
The supreme power of Nirvāṇa, situated above the collection of parts known as Nirvāṇa, possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns; it is profoundly deep,
equal to a ten-millionth part of the tip of a hair, the Mother of all, eternally manifest, and stainless.
A stream flowing from the moon of the pretext of the state of eternal bliss, born of the supportless.
Beyond this is the station of the power of Nirvāṇa, which is higher than the highest—the eternal, immeasurable, stainless, ever-arisen, and actionless state of Śiva.
The wise call that the station of Viṣṇu; some call it the station of Brahmā.

Having meditated in sequence with a concentrated heart upon the single [deity] who, together with the Self, has been placed from his abode in the Lotus-born one into various stations ending with the Command (ājñā)—some as the state of laughter, some as the stainless state, and some as the supportless—having repeatedly projected his power; (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion given.)
Having led [the breath] into the space between the seven lotuses of the sky-going lineage, which begins with the unmanifest (anādi) and ends with the unmanifest (asāna),
one should meditate upon the primordial Śakti, whose nature is consciousness, for the attainment of desired fruits.
Having directly entered the great palace situated on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, which resembles lac-dye in color, she who is like a swan resting upon a lotus,
yellow-hued, and possessing a flood of divine nectar, shall again enter the central region of the Kula.

One should satisfy those deities, beginning with Hākinī, by means of the flow of nectar-essence through the sequence of the wheels; one should satisfy that Kuṇḍalī who resides in the lotus of the heart.
Now, the six practices (*ṣaṭkarmāṇi*).
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "Dhautī, vasti, as well as netī, trāṭaka, naulī, and kapālabhāti."
The skull shines with these; they declare these to be the six rites.
This secret group of six actions, which effects the purification of the vessel and bestows a variety of virtues, is worshipped by the foremost among yogis.
Now, regarding purification (dhauta):
one should swallow a fine cloth four fingers wide; having swallowed it, one should withdraw it again. Through this practice, the act of purification is accomplished.
Cough, asthma, abdominal dropsy, skin diseases, and diseases of phlegm, as well as hemorrhoids—by the power of the *dhautī* practice, these surely vanish; of this there is no doubt.
Then,
the knower of the ritual, having placed his knees in water reaching up to the navel and sitting on a seat made of *nāka* grass,
should perform the contraction of the *ādhāra* [the perineum].
Even gulma, udara, and diseases arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha—
all such ailments are suppressed through the power of the enema (basti-karma).
It bestows clarity upon the elements, the senses, and the internal organs; it grants the luster of ghee and the brilliance of a blazing fire,
and it destroys the entire accumulation of defects.
The procedure of the water enema (jalavasti) being practiced.
One should insert a well-lubricated thread, one span in length, into the nasal passage and draw it out through the mouth; this is indeed declared by the masters of *netī* to be successful.
It is the purifier of the skull and the bestower of divine vision;
it is that which digests the flood of diseases born above, from head to foot.
Now, regarding *trāṭaka*:
One who is composed should gaze with a steady eye at a subtle object until it is overwhelmed by the falling of tears; that is considered *trāṭaka* by the noble ones.
The churning [of the eyes] is a bolt against eye diseases, drowsiness, and the like;
and this *trāṭaka* is to be kept secret, like a casket of gold.
Now, as for *naulī*:
with the force of a rapid whirling motion, one should rotate the abdomen from left to right and back again;
those who know the practice of yoga call this *naulī*.
It kindles the weak digestive fire, acts as the cooking fire for digestion, likewise bestows bliss upon those who are tormented,
and dries up all defects and diseases.
Indeed, this naulī is the crest-jewel of haṭha-yoga practices.
Now, as for Kapālabhātī:
like the bellows of blacksmiths, both the inhalation and exhalation are performed with equal rapidity.
Kapālabhātī is well-known for drying up the disorder of phlegm (kapha).
Now, regarding the mudrās in the *Pavanayogasaṃgraha*:
"The Mahāmudrā, the Mahābandha, the Mahāvedha, and the Khecarī."
Then follow *śakticāla*, *mūlabandha*, and *uḍḍīyāṇa*; after that, the bandha called *jālandhara*, and likewise *viparītakṛti*.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"He is like the leader of those ascending [the mountain], who is the support for the mountains, forests, and nurse-plants."
Kuṇḍalinī is indeed the foundation of all Yoga Tantras.
Awakened by the grace of the Guru, she who was asleep becomes the giver of happiness;
likewise, all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced asunder.
O King, the state of emptiness of the vital breath is such that it is like that of a snake;
likewise is the mind without support, and likewise is the deception of time.
Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort one should be intent on the practice of mudrās to awaken her who is asleep at the entrance of the door of Brahman.
Mahāmudrā, Mahābandha, Mahāvegha, and Khecarī;
Uḍḍīyāna, Mūlabandha, and that which is called Jālandhara.
The one called Karaṇīviparītā, as well as Vaiśakticālana—
this indeed is the ninefold mudrā, which is devoid of old age and death.
It was proclaimed by the Lord who is without beginning, bestowing the eightfold sovereign powers;
it is the beloved of all accomplishments and difficult even for the gods to attain.

It should be guarded with effort, like a casket of jewels; it must never be told to anyone, just as one would not speak of the sexual union of a low-born woman. Now, regarding Mahāmudrā, [it is said] in the Skanda:
The thorough purification of the network of channels, the joining of the moon and the sun,
and the complete drying up of the bodily fluids— this is designated as Mahāmudrā.
In the *Aiśvaraprokte*:
"I shall proclaim the Mahāmudrā, my own beloved, within this tantra—
that which, having attained, the Siddhas of old, such as Kapila and others, reached perfection."
Having carefully pressed the anus with the root of the foot while it is being moistened, one should,
according to the teacher’s instruction, direct [the breath] into the yoni located between the anus and the genitals.
Holding the left leg extended with both hands,
restrain the openings of the body through the *nāḍīs*, and place the chin upon the heart.
Having placed the mind at the crossroads, one should practice the retention of breath;
this is the "Mahāmudrā" proclaimed in all tantras.
Having practiced with the left limb, one should practice again with the right limb;
having performed the breath control (prāṇāyāma) equally, the yogi, with a restrained mind, [should proceed].
Having received this mudrā from the mouth of the guru as it was taught,
even one of meager fortune achieves success in the sacrifice through this procedure.
The movement of all the channels, the retention of the drop,
the digestion of the impurity (kaṣāya), and the destruction of sins.
The heating of Kuṇḍalinī and the entry of the vital breath (vāyu) into the aperture of Brahmā brings about the pacification of all diseases and the intensification of the digestive fire.
It bestows the splendor of the body, the power of desire, the destruction of old age and death,
the strength to achieve desired goals, happiness, and the subduing of the senses.
All these [mudrās] are connected to the yogin who has ascended the path;
indeed, I have declared these mudrās to be like wish-fulfilling cows for practitioners.
It should be practiced in secret and must not be given to just anyone;
indeed, O great adepts, this "Great Seal" (Mahāmudrā) is praised as a dyad.
"By that very [means], the faults arising from the great afflictions—such as death and so forth—are exhausted;
and thus, O best of the wise, one attains Mahāmudrā at the end.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff,
so too the innate power Kuṇḍalinī becomes straightened."
Pressing the perineum with the left foot and holding the extended right foot with both hands,
one should fill the mouth [with air].
Having placed the throat-bind (kaṇṭhavandha) and holding the vital air at the crown of the head,
one thus removes that state of death which is the refuge of calamity.
Indeed, all tastes—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are rendered tasteless;
even dreadful poison, when consumed, is digested as if it were nectar.
For one who practices Mahāmudrā, diseases such as wounds, leprosy, Udāvarta, Gulma, and splenic disorders go to their destruction. Now, the Mahābandha.
As stated by Īśvara:
"Having placed the two feet extended [in the previous posture] upon the thighs,
contracting the anus and the perineum, one should lead the apāna upward."
Having joined [the breath] with the equalizing [air] and having brought comfort,
the wise man should bind the downward-facing apāna and prāṇa for the sake of their upward movement.
This great binding, which bestows the path to perfection, has been described;
it leads the yogi upward, carrying the flowing drops through the channels.
One should accomplish both lotuses with great effort, one by one;
however, some authorities here maintain that one should avoid the throat-lotus.
There, one should paralyze the two "king's rods" (the two channels) at the two tongues;
through practice, the vital air (vāyu) will become established in the center of the Suṣumnā.
By this [body], the cage of bones is firmly bound together, yet it possesses the splendor of a physical form.
The yogis who are subject to this become possessed of a completely fulfilled heart.
By this binding, the lord of yogis shall accomplish all that is desired;
indeed, having effected the union of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths throughout the three worlds.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "One should place the heel of the left foot in the region of the perineum (*yonisthāna*),
and likewise place the right foot upon the left thigh."
Having filled the mouth with air, likewise pressing the chin against the heart,
contracting the perineum and drawing up the anus, one should fix the mind in the center.
One should practice this very slowly; by this, the "Great Bond" (mahābandha) is released.
Indeed, this "Great Bond" is the bestower of great siddhis.
Expert in liberating one from the great bond of the noose of Time,
this [place] indeed obstructs the upward movement of all the channels (nāḍīs).
It maintains the confluence of the three rivers (Triveṇī) and leads the mind toward Kedāra.
Now, the Great Piercing (Mahāvedha): "Just as a weaver, though endowed with beauty and grace, is [useless] without a man,
so too the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) and the Great Piercing are fruitless when devoid of piercing."

Established in the great bond (mahābandha), the yogi, having performed a single pūraka and having restrained the movement of the vital airs by means of the throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā), remains motionless.
Placing both hands upon the buttocks, one should strike them gently;
having pressed down upon the two hollows, the vital air (vāyu) throbs within the center.
The union of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni arises and becomes immortal;
since it is born from the state beyond death, whence can there be any fear of death?
This Great Piercing (Mahāvedha), through practice, bestows great accomplishment;
it destroys wrinkles and grey hair caused by piercing, and is practiced by the most excellent of adepts.
This triad is a great secret that destroys water-born death,
increases the power of fire, and bestows the supernatural qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
It is performed eight times, every watch, day after day;
it always accumulates a store of merit and keeps one far from the flood of sins.
Even for those possessing the vows and the trainings, this is a small amount during the initial practice.
As spoken by Īśvara:
"The wise yogi, established in the great bandha, having filled the abdomen with air, should strike the buttocks; this is celebrated by me as Vedha."
Pierced by this piercing, that bull among yogis was [pierced] by the wind.
He who constantly practices this well-guarded Great Piercing (Mahāvedha) pierces the knots along the path of the Suṣumṇā up to the aperture of Brahmā (Brahmarandhra). For him,
there arises the perfection of the vital wind (vāyusiddhi), which destroys old age and death.
The deities situated within the center of the wheel tremble from the stroke of the wind;
even Kuṇḍalī, the Great Illusion, dissolves into the shoulder of Kailāsa.
Therefore, the yogi should diligently perform the triad in its proper sequence.
He who performs these three [practices] diligently four times [a day] conquers death within six months; of this there is no doubt.
The greatness of this triad is known by the perfected one (siddha), and by no other;
having known it, all those who have attained perfection have obtained the supreme designation of "perfected."
The means of accomplishment must be guarded with great effort by one who desires success;
otherwise, there will be no success at all—this is the definitive conclusion regarding the seals (mudrās).
P.136 Now, Khecarī, from the Yoga-bīja.
One vitasti in length and four aṅgulas in width,
soft and white— these are said to be the characteristics of the support for the wrapping cloth.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā:
"By cutting [the frenum] and moving it, one should lengthen the tongue until it touches the space between the eyebrows; then the Khecarī-siddhi is attained."
Having turned the *kalā* away from the face, one should cause it to revolve in the triple path (*tripatha*).
That is the khecarīmudrā; it is called the vyomacakra.
If one holds the rasanā upward for even half a moment,
the yogi is liberated from sense objects, as well as from disease, death, old age, and the like.
He by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by the Khecarī mudrā—
his bindu does not leak, even when embraced by a passionate woman.
Even when the drop has moved and reached the fire,
it indeed ascends by that power, being restrained by the *yonimudrā*.
In the process of coagulation, the drop becomes pale white and then red;
that which is pale white is called *śukra*, while that which is red is known as *mahārajana*.

The seed resembling vermilion (sindūra) is the *rajas* situated in the place of the sun; the *bindu* should be in the place of the moon. The unification of these two is very difficult to attain. The *bindu* is Śiva, the *rajas* is Śakti; the *bindu* is the moon, and the *rajas* is the sun.
When there is the simultaneous union of the subtle drop (bindu), then the divine body arises;
the semen is joined with the moon, and the menstrual blood is encompassed by the sun.
Of these two, he who knows their state of equal flavor is a knower of yoga.
The semen of men is dependent on the mind, and life is dependent on the semen.
Therefore, one must protect both the mind and the semen with great effort.
That [state] exists at the peak in the sky, at the base of Mount Meru;
and the wise man proclaims this truth in the presence of the rivers.
From the moon, essence constantly flows; by that, death comes to men.
One should bind that with one's own hand-mudrā; otherwise, there is no accomplishment of the body. Just as fire [requires] fuel, or a lamp [requires] oil and a wick.
The embodied soul never abandons the body, which is eternally filled with the digits of the moon;
one should direct the tongue upward and drink the water exuded by it.
I consider him to be of noble birth who constantly eats beef and drinks the nectar-like wine of the gods; others are destroyers of their lineage.
The tongue is denoted by the word "go" (cow), and its entry into the palate is indeed the consumption of cow-flesh;
that [act] destroys even the greatest of sins.
Indeed, that essence which flows from the moon, produced by the fire generated through the entry of the tongue,
is the nectar of the immortals (amaravāruṇī).
The seed-syllable is one, consisting of creation; the Khecarī mudrā is one;
the deity is one, the supportless; and the state of Manonmanī is one.
There is no posture equal to Nāsana, no Kumbhaka comparable to Kevala;
there is no Mudrā equal to Khecarī, and no dissolution (laya) like that of Nāda.

Whoever drinks the pure water of its waves and ripples, which flows from the sixteen-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, forcefully obtained from the vital breath (prāṇa), having restrained the tongue with the upper palate and contemplating the supreme power (parā śakti) within the cavity; who drinks that which fills the tongue.
Free from defects, with a body as delicate as a lotus stalk, that yogi lives for a long time.
P.138 "If the tongue, dripping with flavor, constantly kisses the jewel of the long lower lip—
whether it be like salt, pungent, sour, or milk, or like honey and clarified butter,"
The removal of diseases, the swiftness of internal faculties, the recitation of the scriptures and traditions,
and the attraction of perfected women— these eightfold accomplishments shall belong to him here on earth.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse,
and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that mudrā becomes 'Khecarī'."
Because the mind moves in the void and the tongue has moved into the void,
this is called the Khecarī mudrā, practiced by the perfected ones (siddhas).
As long as the seal of the sky (nabhomudrā) is bound, so long does the drop (bindu) not depart;
as long as the drop is stable within the body, whence can there be fear of death?
He who knows the Khecarī Mudrā is not afflicted by disease, nor is he stained by karma; he is not constrained by time.
Having placed the tongue in the cavity of the palate, [one should drink] the nectar from the upward-facing mouth.
He who, having become firm with his tongue turned upwards, performs the drinking of Soma for six months, shall undoubtedly attain freedom from old age.
Within half a month, there is no doubt, the knower of yoga conquers death by pressing the great cavity of the "royal tooth" with the tip of the tongue.
By meditating upon the Goddess who consists of nectar, one becomes a poet within six months;
for the yogi whose body is filled with nectar, this occurs within two or three years.
For that yogi whose body is eternally filled with the digits of the moon, the semen— arising from the qualities of sattva and the rest— flows upwards.
"Even for one bitten by Takṣaka, the poison does not spread. Thus said Dattātreya.
Having turned back the tongue and placed it within the cavity of the skull,
with the gaze fixed between the eyebrows— this is the *khecarī* mudrā.
"There is no disease nor death for him, no sleep, no hunger, no thirst, and no fainting shall occur for him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā. Thus [it is said]. The Lord said:
When the cavity is situated above the uvula,
the wise man should diligently join the tongue so that it moves in the reverse direction, lest it fall into the pit of nectar.
This mudrā is called Khecarī, taught out of consideration for devotees;
through constant practice, one may drink nectar every day.
By that, there shall be victory over death, which is like a lion for the elephant of mortality;
this is the Khecarī Mudrā, which, when well-stabilized and unrestrained, [grants liberation].
"Even after the passing of a hundred Brahmās, he indeed considers it but half a moment."
Now, the *mūlabandha*:
"Having firmly pressed the anal region with the root of the foot and well-restrained,
one should forcefully draw up the *apāna* wind and practice its upward movement in gradual stages."

This root-lock (mūlabandha) has been described; it destroys old age and death. It effects the unification of the apāna and prāṇa breaths and the depletion of urine and feces. Through this lock, the yonimudrā is most effectively accomplished.

When the *yonimudrā* is perfected, why indeed would one not achieve perfection on this earth? By the grace of this *bandha*, the yogi, having mastered the wind, remains suspended in the sky, having left the ground, while seated in the *padmāsana*.
"If the preeminent among yogis desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, he should practice this binding in a secluded place where no one is seen. Thus it is said.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā:
"Pressing the perineum with the heel, one should contract the anus;
drawing the apāna upward, this is called 'mūlabandha'."
The yogis call that which forcibly draws the downward-moving apāna upward by means of contraction the "mūlabandha," as stated in the *Yogabīja*.
Pressing the anus against the heel, one should forcefully contract the vagina;
thus, time after time, the vital air (samīraṇa) moves upward.
Having brought the prāṇa and apāna under control through the nāda-bindu and mūla-bandha, one attains the perfect accomplishment of yoga; of this there is no doubt.
When the downward-moving breath (apāna) rises upward and reaches the circle of fire,
a long flame of fire, struck by the wind, increases in size.
Then, from that [union], the two fires, Apana and Bahni, were born, whose essential nature was said to be Prana;
by them, the fire born of the body was thus exceedingly inflamed.
By that [means], Kuṇḍalinī, who is perpetually asleep, is thoroughly awakened;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, she certainly attains straightness.
Just as if entering a thorn, so too should one move within the central channel of Brahma;
therefore, the root-lock (mūlabandha) must always be performed by the best of yogis.
Because the great bird (the vital breath) flies upward without rest from this [point],
it is called the Mūlabandha, the "root-binding" of the Lord Uḍḍīyāṇa.
One should practice the upward movement from the navel toward the upper part of the belly;
this is indeed the *Uḍḍīyāna* bandha, a lion for the elephant of death.
The Uḍḍīyāna band is innate, as taught by the Guru;
when practiced, even an old man becomes like a youth.
One should diligently perform the *tāla* (rhythmic percussion) either above or below the navel;
by practicing this for six months, one certainly conquers death—of this there is no doubt.
In the *Iṣṭapradīpikā*:
"When in the vajrāsana posture, one should firmly hold the feet with both hands near the region of the ankles; then one should press upon the abdomen."
One should direct the palm to the abdomen and the chin to the heart,
very slowly, so that the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the cavity of the belly.
Of all the bonds [of posture], the Uḍḍīyānaka is indeed the supreme.
This is the Uḍḍīyāna-bandha, which destroys pain in the throat.
If a yogi performs it daily four times every day,
through that there shall be purification of the navel, and the vital breath (marut) will become perfected.
By practicing this for six months, the yogi who knows reality conquers death;
his digestive fire blazes and an increase in vital essence occurs.
By this, the accomplishment of the body is most certainly achieved,
and for the yogin, the complete destruction of diseases also occurs with certainty.
"A wise person, having received [this] from the guru with effort, should accomplish it in a secluded and well-situated place; [thus one attains] the supreme, most difficult-to-attain bond.
Now, Jālandhara:
"By binding the network of vessels in the throat at the heart with the chin,
the 'Jālandhara-bandha' is proclaimed, which is difficult even for the gods to attain."
The fire at the navel of living beings drinks the nectar dripping from the thousand-petaled lotus like a flavorful juice; for that purpose, one should bind this [bandha].
By means of this bond, the wise man drinks nectar himself;
and having attained immortality, he rejoices throughout the three worlds.
"This is the Jālandhara-bandha, which bestows success upon the Siddhas;
it should be practiced constantly by the yogi who desires accomplishment. Thus, in the Yogabīja.

"Contracting the throat, one should firmly fix [the breath] in the heart by will; this is the 'bandha' called Jālandhara, which brings about the imperishable nectar. Thus it is said in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
It binds the network of vessels here that carry the water of the sky downward;
therefore it is called Jālandhara, the destroyer of the dense suffering in the throat.
When the Jālandhara band, characterized by the contraction of the throat, is performed,
the nectar does not fall forward and the vital wind (vāyu) does not become agitated.
This middle wheel should be known as the binding of the sixteen supports;
this triad of bindings is supreme and practiced by the great siddhas.
Yogins know the practice of all Haṭha-tantras.
Now, the reversal-method (viparītakaraṇī) according to Haṭhayoga:
"The sun, whose nature is burning, resides eternally in the region of the navel."
The moon, whose nature is nectar, dwells eternally in the center of the palate.
The moon rains when facing downward, and the sun devours when facing upward;
that ritual must be performed by which that nectar is attained.
The nectar of the lunar digit, obstructed within the supremely pure supreme wheel,
flows as nectar through that path, bypassing the mouth of the sun.
Having placed the nectar at the cave and gradually reaching the tip of the nose on the peak,
it moves upward by itself and departs, having deceived the mouth of the Sun.
The pure water of the moon’s digits, increased [by the breath], rises from the region of the throat upward;

reaching the tip of the nose, it goes through the peak to the gateway of the sky on all sides. Having descended from that upper space onto the earth, one should drink it with the feet firmly turned upward.
Thus, for one who acts in this way with a collection of conquered senses, there is no exhaustion whatsoever."
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Whatever nectar of divine form flows from the Moon, the Sun devours it all; by that, the physical body is destroyed."
In that regard, the divine process of making the bones— the deception of the Sun’s mouth—
is to be known through the instruction of the Guru, and not by means of millions of scriptural interpretations.
With the navel above and the palate below, with the sun above and the moon below—
this practice known as the "reversal" (viparītakaraṇī) destroys all diseases.
Dattātreya said:
"The sun is above and the moon is below; hear this, O Sāṅkṛti!
On the first day, [the deity] should remain for a moment with head downward and feet upward."
And moment by moment, one perceives oneself as slightly more advanced day after day;
and within half a month, both wrinkles and grey hair are seen.
If one practices this constantly for just one month, he becomes a conqueror of time;
for one who is constantly engaged in practice, there is an increase in the digestive fire.
For him, abundant food must certainly be provided by Sāṅkṛti;
for if he were to have little food, the fire would surely cause a burning sensation.
Now, the activation of the *śakti*. As stated by Īśvara:
"One should firmly awaken Kuṇḍalinī, who is asleep in the lotus of the *ādhāra*."
Drawing up with the apāna wind and contracting the anus, the wise man [should practice].
Indeed, for one who practices the movement of the *śakti* in this manner every day,
there shall be an increase of the digestive fire and the destruction of diseases.
Having abandoned sleep, the female serpent herself indeed rises upward;
therefore, a yogi desiring perfection must practice this.
He who constantly practices the supreme movement of the *śakti*,
by which the perfection of the body is attained, bestowing the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
According to the method of the Guru’s instruction, how could there be any fear of death for him?
For a period of two muhūrtas, one should practice the movement of the Śakti according to the prescribed rite.
Seated constantly upon the vajra-posture, one should practice for half a month;
the fire, ignited by the vital wind (vāyu), incessantly burns the kuṇḍalinī.
Heated by fire like a serpent's hood, that power which deludes the three worlds enters the interior of the mouth of the Suṣumṇā through its adamantine tip.
Together with Vāyu and Agni, having pierced the Brahma-knot,
she then pierces the Viṣṇu-knot and remains at the Rudra-knot.
Then, having repeatedly filled [the body] firmly with breath-retentions (kumbhaka),
the knots in the channel are split, like heated iron rods [piercing] bamboo.
In the same way, there may be a splitting of a knot in the spinal column caused by the wind;
just as when an ant has settled there, an itching sensation arises.
"Likewise, through constant practice upon the Suṣumnā with the vital air (vāyu),
one then pierces the Rudra-knot and proceeds to that which is of the nature of Śiva. Thus it is said.
In Haṭhayoga: "Just as one might forcibly open a door with a key,
so too the yogi should pierce the gate of liberation by means of Kuṇḍalinī."
Having covered with her mouth that gate through which one must go to the stainless abode of Brahmā, the Supreme Goddess fell into a deep sleep.
The Kuṇḍalinī power is above the pit; having bound it for the liberation of yogins and for the bondage of the deluded, he who knows her is a knower of Yoga.
Just as Śeṣa-Kuṇḍalī is the support for the oceans, mountains, and islands,
so too is Kuṇḍalī the support for all the Yoga Tantras.
Kuṇḍalāṅgī, Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujagī, Śakti, Īśvarī,
Kuṭilā, Arundhatī, and Devī are synonymous terms.
Kuṇḍalinī is proclaimed to be curved in shape like a serpent;
he by whom that power is set in motion is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
He who forcibly seizes a young widow ascetic between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Grasping the tail, one should awaken the sleeping female serpent;
abandoning her sleep, she rises straight up by force.
And that serpent remained coiled;
from morning until evening, for about half a watch,
having given birth, she was freed from her solar heat.
Having grasped it, she goes forth, having been moved.
The yogi, seated upon the vajra-posture, having moved the kuṇḍalinī,
should quickly awaken the kuṇḍalinī by means of the bellows immediately following the sun.
One should perform the contraction of the sun (the breath) and then move Kuṇḍalinī;
for one who has thus entered the mouth of death, whence can there be any fear of death?
The breath flowing through the right path in the nose is lengthened by the olfactory organ;
resembling the moon, it first fills the throat-pipe of the deceased body.
Then, piercing the channels of the eyebrows and the multitude of vessels that are under the sway of the vast fire of Time (Kāla), it proceeds.
He makes that body anew again, like the trunk of a withered tree.
Having moved Kuṇḍalinī, one should especially perform the bellows-breathing (bhastrā);
by such constant practice, Yama himself fears the self-controlled practitioner.
Then one should practice Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, and also Śītalī;
for one who is thus engaged in practice, how could there be any violation of restraint (yama) for the self-controlled?
Indeed, by practicing this intensely for a period of two muhūrtas,
it is always beneficial for one who observes celibacy and eats food that is wholesome and moderate.
Success is seen in the maṇḍala for the yogi through the practice of kuṇḍalinī;
it is the purification of the impurities of the seventy-two thousand channels.
Whence can there be a means of cleansing without the repeated practice of *kuṇḍalī*?
In this regard, for the activation of the power (*śakti*), only the *padmāsana* is to be observed, and not the *vajrāsana*, because that would contradict direct experience.
And so it is said in another text: "Having joined the palms together and firmly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana),
placing the chin closely against the chest, one should fix that [object] in the mind through meditation."
Again and again, one should expel the filled downward-moving wind from the head;
as one releases the vital breath (prāṇa), the power (śakti) certainly attains awakening through the arising of its own awakening.
P.147 Thus, nine mudrās have been proclaimed by Śambhu, the primordial Lord;
each one among them bestows great siddhi upon those who practice self-restraint.
Dattātreya says: "The difference arises from the difference in practice, but the fruit is indeed the same.
And the sequence of practice has been described in the *Pavanayogasaṃgraha*:
Having thoroughly practiced Mahāmudrā, one should thereafter certainly perform Mahābandha,
Mahāvedha, and the movement of Śakti.
"Having assumed a very firm posture and having performed the *mūlabandha*,
one should likewise practice the *uḍḍīyāna* bandha and then that called *jālandhara*. This is the connection [of the sentence], as stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
Having drawn up the root-center (mūlasthāna), one should perform the uḍḍīyāṇa lock;
having bound the iḍā and piṅgalā, one should cause [the breath] to flow along the western path.
"One should practice the abode of the wind by this very method;
then death, as well as old age, disease, and the like, do not arise. Thus it is said in the *Yogabīja*:
"When the fourfold divisions have been established in the *kumbhaka*..."
These three bonds, which I shall clearly explain, must be performed by me.
The lock known as Jālandhara should be performed at the end of inhalation (pūraka);
the Uḍḍīyāna lock should be performed at the end of retention (kumbhaka) and at the beginning of exhalation (recaka).
By quickly contracting the lower part [of the body] and constricting the throat,
and by stretching the middle [part] backward, the vital breath shall enter the Brahma-nāḍī.
Having raised the apāna upward and drawn the prāṇa down from the throat,
the yogi, freed from old age, becomes sixteen years of age.

Because the *uḍḍīyāna* [bandha] occurs spontaneously, it should be performed during the state of *kumbhaka*. Regarding this, some say that although Mahāmudrā and the other [bandhas] are accepted only for perfected beings such as Kapila and not for sages such as Yājñavalkya, they nevertheless must be understood as being common [to all]. However, that [view] is due to a lack of comprehension of the meaning of the text.

Nevertheless, in the section on the arising of the *nāda*, in the verse "Having drawn the *apāna* upward with the *praṇava*, being well-composed," the *mūlabandha* is explicitly mentioned by name. By the mention of that, its two associates, *uḍḍīyāna* and *jālandhara*, are also implied, because the performance of all three simultaneously without interruption has been shown previously. Furthermore:
"Having brought the wind into the tongue, one should restrain it at the root of the tongue;
he who, knowing this, drinks the nectar, enjoys every auspiciousness."

In this context, since it is evident that [the practice] is untenable without the *khecarī* [mudrā], it follows that the *mudrās* of Yājñavalkya and others were indeed intended [by the author]. However, it should be understood that their specific presentation has not been made here because they are well-known from other texts. Now, for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who is endowed with the previously mentioned external and internal means and possesses knowledge of the *ādhāras*, *mudrās*, *cakras*, and so forth, the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅgas*)—which serve as the means to liberation by way of purifying the mind and are useful for the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—are being described.

And likewise in the *Pātañjala*: "From the practice of the limbs of yoga, there is illumination of the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). The meaning is that when impurity has been destroyed—that is, when the impurity known as the afflictions (*kleśa*), which is the veil over the luminosity of the *sattva* of the mind, has perished—there arises an illumination of knowledge, which is a *sāttvika* transformation and the cause of discriminative discernment. Furthermore, the aphorism enumerating the limbs of yoga is: "Restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*) are the eight limbs. And Yājñavalkya says: "I shall explain the limbs to you correctly, just as they were heard by me in the past."
O Gārgī, with a concentrated mind, listen together with the sages.
Yama and niyama, as well as āsana,
prāṇāyāma, and likewise pratyāhāra and dhāraṇā, O Gārgī!
O fair-faced one, meditation (dhyāna) and concentration (samādhi)— these are the limbs of yoga;
restraint (yama) and observance (niyama) are proclaimed to be tenfold.
Eight supreme postures are proclaimed, among which the uttama-uttama is the highest;
breath control (prāṇāyāma) is said to be threefold, and withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is fivefold.
Retention (dhāraṇā) is said to be fivefold, and meditation (dhyāna) is proclaimed to be sixfold;
thus, among these, the highest is said to be samādhi, which is of a single form.
Some desire [these virtues] in many ways; listen separately in greater detail:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, and uprightness.
Forgiveness, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity— these are the ten restraints (yamas) toward all beings at all times, through action, mind, and speech.
Non-violence is declared by yogis to be that which does not give rise to affliction;
truth is declared to be speech regarding existing things that is beneficial to living beings.
To be free from longing for the property of others through action, mind, or speech—
that is declared as non-stealing by the seers who perceive the truth.
The renunciation of sexual intercourse at all times, in all circumstances, and in every way— whether by deed, mind, or speech— is declared to be celibacy (brahmacarya).
For those in the stage of studentship, for ascetics, for the lifelong celibate,
and likewise for forest-dwellers, this is declared to be the vow of celibacy.
The union with one's own wife during her fertile period according to the prescribed rule is declared to be the very practice of celibacy for those dwelling in the householder stage of life.
Celibacy is proclaimed for the king as well as for the householder;
constant service to the guru is likewise declared to be celibacy.
Generosity toward all beings is considered to be universal benevolence;
as for other prescribed duties, they are performed through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Uprightness is the state of being of a single form, whether in engagement or withdrawal;
it is the equanimity of embodied beings toward all things, both pleasant and unpleasant.
The learned who proclaim the teachings of the Vedas have declared that this very forbearance is the true wealth,
even in the loss of one's purpose, in separation from kinsmen, or in the midst of prosperity.
And when those two are attained, the steadying of the mind everywhere is fortitude (dhṛti).
Eight mouthfuls are prescribed for a sage, and sixteen for forest-dwellers.
For a householder, however, there are thirty-two [mouthfuls]; for students (brahmacārins), it is according to their desire.
Among these, this [number] constitutes a measured diet, while for others it is merely eating little.
Purity is said to be twofold: external and internal;
that which is performed with earth and water is known as external, while purity of mind is the internal.
And the purification of the mind is to be understood through the Dharma and through inner science (adhyātma-vidyā);
O sinless one, the inner science and the Dharma were obtained from my father and my teacher.
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord,
hearing the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and the observance of vows.
These observances have been declared; now hear of them all individually, [performed] according to the path prescribed by rule through the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances.
They say that the emaciation of the body through austerity is the highest form of asceticism;
however, this should be undertaken only after one has first mastered the practice of yoga.
Since bodily afflictions such as fasting and the like are prohibited during the time of practice,
the characteristics of silence and so forth mentioned in the Bhagavad Gītā are appropriate.
For instance, Yājñavalkya says: "Worship of gods, the twice-born, gurus, and the wise; purity and straightforwardness."
"The sages have declared that contentment is the defining characteristic of happiness— that state which, when perceived, is always sufficient for a person in terms of gain."
Faith in dharma and adharma is called āstikya;
and wealth or food acquired through righteous means that is bestowed [upon others].
This is declared to be the gift given with faith to those who seek it:
that which is offered with a serene disposition to either Viṣṇu or Rudra.
Worship according to one's ability and with devotion is indeed the worship of the Lord;
it is a heart free from passion, untainted by passion, falsehood, and the like.
A body free from violence is the worship of the Lord;
listening to the established doctrine is declared by the wise to be the hearing of Vedanta.
The wise maintain that even for a Kṣatriya, the hearing of the established doctrine is like that of a twice-born.

Some wise men maintain that the hearing of the Siddhānta (the established conclusions) and the hearing of the Vedānta are intended for virtuous and noble Vaiśyas, as well as for Śūdras, Kṣatriyas, and ascetics who abide by their own dharma.

Whatever action may be contemptible within the Vedic or worldly paths, the sense of shame that arises regarding it is proclaimed as *hrī*. Furthermore, that firm resolve which exists toward all prescribed duties is known as *mati*.
"Even when instructed by a guru, one must avoid what is outside the Vedas;
the practice of mantra, known as *japa*, is prescribed according to the path declared by the ritual injunctions."
Having studied the Veda, or the Sūtra, or the Purāṇa along with the Itihāsas—
that which is their study is known as constant practice and recitation (japa).
Regarding the subject of the ascetic, Dattātreya states a specific distinction:
"Non-stealing, celibacy, renunciation, and likewise freedom from greed."
The five vows of the monks are indeed such that non-violence is supreme among them.
"Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and constant study— these are proclaimed as the five observances (niyamas).
This is also stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra]:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*;
purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the *niyamas*. Furthermore, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Compassion, lack of laziness, detachment, and supreme straightforwardness..."
Freedom from fickleness, fortitude, truthfulness, and knowledge—these indeed they know as *yama*.
Compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is the absence of harmful intent.

Purity (*śauca*), regulation of diet (*āhāra-niyama*), detachment (*nirmamatva*), non-attachment (*asaṅgatā*), tranquility (*śama*), forbearance (*kṣamā*), self-restraint (*dama*), and contentment (*sṛṣṭi*)—these eight constitute the observances (*niyama*). Detachment and non-attachment [are included therein].
Tranquility, forbearance, self-restraint, and creation—these are remembered as the eight observances (niyamas).

Now, regarding the posture (*āsana*): Patañjali states therein, "Posture is steady and comfortable. That by which one sits is a posture, such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and others. When it becomes motionless, comfortable, and non-disturbing, then it attains the status of being a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*). Then, for the sake of attaining that very comfort, there is the aphorism: "By relaxation of effort and by meditative absorption in the Infinite. Regarding this, Bhojadeva maintains that the reading is with a suffix denoting abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), namely *anantatā*. The connection is that through relaxation of effort and through meditative absorption in the Infinite, [the posture] becomes steady and comfortable.

When one binds the posture, then even through the relaxation of effort, it is accomplished as if without difficulty; when the mind’s absorption is directed toward the infinite space within, one attains identity with it through focused attention. Then, due to the absence of the notion of "I" regarding the body, the posture does not become a source of pain.

When this mastery of posture is achieved, those obstacles to concentration such as physical trembling and the like cease to arise. Regarding the phrase "by means of the two attainments of Ananta," the traditional interpretation of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that the reading of the *Sūtra* is without the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*). On this point, Vācaspatimiśra explains: "With one's gaze fixed more steadily upon Ananta, the Lord of Serpents, the mind attains a state of absorption within the circle of the earth supported by the thousand [hoods], thereby accomplishing the posture."
The general definition of *āsana* (posture) is that it is a specific arrangement of the hands and feet. As for its specific definition, in the *Dharmaputrikā*, it is said:
"The two feet should be placed upon the ground by the yogin seated in posture;
the right [foot] on the left side, and the left foot on the right."
Facing one another, with both hands forming the *mṛgaśīrṣa* gesture,
this is called the *mṛgasvastika*, performed for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga.
Standing with the left foot and the right knee [on the ground], one should form a hollowed palm; this they know as the "Half-Moon Posture" (ardhacandrāsana).

Having remained seated upon the knees, the yogi should place his hands in cupped fashion at the heart; this is to be known as the *añjanikā* posture. The feet are comfortably extended, well-joined, and resting firmly on the ground.
Sitting with only the upper half of the body [supported] is known as the "staff posture" (daṇḍāsana).
Sitting with only the upper half of the body [supported] is known as the "staff posture" (daṇḍāsana).
"Having placed both feet evenly on the ground while remaining seated,
and having placed the palms of the hands upon the two knees— this is the *pīṭhāsana*," so says Mataṅga.
One should bind [the body] with a yoga-band in the paryanka posture from behind;
having drawn up the knees, one should place the right foot together [with the left].
On the outside of the left calf, one should place the left [foot] below the left [knee], slightly extended outward,
and remain with the knees together.
"The seat known as 'paryaṅka' bestows the perfection of yoga.
(Āgneya Purāṇa, p. 154)
Having doubled both feet, one should place the hands horizontally and vertically respectively,
with the fingers joined and the nails touching as if resting upon a cloth band.

"This is indeed the 'Yogapaṭṭa' posture, which is praised by all. Listen briefly to the 'Half-Moon': having placed both feet in that same manner, with the soles joined to one another, it is called the 'Half-Moon'."
The meaning is that, in the same manner as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), one should place the two feet doubled over;
"in that same way, one should make the two feet [double], but with the face bent down,
having extended both hands resting upon a pillow behind."
This is called *prasāritāsana*, which bestows success in yoga.
Restraining the anus with the two heels in reverse order,
one who is composed [attains] what the knowers of yoga know as *kūrmāsana*.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Placing one foot upon the other thigh and remaining thus,
this is the 'half-seat' (*ardhāsana*), the supreme means for accomplishing yoga."
Yājñavalkya:
"Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees,
sitting with the body straight— that they call 'Svastika'."
Having placed the ankle of one foot at the side of his own groin,
he should place the right ankle upon the side of his back.

Likewise on the right and similarly on the left, with one foot placed upon one thigh and the other thigh likewise placed upon the other, this is declared to be the *vīrāsana* (heroic posture). Just as the *gomukha* [posture] is described, so too is the *gomukha*. Having placed one foot upon one thigh, one remains seated; likewise, having placed the other thigh upon the other [foot], it is called *vīrāsana*.
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineum;
the right ankle with the left [ankle], and likewise the other with the right.
Placing his hands upon his knees and extending his fingers,
Vyāghravaktra, being well-composed, should gaze at the tip of his nose.
This shall be the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), always honored by yogis.
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on either side of the perineal seam;
having firmly bound the hands upon the sides of the feet, one remains perfectly motionless.
This Bhadrāsana removes all diseases and poisons.
Pressing the subtle seam (sīvanī) on the left side with the left ankle,
and the right [seam] with the right ankle, it is called Muktāsana.
Firmly supporting the earth with the palms of both hands,
one should place the elbows at the sides of the navel;
with the head and feet raised, one remains poised in the sky like a staff.
This indeed is the peacock posture (mayūrāsana), which destroys all sins;
all internal diseases and poisons are destroyed by it. —From the Haṭhapradīpikā.
Some postures adopted by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and by yogins such as Matsyendra are now described by me. Since posture is the first limb of Haṭha-yoga, posture is discussed first.
One should practice that which brings stability to the posture, health, and lightness of the limbs.
Having joined the hands between the knees and thighs and placed them on the ground,
one establishes the *kukkuṭāsana* (cock's posture) with the body suspended in the air.

Seated in the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana), having bound the neck with both arms, one should remain supine like a tortoise; this is the *uttānakūrma* [asana]. Then, grasping the two big toes with the hands up to the ears...
One should perform the drawing of the bow; this is called the bow posture (*dhanurāsana*). In it, the right foot is placed upon the root of the left thigh.
Wrapping the right arm around the outside of the knees and remaining with the body turned,
this is the posture called Śrīmatsyanātha, as taught by the Lord.
The seat of Matsyendra is the expansion of the belly; it is the weapon that shatters the circle of fierce diseases.
Through practice, it brings about the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī.
It produces steadfastness in the staff for men.
Having stretched out his feet upon the ground and standing like a staff,
he grasped both feet with his two hands and placed the region of his forehead upon his knees.
"One should expel this; they call it *paścimatāna*.

Thus, *paścimatāna* makes the wind flow toward the west, being the foremost among lotus postures (*padmāsana*). "It causes the rising of the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) and brings leanness and freedom from disease to men in the abdomen. Then, pressing the earth with both hands and placing the sides of the navel upon the elbows—when one has risen into the sky by means of that posture, the virtuous call this *mayūra* (the peacock). It quickly removes diseases along with those of the armpits, such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*), enlargement of the belly (*udara*), and so forth.
The "Śrīmayūra" [elixir] suppresses all defects when taken;
it reduces to ashes everything consumed, even a great variety of food; it kindles the digestive fire and would digest even kālakūṭa poison.
Lying on the ground like a corpse, this is known as the Corpse Pose (*śavāsana*).
The Corpse Pose removes fatigue and is a means for achieving rest of the mind.
Placing the head upon the ground, as well as the elbows on the hands, one should extend the feet in the air like a staff; this is declared to be the Naraka posture.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"There are as many seats here as there are wombs of living beings."
Likewise, Siddha and Padma—these two grant swift accomplishment.
Gorakṣa said: "Each one of the eighty-four sacred fields has been proclaimed;
Maheśvara alone knows all their various divisions."
Then Śiva established one hundred and sixteen seats;
from all those thrones, two were extracted for the purpose of meditation.
"One is declared to be Siddhāsana, the second is Kamalāsana.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Indeed, eighty-four postures were taught by Śiva."
Taking from them that which is the essence, consisting of four parts, I shall speak.
The fourfold [postures] are Siddha, Padma, Bhadra, and Siṃha;
among these, the Padma is indeed the most excellent, and it is then called Siddhāsana.
On the auspicious lion-throne previously described, Yājñavalkya says:
one should press the vein at the suture with the left ankle;
it is subtle, located below the two shanks, and on the left side of the right [leg].
O Gārgī, one should firmly bind the space between the two calves so that it is without any gap;
with the neck, head, and shoulders aligned, the back even, and the abdomen level,
one should remain positioned above, gazing at the right ankle with both eyes.
This is called Siddhāsana, which swiftly bestows spiritual accomplishment.
Pressing the anus with the left ankle and blocking the joint with the other [right] one,
while placing the other hand upon the left hand, [one should remain].
Behold the crest of the fire.

"O Gārgī, when the life-sustaining breath (prāṇa) that obstructs longevity is indeed restrained by means of āsana, it then gradually enters the family of the downward-moving breath (apāna), which carries fire."
In the *Pavanayogasaṃgraha*:
"Having firmly placed the root of one foot joined at the site of the perineum, and having made the body even with the mind fixed on the heart, one should place the other foot upon the penis."
Standing like a pillar with senses restrained, looking at the space between the eyebrows with a steady gaze—
this indeed shall be the "Siddhāsana," which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation.
This they call Siddhāsana; others call it Vajrāsana.
Some call this posture "Muktāsana," the supreme among postures.
As stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "Just as moderate diet is among the observances (*niyamas*), so is non-violence among the restraints (*yamas*)."
The wise know this "Siddhāsana" as being thus positioned at the mouth of all the channels;
among the eighty-four seats, one should practice Siddhāsana,
just as one attends to the Suṣumṇā among the seventy-two thousand channels.
Meditating on the Self and restricting his diet for twelve years,
the yogi shall attain perfection through the constant practice of the Siddhāsana posture.
When the Siddhāsana is attained, what is the use of many laborious postures?
When the vital breath (prāṇānila) is carefully bound in the Kevala-kumbhaka,
it rises effortlessly on its own, just as a flame does.
P.159 Now,
when one is always firmly established in the Siddhāsana alone,
the three bonds (bandhas) arise spontaneously and with little effort.
Now, the six-month practice. Yājñavalkya says: "O best of Brahmins, one should bind the two big toes with the hands in reverse order, having placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs."
"This shall be the *padmāsana*, honored by all. Mataṅga says:
"Having settled oneself with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon a level and pleasant patch of ground..."
The right leg is placed upon the left thigh.
Drawing the right [leg] up so that the two shanks are joined together—
this indeed is the excellent seat of Brahmā, known as the "Lotus."
In the *iṭha* posture: having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left [foot] upon the right thigh,
one should hold [them] firmly with both hands according to the subsequent method.
"Placing the two thumbs upon the heart and gazing at the tip of the nose,
that which destroys the afflictions of single or dual diseases is called 'Padmāsana'. —
Dattātreya.
Having carefully placed the feet flat and the thighs together,
and likewise having placed the palms flat upon the middle of the thighs, one should then fix the gaze [upon the tip of the nose].
O King, one should place the tongue against the root of the teeth at the tip of the nose,
and having raised both the chin and the chest, one should slowly exhale the breath.
Drawing [the breath] seven times according to one's capacity, one should slowly fill the abdomen;
this is declared to be the *Dadma* posture (*āsana*), which destroys all diseases.
It is difficult for anyone to attain, but shall be obtained by the wise man who is destined for it.
Then, according to one's capacity, one should slowly exhale the breath.
The yogi, seated in the lotus posture, filling [the breath] within the openings of the channels;
He who restrains the vital air (māruta) is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, among the various postures (āsana), the lord of yogis has conquered all fatigue.
"One should practice the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*) and the yogic exercises on the breath (*pavana-kriyā*) by means of the *mudrās*.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Yogacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śivānanda Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī.

In the aforementioned place, within a hermitage endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, at an auspicious time marked by favorable stars, a moon-like moment, and a suitable conjunction (*yoga*), one should worship Vināyaka, Śiva, Śivā, Viṣṇu, Kṣetrapāla, and the gurus together with their disciples, as well as the lords of yogis, according to one's capacity. Then, seated upon a seat consisting of *kuśa* grass, a deerskin, and a cloth sixteenfold in size, facing either east or north, and endowed with qualities such as tranquility (*śama*), one should bow to the gods beginning with Śiva, the yogis, and the gurus. Following the path taught by the gurus and the scriptures, one should first perform the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śodhana*), which is the most intimate internal limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

In the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, regarding Rājayoga: "Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place— neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass, one over the other."
Seated comfortably on an excellent seat in a secluded, solitary, pure, and very charming place, he should lean slightly backward.
With all limbs in a state of deep sleep, the self is perfectly steady and utterly pure;
as it is said in the Śruti: "Seated in a comfortable posture in a secluded place..."
Possessing a body with neck and head erect,
situated in the final stage of life, having restrained all his senses and bowed with devotion to his own guru.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa, the words of Śiva are as follows:
"Having paid homage to the lords of yogis, together with their disciples, and to Vināyaka..."
"And then the yogi, well-composed, should unite with both the Guru and me.
Yājñavalkya said:
"One who has acquired knowledge, who has subdued anger, and who is devoted to truth and dharma..."
Devoted to the service of his guru and dedicated to his father and mother.
Abiding in his own hermitage, practicing virtuous conduct, and well-instructed by the learned,
he should worship Vināyaka thoroughly with roots, fruits, water, and other offerings.
Having bowed to one’s chosen deity and the gurus, and then having ascended the seat,
one should thus understand the configuration of the channels as well as the locations of the vital winds.
"Perform the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śodhana*) by the path prescribed in the injunctions. In the *Vasiṣṭha-yoga*:
"One who is engaged in the actions prescribed by the injunctions and is free from all desires..."
He who is endowed with the primordial qualities and is entirely free from all attachments.
Then, having gone to a penance grove provided with fruits, roots, and water,
one should construct a very beautiful hermitage in a pleasant and pure location— either by a river or in a forest— and ensure it is fully equipped with all protections.
Constantly engaged in bathing three times a day, having become pure and composed,
the wise one always wears white ashes while his body is consecrated with mantras.
Having spread kusha grass upon a soft seat, or else a horse-skin,
and having duly worshipped Vinayaka with fruits, roots, water, and other offerings;
and having bowed to one's chosen deity and one's guru, one should then mount the seat.
Facing either east or north, having mastered his posture,
he himself should remain perfectly motionless, with his neck, head, and torso held erect and his mouth closed.
Seated with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose, he should place one hand upon the other;
at the tip of his nose, he beholds the moon, its orb full and its moonlight spread abroad.
Having beheld with both eyes and the mind the fourth letter of this seventh group, conjoined with the bindu and situated in the center of the orb;
One should fill the external air through the *iḍā* for twelve *mātrās*;
then, one should meditate upon the fire as before, endowed with a series of flickering flames.
Meditating on the letter *ra* joined with a *bindu*, situated within the circle of fire,
one should then exhale slowly through the *piṅgalā* channel.
Then, having filled the breath through the Piṅgalā on the right,
the wise and intelligent practitioner should slowly exhale it through the Iḍā.
Whether for three or four years, or even for three or four months,
one should practice this diligently three times a day, six times each.
One attains the purification of the channels, characterized by distinct signs.
Lightness of the body, radiance, and an increase in the digestive fire.
"The manifestation of the internal sound (nāda)—this is the sign that indicates spiritual perfection (siddhi).
As long as one perceives these [signs], one should practice in this manner.

Regarding the phrase "engaged in the actions prescribed by the injunctions," it means being engaged in the performance of those duties ordained according to one's caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), beginning with the restraints (yama) and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (tyādi), the observances (niyamas) and postures (āsanas) are included. The qualities belonging to those [practices]—namely, the observances, the restraints, the postures, and so forth—are the marks of their accomplishment (siddhi): the abandonment of enmity, self-disgust for one's own body, invulnerability to the pairs of opposites (dvandvas), and so on. Endowed with these, the first [type of practitioner] goes to a penance grove (tapovana) and so forth; however, this is not a rule regarding the location for the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi), because the fatigue of the sentence is due to its being subordinate to a higher purpose.

Therefore, this is a restatement of one part of the various locations for yoga practice obtained through the five ancillaries of yoga, such as breath control (prāṇāyāma). In the phrase "having spread kuśa grass, or else (*athavā*) a horse-skin," the word *athavā* does not intend an option; rather, because indeclinables have multiple meanings, it has the sense of "inclusion of what was not mentioned.
Thus, the meaning is:
having placed a skin upon soft kuśa grass, and having also provided a cloth.
And likewise, in the *Bhagavadgītā*:

"Neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, antelope skin, and *kuśa* grass. Regarding the term "covered with *kuśa* grass" (*kuśottaram*), according to the maxim that "the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)," and because Śaṅkarācārya and others have stated that the order of recitation is a sequence of what precedes and what follows, it should be explained as: first the tiger skin upon the *kuśa* grass, and then the *kambala* woolen cloth upon that.

Regarding the phrase "upon which [there is] cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass in ascending order" (*cailājinayoḥ kuśottare*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the commentary that explains it as "that seat upon which cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass are placed in ascending order. As stated in the *Yogasāra*: "strewn with kusha grass, cloth, and deerskin."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "Covered with soft kuśa grass and a sacred antelope skin,
seated there, one should constantly practice the limbs of yoga."
Yājñavalkya says:
"Having spread kuśa grass upon a seat of earth, and over that an antelope skin.
Others, however, say:
Some say that the word "or" (*athavā*) indicates an option (*vikalpa*) between *kuśa* grass and a deerskin (*ajina*).
That is incorrect; for the meaning of other statements must conform to the meaning of the words of the Blessed Vāsudeva, the teacher of all the world.

Furthermore, since clothing is not mentioned in the *Vasiṣṭha-gītā*, if there were an intention to allow an option between *kuśa* and deerskin, it would be established by experience that the practice of yoga is impossible on a seat made of mere *kuśa* grass or on a seat made of mere deerskin.
"Now, [one should prepare] a seat filled with cotton, covered with a white cloth,
and with a black antelope skin as an upper covering, arranged for a gentle ritual."
Thus, in the *Agastyagītās*:
"One who is endowed with fortitude should always wear either a garment or even an antelope skin."

If it is argued that the alternative [of using kuśa grass] is indeed appropriate because even the absence of kuśa is seen in the statement of Dattātreya, "neither too high nor too low" (p. 164), we say no. For even there, according to the principle of the *Sarva-śākhā-adhikaraṇa*, just as two elements are combined when the *trivṛt* is heard, the inclusion of kuśa is likewise necessary. Thus, the definition "the posture is steady and comfortable" (*sthira-sukham āsanam*) is also justified. In this context, however, an āsana filled with cotton and covered with a white cloth should be understood as referring to those other than ascetics (*yatis*), because in the *Dharma-śāstras*, cotton and white cloth are prohibited for them.
