"Explaining [the scriptures], sleeping during the day, keeping a monastery, collecting books, cotton, and cotton cloth— these six lead to the downfall of ascetics."

By this, it is shown that even where only the six limbs beginning with posture (āsana) are mentioned, the inclusion of restraint (yama) and observance (niyama) is implied; for these two are common to all vows, and thus they are not specifically set forth in certain texts—this should be noted. Furthermore, this rule for posture is intended primarily for the purification of the channels (nāḍī), but it should also be understood as being for the purpose of practicing yoga with its constituent limbs, according to the statement of Nārada: "Sitting here, one should practice the yogas.
Regarding the phrase "the orb of the moon at the tip of the nose," it should be understood as "it flows with nectar."

One should take the fourth letter of the group beginning with *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* (i.e., *ha*) as the seed-syllable; "one should fill the air" should be understood as being mixed with nectar (*amṛta*). By this, the inhalation (*pūraka*) which is the means for purifying the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*) is shown. Here, some [commentators] maintain that from the words "then fire" (*tato 'gnim*) up to "again by Piṅgalā" (*punar piṅgalayā*), exhalation (*recaka*) is shown. By the phrase "as before," there is also a reference to the tip of the nose.

Thus, it is taught here that inhalation and exhalation alone—accompanied by the visualization of the moon and fire—are the means for purifying the channels, and not retention (*kumbhaka*) as well. Therefore...
"One should subsequently fill and exhale through the path of the black-pathed one (the left nostril).
Thus it is said in the *Yogasāra*:
"Adorned with the second *oṃkāra* situated in the middle..."
Or, having filled it fifteen times by way of the moon-path, one should offer it to Marut.
"Then one should cause [the disciple] to purge; from even a slight [amount], [the power] will arise," so it is said.
And in the *Nakulīśayogaparāyaṇa* (p. 165):

Some say that only inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*) are prescribed as the means for purifying the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*). If that were the case, since the sequence following inhalation would already be established by the word "then" (*tataḥ*) in the phrase "then [he should meditate on] fire," the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*) in the subsequent passage, "afterwards again through Piṅgalā," would be redundant. Furthermore, because the gerundive suffix in "he should exhale while meditating" (*virecayet*) itself implies a rule for exhalation qualified by meditation, the explicit hearing of the injunction "he should meditate" would be utterly purposeless. Therefore, it should be explained in this way:

Since it is impossible to interpret otherwise the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), which is the primary element of every word, the injunction of meditation (*dhyāna*)—together with its object—is enjoined by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*). In this context, meditation does not consist merely of a continuous flow of consciousness (*cittasantati*), but rather includes breath control (*kumbhaka*), on the strength of the syntactic unity of the preceding and following passages.

For instance, this meditation is not possible during inhalation (*pūraka*), because by the words "one should fill," the completion of the inhalation is stated; according to the maxim that the completion of all [actions] mentioned is the meaning of the word, so it is. Likewise, by the words "then one should meditate upon the fire," meditation is enjoined immediately after the completion of the inhalation. Nor is this possible during exhalation (*recaka*), because by the words "one should exhale afterwards," the exhalation is prescribed immediately after the completion of meditation, according to the same logic as before.

Therefore, because of the force of the authoritative statement which refers to what precedes and follows—namely, "prior to exhalation (*recaka*) and immediately after inhalation (*pūraka*)"—the very meditation accompanied by the restraint known as retention (*kumbhaka*) is prescribed as the means for attaining the fruit. Such is the meaning of Vasiṣṭha’s statement. Consequently, it is logically sound that the capacity for purifying the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*) belongs only to exhalation and inhalation when they are devoid of retention. As stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa* in the section on the purification of the channels: "One should not draw the breath in during the lunar [flow]; having drawn it up at the navel, one should hold it there."
Having restrained it further by one's power, one should exhale slightly in the Āgneya [breath].
In this manner, one should purify the wind situated in the big toes of the feet;
the purification of the channels is desired from the wind that is always omnipresent.

Thus, in other numerous texts as well, the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*) is clearly established in its own section; therefore, it is logical that here only meditation accompanied by breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) is prescribed. It is not so in this [present] commentary.

It should not be argued that because the deities and so forth who constitute the limbs of the *recaka* are obtained through meditation, one should meditate on Agni and the others as before—since the requirement for the oblation produced by that [meditation] would then be satisfied. Rather, in accordance with the syntactically expectant phrase "meditating, one should exhale" (*dhyāyan virecayet*), and given that it is well-known in all Yoga scriptures that Agni is the presiding deity of the *suṣumṇā* and that Sūrya is the presiding deity of the *piṅgalā*, the word "Sūrya" must be supplied here in place of "Agni."

Consequently, the meaning of the sentence is established as follows: one should exhale while meditating upon the sun as having the form of fire (*agni*). For this very reason, with the intention of meditating on the sun in the form of fire, the term "fire" (*agni*) is applied to the sun itself in the *Yogasāra*, the *Nakulīśa-yoga-parāyaṇa*, and elsewhere—such as in the phrase "by the path of the black-trailed one" (*kṛṣṇavartmanā*) referring to the channel (*nāḍī*), and slightly [in the sense of] "the born-with-knowledge" (*jātavedas*). Thus, it is said in the *Amṛtasiddhi*: "The fire that is in the womb is the sun; that which is the sun is the consumer of oblations (*hutāśana*).
These two are seen as one, though they appear distinct through subtle difference."

And thus, even a slight [practice] by Piṅgalā becomes fruitful again; for the syntactical connection is consistent with the phrase "meditating again" (*punardhyāyan*). Since the immediate sequence following the exhalation (*recaka*) performed previously has not been stated, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) in the expression "one should exhale again" (*punar recayet*) would otherwise lack syntactical connection. This point must be considered here: in the verse "the nose is like the orb of the moon," the term "tip of the nose" (*nāsāgra*) indicates the space between the eyebrows (*bhrūmadhya*).

Since it is well-known in all the Yoga scriptures that the space between the eyebrows is presided over by the Moon, meditation upon that [Moon] is prescribed specifically there. In the phrase "one should meditate as before," there is a reference only to the duration measured by twelve *mātrās*, and not to anything else. The word "in the middle of the body" (*dehamadhye*) must be supplied here, because during the *kumbhaka* (retention), the breath is held precisely there.

And thus, this is the meaning: "Having beheld with both eyes the lunar disc, accompanied by the seed-syllable (*vīja*), from which a stream of nectar flows in the space between the eyebrows, one should fill [the lungs] with air mixed with nectar for twelve *mātrās*. Then, meditating upon the triangular mandala of fire, accompanied by the seed-syllable and possessed of flickering garlands of flames, within the center of the body, one should hold the air in the *suṣumnā* for twelve *mātrās*. Then, [one should place it] in the heart or at the navel.

Meditating on the Sun in the form of fire for twelve *mātrās*, one should exhale the breath through the *piṅgalā*. Again, preceded by meditation and so forth, having inhaled through the *piṅgalā*, one should retain it in the heart and exhale through the *iḍā*.
As stated in the *Yogabhāskara*: "One should fill the breath with the *iḍā* and retain it with the *suṣumnā*."

"One who is disciplined should perform the sequence of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) through the *piṅgalā* channel. And in this manner, one should practice six times daily—at dawn, midday, and during the evening twilight—until signs indicating the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*) appear. Thereafter, the yogi whose collection of channels is purified will become capable of breath control. This very point has been stated: 'As long as these [signs] are not perceived, one should practice in this way.'"
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "When the entire network of channels, which was previously clouded by impurities, attains purity,
at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of binding the vital breath."
Seated firmly, one should fill the breath with the moon (the left nostril) according to one's capacity, and then exhale through the sun (the right nostril); this is called vāma-āyāma.
Meditating on the moon as it pours forth a flood of nectar-streams,
the lord of yogis attains bliss in that very moment through the practice of leftward extension.
Having drawn in the vital breath with the sun (the right nostril), the yogi should fill the cave of the belly;
having retained it slowly, he should later exhale through the moon (the left nostril),
while contemplating the hot-rayed sun in his heart, which has the brilliance of a mass of blazing fire.
By this practice of both exhalation and inhalation, the lord of yogis shall become a partaker of bliss;
thus, through three months of practice and the cultivation of both types of breath control.
The yogi who possesses a pure collection of channels is called a perfected one (siddha);
he has the power to restrain the vital breath at will and to kindle the internal fire.
"From the purification of the channels, there shall be the manifestation of *nāda* and freedom from disease.
In *Haṭhayoga*: "If one restrains the breath and drinks [air] through the *iḍā*, one should subsequently exhale in the opposite manner."
Having inhaled through Piṅgalā and then bound the breath with Vāmā, one should exhale;
for those self-controlled practitioners who meditate upon the two orbs of the sun and moon according to this method, their entire network of channels becomes purified after three months.
When the purification of the channels occurs, then thought is eliminated;
at that time, the body's leanness and radiance will certainly arise.
One should practice the kumbhakas four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually increasing up to eighty repetitions each time.
In the lowest stage there is perspiration; in the middle stage, trembling occurs;
and in the highest stage, one rises up while remaining in the lotus posture through the restraint of the vital breath.
One should perform body massage with water and a net of [woven] fibers;
by this, lightness and firmness of the limbs are produced.
In another treatise:
"(1) A person should indeed perform sixty prāṇāyāmas at the beginning of the day,
forty at midday, and twenty at the twilight."
"At midnight there should be twenty; thus is the restraint of the vital breath."
Dattātreya said:
"Having spread out a waveless seat upon this sacred seat (pīṭha),
the wise man, endowed with the lotus posture (padmāsana), should sit down here."
With the body straight and palms joined, one should bow to the chosen deity;
then, having restrained Piṅgalā with the thumb of the right hand,
one should slowly fill the breath through the iḍā.
Then, one should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention) by means of suppression according to one's capacity;
thereafter, one should exhale through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] very slowly and not with force.
Again, having filled [the abdomen] with the piṅgalā, one should slowly fill the belly;
having retained it according to one's capacity, one should exhale slowly through the iḍā.
One should fill with that [breath] by which one would exhale, and hold it without obstruction;
thus one should practice in the morning, performing twenty kumbhakas.
The *kumbhaka* known as *sahita* is devoid of all [forced] suppression.
Thus, at the time of midday, one should perform twenty *kumbhakas*;
one should perform them daily along with the *recaka* (exhalation) and *pūraka* (inhalation).
Therefore, one should perform the "combined" (sahita) breath-retention through both exhalation and inhalation;
thus, free from laziness, one should practice it four times every day.
Thus one should perform the three measures (mātrās), whereby the purification of the channels occurs;
when the purification of the channels has taken place, then the signs of the yogi appear.
"These arise indeed within the body; hear them from me as I speak:
lightness of the body, radiance, an increase in the digestive fire, and emaciation of the body—these certainly arise at that time."
In the *Yogabhāskara*: "By drawing the thread through both nostrils and rubbing [the tongue],
and by consuming long pepper (*jīra*) with more sugar than usual, there is an upward movement (*utkleda*) of water and food."
"The purification of the channels is declared by the sages; such are the means, as well as the aforementioned diet and the binding of the breath—this is my conviction."
Yājñavalkya states: "(1) One should not expel the air through either the prāṇa or the apāna;
rather, by means of that [breath] through which one moves flour-meal held in the hand by the application of breath."
"One should slowly release the breath through the nostrils, but not with force;
one should not cause the body to tremble—that is considered the supreme yoga. Thus it is said.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Alternatively, having placed himself upon whatever external seat brings him comfort,
such as the Svastika and others, the knower of Yoga should apply himself to yoga."
With the feet placed upward on the thighs, having laid the right hand upon the left,
and slightly raising the face while keeping it supported by the chest.
With eyes closed, established in sattva, not touching tooth with tooth,
with the tongue fixed motionless against the palate, the mouth slightly closed, and perfectly steady.
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should then commence the middle and the highest forms of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The characteristics of the three types of breath control—mild, middling, and intense—will now be described:
"Practiced in due order, this leads one wherever one desires;
through disciplined breath control, there occurs the destruction of all diseases."
Through the practice of improper yoga, all diseases arise:
hiccups, labored breathing, coughing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes.
Various diseases arise from the derangement of the wind (vāyu).
One should exhale the wind repeatedly in a controlled manner and fill it in repeatedly in a controlled manner.
One who knows yoga should bind [the breath] again and again as it becomes joined; in this way, success is achieved.
Otherwise, this vital breath, forcibly restrained, will escape through the pores of the skin.
This [anger] tears the body apart and even produces leprosy and other ailments;
therefore, it must be brought under control gradually, like a wild elephant.
Just as a wild elephant or a lion gradually attains gentleness,
one should act according to the vision of the scriptures and not transgress them.
Likewise, this vital breath (prāṇa) residing in the heart, when grasped by the yogi through the practice of sequential yoga and cultivated, attains a state of confidence.
As long as the vital breath remains within the body, so long is it called "life";
when it has departed, that is "death. Therefore, one should restrain the vital breath.
As long as the breath remains bound within the body,
as long as it is supported by the two eyebrows, and as long as the gaze is fixed between them, how can there be any fear of death?
Therefore, since [liberation] is to be accomplished through time, the yogi should always be devoted to the supreme practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma);
for by the perfect regulation of the vital breaths, yogis have attained perfection.
In the Vāsiṣṭha, Rāma said:
"O Brahman, how do yogins live for such a very long time?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O best among all knowers of Brahman!"
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"By the vibration of the vital breaths, they vibrate; when those are stilled, they remain equanimous.
Since they are established in that which is the support of concentration, yogis do not perish."

For one in whom neither the internal nor external vibration exists— whether it be born of the mind, the vital breath, or the bodily wind— for such a person, both transformation and decay remain far away.
When the movement of both the breath and the mind has become tranquil within and without,
the constituent elements of the body never abandon their stability.
"When the king is not properly established, the order of the castes and stages of life [is disrupted]"—thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
And listen, O protector of the earth! to the definition of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
And for those constantly engaged in yoga, such as the seat that has been prescribed.
Having assumed either the lotus posture, the half-lotus posture, or likewise the svastika posture,
one should practice yoga, having placed the *praṇava* within the heart.
Having become level and seated, with both feet drawn together,
with the mouth closed and likewise the thighs firmly pressed together in front.
Standing with self-restraint, touching his penis and testicles with his heels,
with his head slightly raised, he touched his teeth with his tongue.
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction,
the yogi, thus restrained in diet and devoted to the practice of breath control, [should meditate].
One should ascend each stage conquered one by one, slowly, as if returning to one's own home;
for the faults of passion, disease, and delusion lie in wait upon the stages already traversed.
One should not mount ground that has not been mastered;
therefore, a method for this has been taught here by the supreme sages who are practitioners of yoga.
By this means, indeed, defects such as disease do not arise for the yogi;
just as one seeking water gradually draws it up by means of machines, pipes, and the like.
Likewise, the yogi who has conquered fatigue should drink air;
for even lions, tigers, and elephants become mild when they are being served.
Just as they move, so the vital breaths become subject to the control of the yogin;
like a mahout leads an elephant at his will once it has been brought to trust, he leads the breath according to his desire.
In the same way, the yogi leads the mastered breath according to his own will;
for just as a trained lion kills deer and not human beings.
"In the same way, one whose breath is restrained does not [retain] sin within the body of men;
therefore, a disciplined yogi should always be intent upon *prāṇāyāma*. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
Therefore, O lady of excellent hips! perform your daily rites constantly;
or else, always practice the restraint of breath during the periods of the twilights.
All those who are devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), who have breath control as their ultimate goal,
and who are purified by breath control— they go to the supreme state.

"There is nothing other than *prāṇāyāma* that delivers those submerged in the ocean of *saṃsāra* from the hells and other realms; the restraint of breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*) is the deliverer. Thus [ends the citation].
Now follows the definition of *prāṇāyāma*. Regarding this, the venerable Patañjali says:

"In that [state] existing, the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)" (YS 2.49). Regarding this, the Commentator [Vyāsa] says: "Inhalation (*śvāsa*) is the drawing in of external air; exhalation (*praśvāsa*) is the expulsion of the abdominal air; the cessation of their movement is the absence of both, which is breath control. (YBh 2.49) Regarding this, Vācaspati’s explanation is: "In exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*), there exists the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation; this is breath control. This is the general definition; for instance, where...

When external air is inhaled and retained internally during inhalation (*pūraka*), there is a cessation of the movement of both inhalation and exhalation therein. Likewise, when the abdominal air is expelled and retained externally during exhalation (*recaka*), there is a cessation of the movement of both inhalation and exhalation situated therein. Thus, in the *kumbhaka*, there is the absence of both. According to Bhojadeva, however: "(4) When stability has been achieved in that posture, the specific limb of yoga characterized by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which is caused by that [stability], is to be practiced."

"What is the nature of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)? It is said that *prāṇāyāma* is the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation through the threefold process of expulsion, filling, and retention, within the external and internal locations—namely, at the tip of the nose, the heart, and the navel.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The *haṃsa* (the vital breath) moves thirty-six finger-breadths outside."
By means of that movement to the left and to the right, it is designated as the vital breath (prāṇa).
"The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind located within the body; *āyāma* is that which has it as its basis. (1)
In the Ādipurāṇa: "The internal restraint of the winds that move within, as well as their external and internal suppression, is declared to be prāṇāyāma; it is described as being of two kinds."
It is of two kinds: with seed (*sabīja*) and without seed (*abīja*).
Yājñavalkya says: "The conjunction of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths is called *prāṇāyāma*."
Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold: by means of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
The definition of *pūraka*:
"The filling of air from the outside into the abdomen is indeed *pūraka*.
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "*Pūraka* is so called because of filling (*pūraṇāt*)."
Devala says: "The restraint and filling of the breaths," and in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One should fill the body with external air, like a leather bag."
One should remain thus when [the breath] is full; because it fills, it is known as the "filler" (pūraka).
Yājñavalkya says:
Having drawn in slowly from all sides the air situated outside through the nostrils by means of that very [nostril], [one should retain it].
He who completely fills all the channels is the great cessation known as Pūraka.
Devala says: "The entry into the interior of that chest [of the abdomen] by that very same path [is the practice];
it is called 'filling' (pūraka) because of filling."
Thus, by that which is characterized as the nostril-cavity, the mouth, and the *brahmarandhra*;
as stated in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*:
"Having pressed one nostril with the finger, [one should inhale] through the other."
It is known as *pūraka* because of filling [the breath] through the other nostril.
Regarding the definition of *kumbhaka*, Yājñavalkya states: "(2) Retention of the breath like a filled jar is *kumbhaka*.
In the *Kanda Purāṇa*:
"He neither exhales nor inhales the air situated within or without;
remaining motionless like a filled jar, that indeed is *kumbhaka*."
Yogi Yājñavalkya says:
"Neither exhaling nor inhaling, this breath remains fixed at the tip of the nose;
when one holds it perfectly still in due order, those who know the truth call this 'kumbhaka'."
"Having abandoned both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), that retention of the breath which is blissful is called prāṇāyāma;
this indeed is the pure kumbhaka.
That which one performs after exhaling and filling [the breath] along with the *mātrās* is the *sahita-kumbhaka*.
Other specific varieties of *kumbhaka* will be described later.
Regarding the definition of *recaka*, Yājñavalkya says:
"The exhalation of the air from the abdomen is known as *recaka*.
Likewise: 'Exhaling the entire breath through the nostrils until it is as if empty of air outside...'"
When the upward-moving breath (ūrdhvavāyu) remains after being restrained,
that is the great restraint (mahānirodha) known as recaka.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "The sun, as the presiding deity, releases the wind joined with all the limbs;
that which begins with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava is known by the name recaka."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Having pressed the nostril with a finger by the other hand, one should expel the air from the abdomen; because of this expulsion, it is known as recaka."
Devala says:
"The exhalation (*recaka*) is the constant out-breath. 'Constant' means uninterrupted; 'out-breath' means the emission [of air].
That which [is emitted] through the *brahmagandhra* [aperture], and neither through the mouth nor externally..."
The expulsion of feces through evacuation is called *sārecaka*.
In the *Jaigīṣavya-yoga-śāstra*:
"Exhalation (*recaka*) is proclaimed to be the expulsion of the abdominal air.
The threefold nature of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is described according to the distinctions of minor, middling, and superior.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"The light [breath] consists of twelve mātrās; that which is double that is the medium."
The upper garment is said to consist of three folds.
By the first [application], one should conquer perspiration; by the second, trembling;
and by the third, dejection—one should thus conquer the humors (doṣas) in their proper sequence.
In the Nandipurāṇa:
"Since the youngest [breath] is established with twelve mātrās,
the middle one is proclaimed to have twice as many mātrās."
"Thus, the eldest [breath] is indeed remembered as having three qualities; it brings about stability. Devala says:
"Furthermore, by means of one, two, or three upward breaths, it becomes mild, moderate, or sharp."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The lowest [breath-control] consists of a single exhalation and lasts for twelve mātrās;
the middling, however, consists of three exhalations and lasts for twenty-four mātrās."
The superior [breath-retention] is said to consist of thirty-six mātrās with three upward thrusts;
it is considered the best because it generates perspiration, trembling, and physical impact.
"The yogi should recognize that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been mastered by these signs.
In the *Vāyu Saṃhitā*: "The restraint of *prāṇa* and *apāna* occurs through the sequence beginning with the little finger (*kanyasā*)."
That is taught to be fourfold, according to the division of measure and quality.
The lowest [breath] has a single exhalation and consists of twelve mātrās;
the middle, however, has two exhalations and consists of twenty-four mātrās.
But the superior [prāṇāyāma] is known to consist of thirty-six mātrās and three suppressions;
that which produces perspiration, trembling, and so forth is the highest prāṇāyāma.
At this stage, for the yogin, there arise bliss, horripilation, the rolling of the eyes, trembling of the limbs, as well as talkativeness, wandering, fainting, and so forth.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "The measure of prāṇāyāma is traditionally held to be twelve mātrās;
a low [level] consists of twelve mātrās, accompanied by a single udghāta. (+)
The middling [breath] consists of twenty-four measures due to its being twice obstructed;
however, the primary [breath], which is thrice obstructed, is said to consist of thirty-six measures.
Perspiration, trembling, and rising occur in succession;
here, bliss arises, as well as a sense of intoxication and dizziness.
When one conquers the experience of horripilation, sounds, bodily movements, trembling, whirling,
perspiration, muttering, and so forth, as well as the experience of fainting;
Then the most excellent Prāṇāyāma, which is exceedingly beautiful, is described:
there is whirling, the oscillation of the mind, sound, self-awareness, and the manifestation of the internal resonance (nāda).
In the Vasiṣṭha-yoga: "That which produces perspiration during the breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) is the lowest;
that which causes trembling is said to be middling; and it becomes the highest through rising [of the body]."
As for the definition of a *mātrā*, it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*:
"A *mātrā* is the closing and opening of the eyes, or likewise the pronunciation of two short syllables.
And in the *Nandi-purāṇa*:
"It is taught [in the Skanda Purāṇa]: 'It should be performed quickly with light breaths in twelve measures (+).
Having circumambulated the knee, neither too fast nor too slow. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"She makes a snapping sound with her fingers until she is called 'Mother'. Thus it is said.
Dattātreya says:
"One should release three fingers and rub the two knees."
"One should snap the fingers once; in that manner, the number of *mātrās* is counted.
Likewise:
"The shortest exhalation (*ucchvāsa*) consists of twelve [mātrās]; the middle one is said to be double that."
"It should consist of three times the highest measure; this is proclaimed as the division of measures."
Yājñavalkya says: "The release of three fingers, the wiping around the knees,
and also the clapping of the hands three times— those who know it praise these as the designation for the *mātrā*."
"The milking of a cow, the suckling of a calf, or the flight of an arrow, as well as the ringing of a bell—these are declared to be excessive [distances].
They should always be practiced gradually, in accordance with the place and time. Thus it is said.
And the definition of *udghāta* is as stated in another treatise:
"When the *apāna* is oppressed by the *prāṇa* being expelled,
and having gone upward, it turns back— this is the definition of *udghāta*."

Now, the specific meditations and recitations (*japa*) for *pūraka*, *kumbhaka*, and *recaka* are demonstrated. Vyāsa says: "One should meditate upon [the deity] seated on the navel-lotus during *pūraka*."
One should meditate upon Janārdana, who has the luster of a blue lotus, within the heart-lotus by means of breath-retention (kumbhaka).
One should contemplate the white Śiva situated on the forehead by means of exhalation (recaka)—
pure like a crystal, stainless, and the destroyer of sins.
Bṛhaspati says:
"One should meditate on Prajāpati as red, Viṣṇu as having the luster of a blue lotus, and Śaṅkara, the three-eyed one, as white; by meditating thus, one shall be released from bondage."
Yājñavalkya says:
"By means of kumbhaka, one should meditate upon the Lotus-seated One in the region of the heart."

One should contemplate with the *pūraka* breath the Great-Souled Brahmā, the Grandfather, who has four faces, a ruddy and fair-complexioned body, is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, and is established in the center of the navel.
By means of exhalation (recaka), one should know Īśvara to be situated in the forehead;
he is Maheśvara, resembling pure crystal, stainless, and the destroyer of sins.
Through inhalation (pūraka), one attains union with Viṣṇu; through retention (kumbhaka), proximity to Brahmā;
and by means of the third, exhalation (recaka), one may attain the state of the Lord (Īśvara).
When the contemplation of the three deities occurs through the application of restraint, [this result is achieved].
Through union with fire, wind, and water, one becomes pure by these three.
From cessation wind is born, and from wind fire is born;
from fire water is produced, and thereafter one becomes pure through these three.
"Prāṇāyāma" is said to consist of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka);
indeed, these—pūraka, kumbhaka, and recaka—are composed of the three syllables [of the praṇava].
This very one is declared to be the Praṇava, and the prāṇāyāma consists of that;
having drawn the breath through the iḍā and filled the belly, one remains [therein].
There, one should gradually recollect the letter *A* for sixteen *mātrās*;
thereafter, one should retain the breath, which has been filled and joined with the external air.
O Gārgī, again slowly with thirty-two mātrās by means of Piṅgalā, being well-composed,
one should here likewise meditate upon the form of the syllable *Makāra*.
This is prāṇāyāma; one should practice it again in this manner.
That which causes perspiration during the prāṇāyāmas is said to be inferior;
from trembling it is declared intermediate, and from levitation it is remembered as superior.
One should perform each preceding stage until the highest stage is attained. O Gārgī, when the highest stage is attained, one becomes happy through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
By that very means, one conquers the vital breath even further within the body.
By that [power], the body rises up, having assumed a steady posture;
for it, inhalation and exhalation never exist at any time.
Although both of these qualities may be natural to the body,
nevertheless, they are destroyed by the supreme practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Upon the mastery of those two, one would be capable of performing the solitary *kumbhaka*.
When there is success in the solitary [breath-retention], which is devoid of exhalation and inhalation, then one should practice the combined [breath-retention].
Once the solitary *kumbhaka* is perfected, it is free from both exhaling and filling.
For one who has performed this dance, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
he attains swiftness equal to that of thought, and his sins are destroyed.
This great path to liberation, known by the letter 'M', is the inner self;
it generates the internal sound (nāda), being the retention of breath (kumbhaka) through the restraint of the vital energy (prāṇasaṃyama).
"The restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa-saṃyamana) is the holding of the breath within the body;
this is the means for conquering the vital breath, which destroys all death."
In Haṭhayoga: "From the practice of Kumbhaka, the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī occurs;
from the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, the unimpeded [flow] to the end of the Suṣumṇā arises, and the perfection of Haṭha is born."
In the Vāyusaṃhitā:
"This triad beginning with exhalation (recaka) should be neither too rapid nor too slow;
through the application of the sequence of upward impulses (udghāta), you should consider this the means for accomplishing yoga."
The practice of the three breath-controls, beginning with *recaka* and preceded by the purification of the channels,
extending up to the gradual mastery over the breath, has been taught by those who follow the path of yoga.
That breath control (prāṇāyāma) is of two kinds, distinguished as "with seed" (sagarbha) and "seedless" (vigarbha). For instance, it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
One should practice the yoga of creation while remaining unreceptive to the womb, restrained by the breath;
for him, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the churning, and its application is described first.
"It is proclaimed to be of two kinds: *agarbha* (without seed) and *vigarbha* (with seed).
The "churning" (*mathana*) of this wind called *prāṇa* is *prāṇāyāma*, because it stands in the same relation to the self as churning does to butter. Of these two—
As for its definition, the *Liṅgapurāṇa* states:
"That which is 'with seed' (*sagarbha*) is called 'with recitation' (*sajapa*), and that which is 'without seed' (*agarbha*) is called 'without recitation' (*vijapa*), respectively.
And in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*:
"Breath control (prāṇāyāma) without recitation and meditation is 'without seed' (agarbha); that which is endowed with them is 'with seed' (sagarbha).
Breath control joined with the 'with seed' [practice] is a hundred times more effective than the 'without seed'."
Mental recitation is the counting by mind.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "One should perform the recitation with the mantra, neither too slowly nor too quickly."
"One should always practice mental discernment during the performance of breath control."
By *jāpya* is meant recitation with mantras such as the *gāyatrī*. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"A mantra accompanied by meditation on the deity is proclaimed to be 'with seed' (*sagarbha*)."
The mantra is declared to be the tranquil Vidyā;
the mantra is said to be the syllable Oṃ, which is the conqueror of all mantras.
He is the support for all doubts regarding the deities for all yogins;
within his belly, the entire collection of mantras and all the gods are established.
Together with three mātrās, they are remembered as *i*, *u*, and *m*.
Within these three measures (mātrās), all existence and non-existence are established.
The three measures are traditionally held to be, in order, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna. Skanda, Umā, and Śaṅkara are also said to be these, and they are celebrated as Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
These three fires are said to be joined with the Mātrā and the Praṇava.
Prāṇāyāma accompanied by smoke occurs from meditating on the three measures (mātrās) of that [breath];
it is proclaimed as "with flame" (sajjvāla) from meditating on the deity who is a portion of a kalā.
The objectless state, free from the particles of smoke and measure, arises through reliance on the yoga-nāḍī.

"The 'tranquil' (praśānta) is described in the scriptures as being free from all objective entities. These are the divisions of that which possesses the internal object (*sagarbha*). Here, three divisions of *prāṇāyāma* with an internal object are shown: "with smoke" (*sadhumaka*), "with flame" (*sajvāla*), and "tranquil" (*praśānta*). Among these, it is "with smoke" due to meditation on the three measures (*mātrā*). It is "with flame" due to meditation on the portions of the vital breath (*prāṇavāṃśa*) in the form of measures, and on their respective deities. But the "tranquil" is "pierced by the non-utterance of mantra. The non-utterance of mantra is its mental contemplation; it is joined with that piercing. By this, it is implied that it is also devoid of meditation on the meaning expressed by the mantra.

Regarding the passage beginning with “*kalāmātrādhūmāṃśa*,” the term *mātrā* refers to one who is devoid of meditation on its parts and is thus tranquil (*praśānta*). Here, by the word *aṃśa*, the deities denoted by the *mātrās* are understood. The *mātrā* has emerged from the form of the smoke-deity and the tuft of hair (*jābāla*) due to the speaker’s reliance; and it is tranquil due to the reliance upon the *yoga-nāḍī*. The *yoga-nāḍī* is the *suṣumnā*. Thus, the *prāṇāyāma* with its internal essence (*sagarbha*) has been shown. In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
“By the utterance of ‘Oṃ,’ everything that exists and does not exist is grasped.”
This is the imperishable Brahman, known by the supreme designation of Oṃkāra.

"The Praṇava is the bow, the Self is the arrow, and the Brāhmaṇa is the one equipped with the weapon; with heedfulness, one must pierce [the mark], for like the arrow, one shall become absorbed in That. (1)
Yājñavalkya says:
"The syllable Om is declared to be the ultimate goal of all established doctrines, as well as of the Vedas and Vedānta, and of other scriptures as well."
The Vedas, beginning with the Praṇava, are established within the Praṇava;
the entire realm of speech is the Praṇava; therefore, one should practice the Praṇava.
Likewise: "A twice-born man, when restraining his breath, should recite the three Gāyatrīs conjoined with the Praṇava and joined with the Vyāhṛtis."
By this, the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) containing the Gāyatrī has been shown.
Regarding its definition, Manu says: "The Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras..."
Reciting [the mantra] three times while the breath is restrained is called prāṇāyāma.
The seven well-known *vyāhṛtis* begin with *bhūḥ*.

As stated in the *Yogiyājñavalkya*: "The seven *vyāhṛtis* are declared to be used constantly during breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*): *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *mahaḥ*, *janaḥ*, *tapaḥ*, and likewise *satyam*.
And here, Śiva [recites] the Yajurvedic mantra beginning with *oṃ āpo jyotiḥ*.
And so says the Kyāsa: "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ—this [mantra] [is applied] in all nine [levels], beginning with Bhūḥ.
Yājñavalkya states the application of the *praṇava*:
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, mahar, janaḥ, tapaḥ, and likewise satyam—
each joined with the syllable *oṃ* (*pratyoṃkāra*), and then that which is beyond Savitṛ."
"One should subsequently employ the mantra 'oṃ āpo jyotiḥ' as the head;
indeed, through the practice of repeating this three times, it is designated as 'prāṇāyāma'.
In this context, the syllable *oṃ* should also be understood as being included within the mantra.
And likewise Yama says:
"One should mutter the seven vyāhṛtis preceded by the syllable Oṃ, together with the Śiras and the Gāyatrī; this is the supreme austerity of prāṇāyāma."
In the phrase "one should mutter," it should be understood that this is done mentally. Thus, Saṃvarta says:
"The seven Vyāhṛtis, constantly joined with the Praṇava..."
A twice-born man should recite the Sāvitrī together with the Śiras three times mentally.
Yājñavalkya says:
"A Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with Vedic learning and always devoted to his own duty..."
He should recite Vedic mantras, and never those that are worldly.
Some desire to recite Vedic mantras for the sake of benefiting living beings;
however, the recitation prescribed for a twice-born man or a kṣatriya is that performed during the restraint of the breath.
O Gārgī, for Vaiśyas engaged in dharma, for women, Śūdras, and ascetics,
there is no mantra at the time of restraining the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyamana) other than the syllable Om (praṇava).
The wise prescribe that either a mantra ending in "namaḥ" dedicated to Śiva or one dedicated to Viṣṇu should be used;
or else, a Śūdra may practice a worldly mantra according to the prescribed rules.
"A Śūdra and women should never recite Vedic mantras.
Thus, the varieties of *sagarbha* [mantra] have been described; in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, p.
Exhalation (recaka), the void (śūnyaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka)—
the suspension of the movement of breath is thus fourfold, known as prāṇāyāma.

Among those, some characteristics such as *recita* and others have already been indicated, and some will be explained later. Regarding the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyalakṣaṇa*), the *Kālikāpurāṇa* states:
"Then, one should contemplate knowledge in the center, which is entirely devoid of appearances."
One should awaken the wind situated in the exterior; that one should designate as Śanaiścara (Saturn).
"Then," meaning: having performed exhalation (*recaka*) through the *nāḍī* presided over by the deity Bhānu, preceded by the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*.
As it is stated in Jaigīṣavya’s *Yogaśāstra*: "One who is fatigued by the five types of *āyāma* [breathing exercises] should perform exhalation and the others in their proper order."
Exhalation, inhalation, retention, upward movement, and downward movement.
The connection is that the yogi attains perfection.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Prāṇa is composed of breath; breath is called air (*vāyu*); air is declared to be the self (*ātman*)."
Its extent has been declared by the skilled teachers to be of six kinds.
"One who is disciplined through the restraint of even the vital breath is rightly so called."
And its sixfold nature consists of: two types of exhalation and inhalation (recaka and pūraka), the combined (sahita) and the isolated (kevala),
and two types of retention (kumbhaka)— the superior and the inferior.
Devala says:
"The *kumbha* (retention) is to be known as sevenfold, according to its divisions beginning with *recita*. These are:
*recita*, *pūrita*, *śānta*, *pratyāhāra*, *uttara*, and *adhara*."
"Kumbhaka has been thus described as being of seven types.
Likewise, he states the definition of the sevenfold [breathing], beginning with *recita* (exhalation),
on page 187:
The retention of exhaled air is called *recita-kumbhaka*;
the obstruction of inhaled air within the abdomen is declared to be *pūrita-kumbhaka*.
The pervasion of the body both internally and externally is the *śānta-kumbhaka*;
the restraint [of the breath] between two stations is the *kumbhaka* called *pratyāhāra*.
Having filled [the body] in sequence, the subsequent kumbhaka occurs by blocking [the breath] higher and higher in the heart and other locations;
the lower kumbhaka occurs by blocking it lower and lower from the top.
Having abandoned both exhaling and inhaling, the retention of the vital air (marut) by means of the mind—
whether it be equalized at the regions of the navel and so forth— is proclaimed as "kumbhaka" (the pot-like breath-retention).

Regarding the phrase "of the body," the meaning is that after setting aside exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) resulting from the retention of the vital air (*vāyu*) within and without the body by means of the mind. In the expression "of the two places" (*sthānayoḥ*), the boundaries are to be understood. The locations are: the soles of the feet, the private parts, the navel, the heart, the abdomen, the throat, the uvula, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). The retention of the vital air in the intervals or middles between these pairs of locations is the *kumbhaka* known as *pratyāhāra*. From the distinction of locations—from the head down to the heart—there is a difference between *śama* and *śānta* due to the difference in the processes of exhaling and filling.

The Blessed Patañjali states the definition of the fourfold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), beginning with exhalation (*recaka*): "It has external, internal, and stationary movements; it is observed by place, time, and number, and is long and subtle"; "the fourth is that which transcends the objects of the external and internal.
(1) The meaning of this is as follows:

The outward movement of the breath is *recaka* (exhalation); the inward movement is *praśvāsa* (inhalation), which is *pūraka* (inhalation); and the internal suspension of movement is *kumbhaka* (retention). When both exhalation and inhalation are abandoned and the breath is obstructed by a single, powerful effort of retention, the vital air (*prāṇa*) is made to remain motionless like water; thus it is called *kumbhaka*. Just as water placed on a heated stone dries up from all sides and undergoes contraction, so too the subtle [breath] within the body becomes rigid; this is the "suspended" (*stambha*) movement. This threefold *prāṇāyāma* is described on page 188.

Characterized by location (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), and number (*saṃkhyā*), it is designated as "long" and "subtle. Characterized by location—such as from the nose up to the *dvādaśānta* [the point twelve finger-breadths above the head]—by time—such as by the snapping of fingers (*tālachoṭikā*) and so forth—and by number—as previously mentioned—it is likewise measured by thirty-six *mātrās* and so on. Furthermore, for the sake of knowing that "this many times it has been performed, or by this many inhalations and exhalations, the first *udghāta* occurs," the inclusion of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is employed as a defining characteristic.

Udvāta is the striking of the head by the upward-moving breath (prāṇa) originating from the base of the navel. Indeed, when this [striking] is practiced in the sequence of days, fortnights, months, and so forth, it becomes designated by the term "long-subtle" (dīrghasūkṣma), because it is perceived as long in its extension over space and time, and because it is subtle.

The meaning of the second [type] is as follows: having directed attention toward and reflected upon two objects—the external object, such as the *dvādaśānta*, and the internal object, such as the heart-wheel (*hṛdaya-cakra*) or the navel-wheel (*nābhi-cakra*)—the cessation of movement in the form of suspension (*stambha*) is the fourth *prāṇāyāma*. The distinction of this from the third [type], *kumbhaka*, is that while the latter is accomplished suddenly through a state of suspension by means of reflecting on the external and internal objects simultaneously—like water fallen upon a heated stone—this [fourth type] depends upon reflection.

By practicing with great effort, one attains that particular state through the successive mastery of each stage. Regarding the fruit of all four types of *prāṇāyāma*, the venerable Patañjali says: "From that, the veil over the light is destroyed, and there arises fitness of the mind for concentration (*dhāraṇā*)" (Yoga Sūtra 2.52).

Therefore, from this breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), that obscuration of the light—which consists of the nature of omniscience residing in the *sattva* of the mind—is diminished and destroyed, being of the nature of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Likewise, the mind acquires fitness for the concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) whose characteristics will be described hereafter. The meaning of the aphorism is that the mind, its defects diminished by breath controls, becomes steady wherever it is held.
Just as clarified butter is perceived by the wise through the application of methods such as milk,
or as fire is obtained from wood by means of the wind, so too is the imperishable Self realized.
The exertion of the vital breath is its friction; therefore, yoga is said to be the means [for its cessation].
Likewise: [p. 189] —
The vital breath (prāṇa), which is the wind, is declared to be the collective function of all the senses;
indeed, by its conquest, the senses themselves are conquered.
Since the non-difference between the function and the possessor of the function has been proclaimed,
therefore, by the mere conquest of the function, the possessor of the function is conquered.
Having conquered the horses of the senses— which have been weakened by the scrubbing-stone of *prāṇāyāma*— through the two lamps of knowledge and dispassion, everything indeed becomes conquered;
for both heaven and hell are nothing other than the senses themselves.
When restrained, these [faculties] lead to excellence; when unrestrained, they lead to heaven or to hell.
They say the body is the chariot; the senses are its horses;
the person (puruṣa) is the ancient charioteer; and breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is known as the whip.
The mind, drawn in and held steady by the two rays of knowledge and dispassion, and cleansed by the friction of breath control, gradually attains immobility.
In Haṭhayoga: "Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, as well as Sītkāra, Śītalī, Bhastrikā,
Bhramarī, and Mūrcchā— these are the eight types of Kumbhaka."
In that regard, the definition of the concomitant has already been stated by me previously.
Bhramarī: "The inhalation (pūraka) is the intense roar of a bee, the exhalation (recaka) is the soft, low hum of a female bee;
through the constant practice of yoga by the lords of yogis,"
"A certain play of bliss has arisen from the awakened mind."
Mūrcchā:
"At the end of the inhalation (pūraka), one should perform the Jālandhara lock very firmly; then, one should exhale slowly.
This is called 'mūrcchanā,' which bestows the bliss of mental absorption."
One should produce the sound "sīt" in the mouth and likewise release it through the nose;
by practicing in this manner, one becomes Kāmadevī, the second [type].
Having fully served the circle of Yoginīs, one becomes the agent of creation and destruction;
neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep, nor drowsiness, nor laziness arises.
By this method, the body of that lord of yogins upon the circle of the earth shall become independent and free from all calamities.
"He who constantly drinks the vital breath (prāṇa) through the rasanā at the root of the palate will,
within half a year, experience the complete destruction of all diseases."
In the *Yogabīja*, regarding the piercing of the solar channel (*sūryabheda*):
"Then, on a comfortable seat, the yogi, having assumed the bound vajra posture (*baddhavajrāsana*),
should slowly draw in the external air through the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*)."
Performing the kumbhaka (retention) from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails, up to the very crown of the head,
one should then slowly exhale the breath through the left channel (nāḍī).
"The purification of the skull, which destroys wind disorders and removes the defects of worms—
one should perform this supreme 'Sūryabheda' again and again."—
Ujjāyī.
Having restrained the mouth and drawn the breath back through the two nostrils,
it should be made to reach from the heart and throat down to the base of the spine with a sound.
One should retain the breath as before and then exhale through the northern direction (the left nostril);
this removes defects of phlegm in the throat and increases the channel of the body.
The practice known as *Ujjāyī* Kumbhaka should be performed while walking or standing; it destroys the defects located in the channels, the abdomen, and the bodily constituents (*dhātus*).

Having placed both soles of the feet likewise upon the thighs, the *padmāsana* is properly formed; it is the destroyer of all sins. (Bhastrikā) — [and] having placed both soles of the feet likewise upon the thighs... [the *padmāsana* is properly formed; it is the destroyer of all sins].
Having properly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with the neck and belly held straight and the body well-composed,
one should carefully control the mouth and exhale the breath through the nose.
Just as it settles in the heart and throat, one should fill [the breath] up to the skull;
one should properly fill the vital air with force up to the heart-lotus.
One should likewise cause it to be evacuated again and again after filling it,
just as the bellows of smiths are moved with force;
even so, the wind residing within one's own body is moved by means of the intellect.
One should fill [the body] in such a way that the vital breath (āśrama) remains within the body.
Just as the abdomen becomes full [with air], so too it becomes light;
one should hold the nose firmly with the middle and index fingers, excluding the thumbs.
Having performed the retention (kumbhaka) as before, one should then exhale through the iḍā;
this removes wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases the digestive fire of the body.
One should perform the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, which destroys sin, bestows happiness, and is auspicious;
it resides at the mouth of the Brahma-nāḍī and removes the bolt of the door.
This kumbhaka, known as "the bellows," must be performed specifically for the purpose of breaking the three knots produced in the body in a proper manner.
Śītalī:
Having drawn in the air with the tongue as before, following the retention (kumbhaka),
the wise practitioner should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils.
The kumbhaka known as śītalī also destroys abdominal tumors, enlargement of the spleen, disorders of wind and bile, hunger, thirst, and poisons.
Yājñavalkya says:
"Furthermore, I shall tell you in truth the means for mastering the vital breath (prāṇa):
having drawn the breath from the outside and filled the belly, one remains [in that state]."
One should diligently hold the vital breath (prāṇa) with the mind at the center of the navel, the tip of the nose, or the big toe, either during the periods of twilight or at all times.
Freed from all diseases and devoid of fatigue, the yogin shall live;
O Gārgī, the concentration on the tip of the nose is the cause of victory over the vital breath.
By holding [the breath] in the center of the navel, there shall be the destruction of all diseases.
The man who, having mounted the rasanā with the breath, drinks [the amṛta] constantly, for him there is neither fatigue nor burning; likewise, his diseases perish.
He who, at the two twilights or during the time sacred to Brahmā, draws in and drinks the air,
will within three months attain eloquent speech like that of Sarasvatī.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, one is liberated from great diseases;
having projected the self into the Self, one should fix it within Kuṇḍalinī.
Others know that his diseases such as consumption and the like are destroyed;
having brought the breath into the tongue, one should restrain it at the root of the tongue.
The wise man who drinks it unoffered enjoys complete prosperity.
Having drawn the self into the self within the space between the eyebrows by means of the senses,
he who drinks the food of the thirty gods is liberated even from diseases.
Having drawn in the breath through the tongue during the twilight for one month,
he who drinks the food of the thirty gods should hold it within the middle of his belly.
Furthermore, abdominal tumors, hard masses, and splenic enlargements, as well as other diseases arising from the three humors—
all those ailments located within the belly, including their underlying sins, are destroyed.
All fevers are destroyed, as are various kinds of diseases for many years; O Gārgī, what is the use of saying more? Even gray hair and other such signs of age perish.
In the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
"Without touching the space between the pair of 'royal teeth' [the two upper incisors], having placed the tongue near them..."
One should drink the wind through the hollow of the crow’s beak;
this is the supreme restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Furthermore, that man who, having drawn together the joints of his arms, draws [them] like a bird with its beak and the wind;
If one places it at the mouth of one's own Kuṇḍalinī,
one lives having been liberated from the disease of consumption (tuberculosis).
The man who, free from sloth, drinks the wind with his tongue like a parrot's beak day and night,
will certainly become so within a year.
Even hearing and seeing [it] are exceedingly far off.
What is the use of these many words?
By drinking the wind through the beaks of two cranes,
one's destruction occurs swiftly along with old age.
The intense fear of death caused by Mṛtyu for mortals.
Having placed the tongue against the root of the palate without agitation,
and having pressed the teeth firmly against the teeth,
he who should drink the wind very slowly;
Together with palaces and cities, from which [blood] flowed within;
Within six months, the lord of practitioners, freed from all diseases and sins, is liberated;
within one year, he overcomes the uneven messenger of death.
Having conquered on earth, one may live for a long time.
O you with hair as black as a swarm of bees, by virtue of three years of practice, he knows whether poison has passed or is yet to come; it does not spread through your body.
Even when bitten by the most terrible lords of serpents, [he remained unharmed].
Neither artificial poison, nor that which is stationary or mobile, nor even other *kālakūṭa* poisons can [overcome] it.
Or perhaps Bhairava himself, having assumed the eight qualities under the influence of time, sports upon the surface of the earth.

He who places within the cavern of his own belly that white stream known as the *vajra-nāḍī*— which flows from the hollow of the sky-lotus, carrying the pure essence of food that has passed through the cavity between the formidable fangs of Yama’s consort, Gaurī— [attains the supreme state].
For him, there would be a dense mass of clouds for the dissolution of the vessel of the universe, and a density even greater than that of the death of Death itself.
When it has reached a state of swoon, it truly removes all disease;
when increased, it enables men to travel through the sky. Vāta, like nectar, extends the entirety of immortality.

P.195 For, through many statements, the practice of yoga has been prohibited during a state of illness, as was already demonstrated at length previously; furthermore, because it contradicts direct experience. As for the scriptural mention of the fruit consisting of the destruction of disease, that refers to the practice of all its constituent parts taken together, not to merely two or three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

For it is clearly observed in all the Yoga scriptures—and has been demonstrated by us as well in various previous contexts—that within all living beings on this earth, all diseases, ailments, fevers, and so forth exist in a subtle form like seeds; and that some of these are destroyed by postures (*āsanas*), some by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), some by withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and some by concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Thus, the propitiation of the Supreme Lord alone is the remover of all obstacles, such as the diseases and ailments born of fate.

"By the union of the seed-syllables of the [five] elements and so forth, having unified [the breath] from its own place, the heart-lotus, and leading it while simultaneously meditating upon Brahmā and Fire.

Having joined the function of the prāṇa with the apāna and drawn it up into the heart,

Having led [the breath] from the middle of the thighs to the middle of the throat,
the palms, the face, the tip of the nose, the eyes, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and finally to the crown of the head;

Clarity of sound, clear vision,
freedom from disease, mastery of the *bindu*, stimulation of the digestive fire, and purification of the channels— these are the signs of mastery over the body (*haṭha*).
As proclaimed by Īśvara:
"In all yogas, these states of yoga occur: the beginning, the pot, the refinement, and the accomplishment."
For it is said:
"When there is purification of the channels for the yogi who perceives reality, then,
for one whose sins have been destroyed, the possibility of undertaking [spiritual practice] arises."
The signs in the body of a yogin are seen through the purification of the channels;
they shall be described by me in brief for my devotee.

He has a symmetrical body, is fragrant, possesses great luster, and has a voice like that of a celestial being; he has a powerful digestive fire, enjoys excellent pleasures, is happy, and is beautiful in all his limbs.
With a fully expanded heart, the yogi becomes endowed with all enthusiasm and strength;
thereafter, the yogi shall possess the power to retain the vital air (vāyu) as desired.
By retaining the breath as desired, the practice of *kumbhaka* (breath retention) is certainly perfected.
Once *kevala-kumbhaka* (the absolute retention) is accomplished, what is there that remains unattained for the yogi in this world?
Sweat arises in the body of the yogi; this is the first, lowest stage.
The second stage is trembling, which is difficult to overcome and is considered the middle stage.
When the sufferings of existence have been withdrawn, then meditative absorption (samādhi) arises;
when that absorption is perfected, it is filled with innate bliss (sahajānanda).
This mind, when perfected, brings an end to all suffering and existence;
whatever the yogi performs at that time, all of it comes to fruition in that very instant.
One should certainly know the characteristics of the yogin who has attained the perfected body,
as well as the emanation of bodies and so forth, and the entry into another's body.
Seeing and hearing from a distance—these are established as the characteristics of Vāyu;
that should be known as liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which bestows the fruit of all desires.
The yogi who has attained liberation while living shall proceed to the state of great liberation;
then that lord of yogis becomes perfected in pure samādhi.
Then there is the great samādhi called "Dharmamegha" (Cloud of Dharma).
At that time, the yogin, consisting of bliss, becomes omniscient and all-seeing.
He was always worshipped in the three worlds, his command never obstructed;
he possessed unimpeded movement, was wise, and was filled with unimpeded bliss.
Endowed with all sovereign qualities and possessed of all perfections,
he is unbound by all beings, a lord of yogis, and free from all defects.
Therefore, the yogi who consists of all things and who consists of all beings—when satisfied, he delivers the world; when angry, he is the destroyer of all.
When a yogin has attained the perfection of knowledge, he is no longer fearsome;
thus for thousands of years and hundreds of lakhs [of years].
"The blissful perfected yogins dwell in caves on the mountain peaks," as stated by Īśvara in the *P.215*.
Then, by the very sequence of practice, the triad beginning with the jar shall manifest;
by means of which the complete perfection of the yogin will certainly be attained as instructed.
Mastery over speech, the power to move at will, vision from afar,
likewise hearing from afar, perception of the subtle, and entry into another's body.
By applying an ointment of feces and urine, gold becomes invisible; likewise, these [powers] arise for the great ones, as does the state of moving through the sky for yogins.
When the supreme state of the "pot" (ghaṭāvasthā) is attained by those who practice breath-control,
then there is nothing in this wheel of saṃsāra that they cannot accomplish.
O Lord, the yogi and the man of knowledge alike should be firm in posture;
when the posture is well-stabilized, he enters into the midst of the vital air (vāyu).
Through even a slight entry of the vital air, the arising of knowledge occurs for the yogi.
Once the equipment of knowledge has been produced, one becomes equal to a yogin indeed.
Free from defects, suffering, hunger, sleep, old age, and death,
he becomes the creator of creation and dissolution, equal to the Lord of Yogins.
Whether it be so or not, here indeed is the unbroken state of liberation.
Because the prāṇa and apāna, the nāda and bindu, and the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) unite and become one, it is therefore called vighaṭa.
When one is able to maintain [the breath] for at least one watch (yāma) without effort,
then the withdrawal (pratyāhāra) should certainly take place, and not otherwise.
Whatever the lord of yogis knows, that he should contemplate within himself.
By means of those senses through which one is not agitated, that constitutes the conquest of the senses.
When, through the practice of yoga, [the breath] remains full for the duration of a watch (yāma),
then the yogi should perform the kumbhaka once.
When the eight staffs (daṇḍās) have subsided and the vital breath (vāyu) becomes motionless within the yoginī, [then that state is attained].
Then, being incapable [of further distraction], the wise one should remain hidden like a blade of grass;
thereafter, through practice, the stage of familiarity arises for the yogin.
When the vital breath (prāṇa), having abandoned the moon and the sun, remains motionless, the breath,
as if enveloped by the wind, shall move through the *suṣumnā* into the ether.
Having grasped the power of action and having pierced through the wheels without doubt,
then the state of mastery arises through the yoga of practice.
Then the yogi certainly perceives the Trikūṭa-karman;
thereafter, for the sake of experiencing his own karma, he should perform the "emanation of bodies" (kāyavyūha).
At this time, the great yogi should practice the fivefold concentration (pañcadhā dhāraṇā).
By means of which there shall be the attainment of moving through the earth and the removal of fear from those very elements;
likewise, there are five ghaṭikās in the base (ādhāra), and similarly in the navel and between the eyebrows.
Likewise, the wise one should hold [the breath] for five ghaṭikās above the middle of the eyebrows;
then, indeed, the lord of yogis will certainly not be lost to the earth and other elements.
The wise man who practices the retention of the five elements does not face death, even when the hundred-fold Brahman has departed.
Then, through the very process of practice, the perfection of yogis shall arise;
by which, having severed the seeds of beginningless karma, they become immortal.
When concentration becomes perfected according to one's own desire, then,
within a month, the wise yogi shall become liberated while living.
Having seized the wind and the power of action,
the impetuous one swiftly pierces all the wheels and dissolves into the power of knowledge.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "trikūṭaṃ karmaṇaḥ" is as follows: some actions are to be experienced exclusively in heaven, while others, however, are to be experienced in hells such as Avīci and the like. (P.217)

The three-peaked nature of actions (*karma*). For the sake of experiencing those [fruits of action] and for the sake of experiencing his own sovereignty, the yogi should practice the emanation of a multitude of bodies (*kāyavyūha*). The procedure for this is as stated in the *Pātañjala*:

"For the yogi who has directly realized reality, the primary causes—consisting of pure egoity (*asmitāmātra*)—originate simultaneously within the bodies that have been manifested for the simultaneous enjoyment of the fruits of karma and for the experience of the eightfold sovereign powers such as *aṇimā*. Like sparks from a fire, because those minds are directed by the single root-mind which existed at the time of yogic practice, they follow its lead."

Having stated that the cause for their distinctness of mind—consisting in the attainment of birth and so forth—is the absence of karmic impressions (vāsanā), it is further declared that the karma of the yogi is neither white nor black, because it is performed with the intention of renouncing the fruits of action and is thus distinct from other types of karma.

Because actions are performed with the intention of renouncing their fruits, there is no commencement of those fruits. Even for the latent impressions (vāsanā) of knowledge acquired over thousands of previous births, their beginninglessness is not contradicted by the fact that they produce results such as memory upon experiencing them in various bodies; for even though they are beginningless, they are rooted in experience, attachment, and ignorance which occur in a sequence. Alternatively, through the practice of knowledge and yoga, ignorance is rendered as if burnt away, thereby uprooting [the impressions] and making actions easy to abandon.

If it be objected that the exhaustion of karma occurs solely through the exhaustion of its fruits, then the scriptures, law codes, epics, and Purāṇas that prescribe expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) would be invalid; this is not so, because of the diversity of karma. To explain: among the karmas of all living beings, some are to be destroyed by expiatory rites such as the *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* performed while the body still exists, while others are to be destroyed solely by experience. In that regard, for those karmas that are to be destroyed solely by experience, the yogi must indeed create a plurality of bodies (*kāyavyūha*) for the purpose of experiencing them.

Furthermore, the statement that "karma is not destroyed without being experienced," and so forth, should be understood as referring to *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma), which is destroyed solely by experience; or else, it refers to those living beings who have not performed expiation (*prāyaścitta*), meaning that for them, karma is not destroyed without experience. Otherwise, the lack of authority of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas—which teach expiation—would be unavoidable. (18.07.2017—P.218)

Thus it may be said. These stages arise—whether over a long period or a short time—according to the distinction between practitioners who are dull, middling, or superior, and those who are dull, middling, superior, or even more superior, and are designated as *tāmasa*, *rājasa*, or *sāttvika*.
Accordingly, it is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi*:
"Those afflicted by disease, the weak, the elderly, the spiritless, and householders..."
Those men who are weak in spirit and weak in vigor should be known as soft-natured.
Within twelve years,
these [qualities] become established as a single state for those who are mature in conduct, well-practiced, energetic, and possessed of equal intelligence.
They are to be known as standing in the middle regarding the paths of yoga, likewise middling in their application of yoga;
they possess middling resolve, middling passion, and middling prowess.
Within eight years, one of these stages is accomplished:
they become heroic, successful, patient, and high-minded.
Established in their own place, those of steady intellect would become healthy;
they would always possess their own syllables through constant practice and be ever endowed with honor.
Those who possess meritorious karma and are intensely devoted to yoga should be known as such;
for those at the highest stage of intensity, success is achieved within six years.
Possessing great strength, great bodies, great heroism, and great voices,
these men were freed from great delusion, peaceful, and possessed of great compassion.
They had practiced all the scriptures, were adorned with every auspicious mark,
possessed forms resembling those of the Omniscient One, and were free from all diseases.
Endowed with the prime of youth, these best of men were free from change,
stainless, free from fear, unimpeded, and undisturbed.
Those of noble lineage and great resolve, who have practiced in previous lives,
deliver other beings and cross over themselves as well.
It should be understood that there are beings who possess all the marks in an even more superior degree.
Through three years, this one state becomes well-known;
and through these three states, yoga shall attain perfection.
In the Yogaśāstra:
"Having blocked the gates to hell and having drunk the vital air (marut), it is firmly retained; having led the apāna and fire together into space, it is raised upward by means of the śakti."
Having performed the placement [of the syllables] upon the head according to this rite, joined with meditation on the self,
as long as one remains thus, there arises a union with the winds of the gods.
Having restrained the mind at the navel and having diligently suppressed the downward movement of the vital air, one should contract the root of the apāna; then,
having led that subtle form which resides with the fire and the moon into the heart-lotus, and subsequently into the eyeball, the palate, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having pierced through the void and the supreme void, he enters the sky where the god Maheśa dwells.
In the Vāsiṣṭha: "Know Kuṇḍalinī to be the life-force of the living being— she who is also called the 'latter Aṣṭakā'—
like a flower-cluster of the inner fragrance."
Having filled that power through the practice of inhalation (pūraka), one remains steady;
then there arises the stability of Bhairava as well as the plumpness of the body.
When the vital breath (prāṇa-māruta), having filled the interior through inhalation,
is led upward by consciousness alone, it endures the sequence of the exertion of dharma.
Like clarified butter, it moves swiftly upward, reaching the state of being like a staff;
having taken hold of all the channels that are bound to the body and resemble creepers, it ascends.
Then, it completely drenches this entire body.
Like a bellows filled with an unceasing wind, it [the body] expels the person who has entered within.
Thus, through yoga— the playful exercise of practice—
yogins attain the lofty state of moving through the sky, just as the wretched [demons] attained the status of Indra.
When the Kuṇḍalinī power, by means of the flow through the fire-channel,
emerges externally above the door-panel at a height of twelve finger-breadths;
By means of the practice of exhalation (recaka), which restrains hundreds of channels, one attains stability for a muhūrta; then, the vision of the space within the body arises.
O Rāghava, by means of the eye of the intellect established upon the ascent of consciousness,
the Siddhas moving through the sky are seen, bestowing their own purposes as if in a dream;
[they are perceived] from the mouth at the end of the twelve [fingers] through the practice of exhalation (recaka).
When the vital breath has been made to remain for a long time, it enters the supreme city.
If one should abide entirely within the Self, having abandoned both coming and going,
then the disease of that person is destroyed, like wind driven from within.

O descendant of Raghu, all attainments from sovereignty up to liberation are achieved solely by means of controlling the vital breath within the body; so it is for all beings, both mobile and immobile.
P.221 Now follows the examination of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).

Regarding that, Patañjali states the nature and the fruit of *pratyāhāra* in the two sūtras: "Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the senses from their respective objects so that they conform to the nature of the mind itself" (YS 2.54), and "From that, the supreme mastery over the senses [is attained]" (YS 2.55). The meaning of this is as follows: *pratyāhāra* is that wherein the senses are withdrawn (*prati-samāhriyante*) from their own respective objects.

To explain how this is accomplished, he says: the objects of the senses, such as the eyes and so forth, are the *upādāna* (material cause). Their conjunction with that [object]—that is, their functioning by being directed toward it—is their state of being one with it. By abandoning that state of being directed toward the object and remaining established in their own essential nature alone, they become conformers to the mind (*citta*) when that condition exists. Consequently, following the mind like bees following the queen bee, all the senses proceed accordingly. Therefore, through the restraint of the mind, they are withdrawn.

The meaning is that when withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is practiced in this very way, the senses become so necessarily dependent [on the mind] that even when led toward external objects, they do not go there.
As stated in the *Śivagītā*:
"Of the senses wandering among objects by their very nature..."
That which is called restraint by the virtuous is declared to be withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
In the Yogaśāstra, page 222:
The sun draws back the stream consisting of lunar nectar;
that which is its drawing back is called *pratyāhāra*.
Just as the sun, situated in its third phase, withdraws its radiance, so too the yogi,
established in the third part, withdraws the modifications of the mind.
Yājñavalkya says:
"The forceful withdrawal of the senses as they wander among their objects by their very nature is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal)."
Whatever one perceives, one should perceive all that as being like the Self within the Self;
this is declared by the great-souled masters of yoga to be withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Regarding those obligatory rites prescribed for embodied beings,
their performance within oneself is that which is carried out mentally, without external action.
That withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is also the supreme means for achieving yoga;
it is highly praised in withdrawal and is always practiced by yogis.
The eighteenth [method] is the retention of the vital air within the locations of the vital points (marmans);
withdrawing it from each location to each successive location is called pratyāhāra.
O Gārgī, may the two Aśvins, the supreme physicians of the gods,
likewise protect the vital points (marmas) within the body for the sake of success in both yoga and liberation.
