I shall describe all of them correctly; listen, O lady of excellent vows!
[The first is] on the big toe and the ankle, and likewise on the left calf.
In the heart, at the root of the navel, in the middle of the two thighs,
at the root of the anus, and thereafter in the middle of the body, [is] the generative organ.
And the navel, O Gārgī, the heart, and likewise the pit of the throat;
The root of the palate, the root of the nose, and the circles of the eyes.
O best of sages! The space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the crown of the head—these are the vital points (marmasthāna), and they are measured separately at these locations.
The measure from the foot to the ankle is four and a half finger-breadths;
from the ankle to the middle of the calf, it should be known as ten finger-breadths.
From the middle of the shank to the base of the altar is one finger-breadth;
from the base of the altar, O lady of beautiful hips, the knee should be two finger-breadths.
The lords of sages have stated that the middle of the thigh from the groin measures nine finger-breadths;
likewise, O Gārgī, the knee should be two finger-breadths from the middle of the thigh.
O Gārgī, the lords of sages say that the middle of the thighs is nine finger-breadths from the knees;
likewise, the root of the anus is nine finger-breadths from the middle of the thighs.
Likewise, from the base of the anus to the middle of the body is two and a half finger-breadths;
similarly, from the middle of the body to the genitals is likewise two and a half finger-breadths.
O Gārgī, one should know that from the genitals to the navel is ten fingers' breadth;
from the navel to the middle of the heart is fourteen fingers' breadth, O best of the twice-born.
Six finger-breadths from the center of the heart is the pit of the throat;
likewise, from the pit of the throat, the root of the tongue is four finger-breadths away.
One should leave a space of four finger-breadths at the root of the nose;
the location of the eyes is desired to be half a finger-breadth from that root.

Therefore, the distance between the two eyebrows is considered to be half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula). From the middle of the eyebrows upwards, there should be three finger-breadths (aṅgula) for that which is called the forehead (lalāṭa).
Above the forehead, there is the space known as Vyoma, which is likewise three finger-breadths.
Having mounted the vital air upon these locations with the mind, one should hold it there.
For one who performs pratyāhāra by drawing [the senses] back from every single object,
all diseases perish and his yogic powers indeed become perfected.
Certain practitioners, men skilled in yogic disciplines, declare: [P.224]
O lady of excellent hips, listen to the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra); I shall describe it to you.
Having filled the air like a jar from the middle of the earth and the oceans,
one should mentally retain the wind impelled by the *prāṇāyāma*.
Having drawn [the breath] from the aperture of space, one should hold it again at the forehead;
having drawn the wind from the forehead, one should restrain it between the eyebrows.
Drawing [the breath] from the middle of the eyebrows, one should restrain it within the center of the eyes.
Drawing [the breath] evenly from the middle of the eyes, one should restrain it at the root of the nose.
One should restrain the prāṇa at the root of the tongue from the base of the nose;
having drawn it back from the root of the tongue, one should fix it in the hollow of the throat.

From the throat to the center of the heart, from the center of the heart to the center of the navel, from the center of the navel back to the genitals, and then one should move it from the genitals upward.
O Gārgī! From the middle of the body [it goes] to the anus; from the anus indeed to the root of the thighs;
from the root of the thighs, between those two, one should restrain it from the knees.
Then, from that root of the consciousness, one should likewise draw [the breath] into the middle of the two shanks;
having drawn the wind from the shanks, one should restrain it like a bubble.
Therefore, O Gārgī, one should restrain that [breath] between the two big toes of the feet;
having drawn it from place to place, he who thus holds it with his intellect.
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall live as long as the moon and stars endure;
this was proclaimed even by Agastya for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga.
Among all forms of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), this is praised by yogis:
having drawn the breath through the two channels (nāḍīs) into the sides of the Kuṇḍalinī, the man [should practice].
Even one possessed of passion should maintain [this concentration], and he is liberated from the disease of worldly existence;
having ascended the vital air as before, he should hold it in the heart and in the sky.
O lady of excellent hips, that man also goes to the state of the Supreme Self.
How much less, then, could diseases—whether existing externally or internally—affect him?
Having drawn in the breath through both nostrils and filled the belly, he remained composed;
then, with concentrated mind, he fixed his gaze between the eyebrows.
Even he who holds it for a mere moment attains the supreme goal; what need is there for much speaking? Perform your daily duties.
Having projected the vital breath of the self from the middle of the eyebrows through the *suṣumnā*,
practice restraint therein until the dissolution of the mind occurs.
Dattātreya, however, says:
"The yogi who clearly withdraws the senses from the objects of the senses while established in kumbhaka is said to be practicing pratyāhāra."
Whatever one sees with the eyes, one should contemplate that within oneself; whatever one hears with the ears, one should contemplate that within oneself.
Whatever the tongue tastes, the yogi should contemplate that within himself;
whatever the skin touches, the yogi should contemplate that within himself.
In this manner,
the yogi, diligent and unwearied, should daily with effort meditate upon that [state] within the self for at least one watch (three hours).
At that time, inconceivable power certainly arises for the yogin.
He possessed the power of hearing from afar, seeing from afar, and likewise the ability to travel great distances in an instant.
Mastery of speech, the power of moving at will, and likewise the power of becoming invisible.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Yogacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śivānanda Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī.
Now, concentration (dhāraṇā) is being defined.
Regarding this, Patañjali states the definition in the sūtra: "Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to a location" (Yoga Sūtra 3.1). The meaning of this is as follows:

the binding of the mind to a location—whether internal, such as the *ādhāra*, the heart, the throat, the mouth, the space between the eyebrows, the crown of the head, and so forth; or external, such as a mountain and the like—wherein the mind is fixed by abandoning other objects, is called concentration.

The meaning is this: by a yogi who possesses friendliness and other virtues, whose internal organ is tranquil, who observes the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), who has mastered posture (*āsana*), who has restrained the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through its withdrawal, who has drawn back the collection of senses, whose body is upright, and who has conquered the staff [of anger], the mind should be made to rest upon the tip of the nose or another such spot for the practice of *samprajñāta-samādhi* in a place free from disturbance. As it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

"Having brought the vital air under control by means of breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*), and the senses by means of sense-withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), one should then direct the fluctuations of the mind toward a virtuous object."
In the Śivagītā: "In the heart-lotus, at the tip of the nose, at the crown of the head, or wherever it may occur—
concentration (dhāraṇā) is the binding of the mind in such locations as these."
P.228 In the Skanda Purāṇa:
Endowed with the practice of posture (āsana), joined with breath control (prāṇāyāma),
and fully established in withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), one should thoroughly practice concentration (dhāraṇā).
The separate concentration upon each of the five elements within the heart,
through the immobility of the mind— that is prescribed as dhāraṇā.

One should meditate upon the earth in the heart as being like yellow orpiment, marked with the syllable La and the syllable Va, and quadrangular; by this, the retention of the earth (kṣitidhāraṇā) is accomplished.

One should meditate upon the syllable *va*, which is like the moon on the throat, resembling the moon at the top of the reality (tattva), accompanied by Viṣṇu, and shining like a kunda flower; meditating thus, one should conquer the lotus.

Having meditated properly upon the fire situated at the palate—triangular, resembling an indragopa insect, joined with the letter *ra*, and presided over by Rudra—one conquers it; thus [one masters] the air element. [Then one meditates on] the air element between the eyebrows as circular and resembling collyrium.
"Meditating upon that seed-syllable whose deity is Īśa, one shall conquer Vāyu."
And the pure space resembling water which resides in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
together with its Lord Sadāśiva, is the tranquil syllable *ha*.
Having restrained the vital breath (prāṇa) there for five ghaṭikās, one should hold it together with the mind;
this is declared to be the space-dhāraṇā, which is skillful at shattering the door-panel of liberation.
It is likewise [known as] the paralyzing, the floating, the burning, and the whirling.
"These fivefold concentrations of beings lead to tranquility.
Yājñavalkya said:
"The steadiness of the mind, endowed with qualities such as self-restraint (yama) and so forth, within the Self."
This is called "retention" (dhāraṇā) by the virtuous who understand the purport of the scriptures.
O Gārgī, within one's own city of Brahman is this lotus of the heart.
In that very internal space, there is the concentration upon the external space.
And this is called "dhāraṇā" by those expert in the Yoga-śāstras—
by contemplators, by knowers of the Yoga-śāstra, by the learned, and by those who are well-informed.
The dhāraṇās are said to be fivefold, and they are each distinct:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
Among these, the fivefold abiding of the gods is intended;
that which extends from the feet up to the knees is said to be the station of the Earth.
The region from the navel down to the anus is proclaimed to be the abode of water;
that which extends from the anus up to the heart is said to be the abode of fire.
From the center of the heart up to the midpoint between the eyebrows is known as the family of air (vāyukula);
from the midpoint between the eyebrows up to the crown of the head is likewise called the ether (ākāśa).
O Gārgī, one should place Brahmā Parameṣṭhin upon the earth;
Viṣṇu in the ether; and Rudra Īśvara in the sphere of wind.
Then, being composed, one should meditate upon Sadāśiva in the ether,
having ascended the wind from the earth while it is conjoined with the syllable *la*.
Meditating on Brahmā, the cause of creation, who has the form of a face with a hide, one should hold [the breath] for five ghaṭikās; thus one shall attain victory over the earth.
Having placed Vāyu within the western [quarter] and joined it with the syllable *va*,
one should remember the pure Lord Nārāyaṇa, who possesses four arms and three eyes.
One should meditate upon [the deity] who resembles pure crystal, is clothed in yellow garments, and is immutable;
by holding this for five *ghaṭikās*, one is liberated from all diseases.
Having established the wind (*anila*) within the fire (*vahni*), it is conjoined with the syllable *repha* (the letter *ra*).
Rudra, the three-eyed bestower of boons, resembling the rising sun—
Meditate upon him with all his limbs smeared with ashes, appearing most serene.
One should retain [the breath] for five ghaṭikās; by means of the fire, that which is impure is not burned.
One should place the wind in the station of the winds, accompanied by the deity of the phoneme.

One should retain [the breath] for five ghaṭikās, and the vital air (vāyu) shall become situated in the ether (vyoma). Having ascended the vital air into the ether above the letter *ha*, one should place the conch-shell [sound].
Mahādeva, whose form is the drop (bindu), who is Sadāśiva in the form of space,
resembling pure crystal, and bearing the crescent moon upon his crest.
Endowed with five faces, peaceful, possessing ten arms and three eyes,
with all weapons raised in his hands and adorned with every ornament,
having Umā as half of his body, the bestower of boons, the cause of all causes.
He who, reflecting with his mind, should retain it even for a moment.
That very [Self] is joined by those practitioners of Tantra who are trained in the yoga of the chariot.
This is what is meant here, O Gārgī, O sky of the knowers of Brahman:
having withdrawn the effects, beginning with Brahmā, each into their own respective cause.
The ascetic should dissolve his vital breath and mind into Sadāśiva, their own ultimate cause.
With a disciplined mind, he always united his self with the Supreme Lord;
regarding this matter, other yogis who are the best among the knowers of Brahman say that one should withdraw all effects into their respective causes by means of the syllable Om.
In this Sadāśiva, who is the supreme embodiment of bliss at the end of the Nāda of the Praṇava, one should dissolve the vital breath and the mind into their own ultimate cause.
The virtuous perceive with their minds the Supreme Brahman as Ṛta and Satya, as the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny— the medicine for the cycle of worldly existence.
Therefore, by means of the *praṇava* alone, through three *prāṇāyāmas* each,
you should dissolve the effects, beginning with Brahmā, into their respective causes.
Others, namely yogins who are the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, declare that in this matter one perceives the Supreme Lord at the end of the taking [of breath] with a purified mind.
O lady of excellent limbs, the best of physicians are thoroughly proficient in these applications;
for this body indeed consists of the five elements.
O lady of excellent hips, there may arise a condition consisting of wind, bile,
and phlegm among all those of self-restrained mind who practice these yogas, provided they are of a windy temperament.
By the very restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇa), they dry up the body;
for those of a bilious temperament, the body withers away without delay.
For those of a phlegmatic (kapha) nature, the desired effect shall be fully realized without delay.

For one who performs dhāraṇa upon the fire element, all disorders born of wind (vāta) are destroyed. For one who constantly performs dhāraṇa upon the earth element and the water element, [the same result follows].
Diseases born of the three humors are destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
In this matter, the Aśvins, the best of physicians, have likewise declared that the pacification of the three doṣas in men occurs through the very restoration of the vital breaths. —
Dattātreya.

Having understood in secret both auspicious and inauspicious matters, one who performs sacrifice should perform the fivefold retention (*dhāraṇa*), which removes the fear of those respective elements.
One should hold the breath for five ghaṭikās below the navel and above the anus;
from that, the earth element arises, and this dhāraṇā removes all fear.
Death arising from the earth shall not occur for that yogi;
therefore, he should hold the vital air at the location of the navel for five nāḍikās.
P.232 Then, there is no fear from water; for the yogi, death does not come by way of water. One should hold the breath within the circle above the navel for five nāḍīs.
This is the Āgneyī Dhāraṇā;
for him, death by fire does not exist, nor is his body burned even when he has entered into a bed of flames.
One should hold the breath for five ghaṭikās in the space between the navel, the eyebrows, and the nose, measuring three prādeśas; this indeed is the Vāyavī mudrā.
Indeed, by the mere retention of the breath, fear arises for the yogin;
he should therefore hold it above the space between the eyebrows for five nāḍīs.
The yogi should diligently master the wind; this is the concentration on space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā). By performing the concentration on space, one conquers eternal death.
And thus the wise yogi should perform the five dhāraṇās;
then, for one whose body has become firm, death no longer exists.
Thus, for one who practices these fivefold elemental concentrations (dhāraṇās),
even through the dissolution of Brahmā, death does not exist for him.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"A yogi who is always engaged in yoga, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses,
should maintain the seven subtle dhāraṇās, beginning with Bhūḥ, up to the crown of the head."
The yogi should support the earth;
he attains its subtlety, considers himself as the earth, and abandons its odor.
In the same way, one should likewise perform the concentration (dhāraṇā) upon that subtle form of the wind in the mind, as well as its touch, while it moves swiftly.
And when he abandons the subtle activity of space as well as sound,
and enters the minds of all beings with his own mind, then [he attains that state].
'Maintaining mental concentration (dhāraṇā), the mind becomes subtle;
having attained that state, the knower of yoga reaches a wisdom that is unsurpassed by all beings.'"
Having attained supreme subtlety of intellect,
the knower of yoga abandons these seven subtle elements.
O Alarka! For one who has correctly understood this, there is no return to worldly existence. Indeed, the self-possessed man attains subtlety through these seven dhāraṇās.
Having seen and seen, he should then abandon one attainment after another and move on;
for toward whichever being he directs his passion, toward that he becomes great.
Having attained attachment to this or that, one perishes;
therefore, knowing these subtle things to be mutually attached, [one should not be attached].
The embodied soul who renounces these seven subtle things, O King, shall attain the supreme state; yet these very same things lead to bondage.
Dispassion toward the elements beginning with earth is necessary here, because its existence leads to liberation;
for this entire world is intensely attached to odors and other such qualities.
O King, having transcended these seven worlds— including those of Brahmā, the gods, and humans— the yogi of dhāraṇā may, if he so desires, return again.
O lord of men, in each respective subtle element, there occurs the dissolution of the gods,
the Suganas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rakshasas.
He attains dissolution within the bodies and does not incur attachment anywhere.
Likewise:
first in the navel, then in the heart, then in the third place, and likewise in the chest.
In the throat, the mouth, the tip of the nose, the eyes, the center of the brows, and the crown of the head.
When that concentration (dhāraṇā) is directed toward something slightly beyond that, it is released as supreme. Having attained these ten concentrations, one attains equality with the Imperishable.
P.234 Now, regarding meditation (*dhyāna*), Patañjali states its definition:

"Meditation is the one-pointedness of thought upon that [object]. In this context, "that" refers to the object made the support (*ālambana*) by means of concentration (*dhāraṇā*). One-pointedness of thought is the continuous flow of similar mental modifications (*pratyaya*) upon that object, achieved by setting aside heterogeneous mental modifications; this is called meditation.
In the Śivagītā:
"The continuous succession of the turning back of the intellect,
based on its abiding in the [Supreme] Deity and untouched by other duties— that the wise know as meditation (dhyāna)."

In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O King, that continuous flow of one-pointed cognition characterized by steadiness and free from desire for anything else— that is meditation (dhyāna), which is accomplished through the first six ancillaries."

In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The verbal root *dhyai* is traditionally understood in the sense of 'thinking' (*cintā*). When the mind becomes steady upon the principles of thought, that is declared to be *dhyāna*. It is of two kinds: with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*)."
That which possesses qualities is considered to be differentiated, while that which is devoid of qualities is held to be absolute.
Know that which is accompanied by mantras to be with qualities, and that which is free from mantras to be without qualities.
As long as the subtle elements of sound and the rest remain within the objects of action and so forth, for that long it is considered meditation (dhyāna); beyond that is concentration (samādhi).
"That merit is not obtained by the horse-sacrifice, nor by the Vairāja-sacrifice;
that same merit a yogi with a steady posture may obtain through single-minded meditation."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (P.235):
Having abandoned attachment, subdued anger, moderate in diet, and having conquered the senses;
Having closed the doors of the senses with the intellect, one should fix the mind in meditation.
Whether in empty places, in open spaces, in caves, or in forests,
the ever-disciplined yogi should always properly undertake meditation.
"The Vedas are the best among all sacrificial rites; they say that recitation is superior to sacrifice, and knowledge is superior to recitation.
From knowledge comes meditation, which is free from all passion."
When that is accomplished, there is the perception of the Eternal One—
by one who is composed, devoted to Brahman, vigilant, pure, delighting in solitude, and having conquered the senses.
That great-souled one shall attain this very sky,
and from that, through yoga, he attains liberation.
Yājñavalkya said:
"I shall now explain meditation; listen, O Gārgī of lovely countenance!
For meditation alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for living beings."
Meditation (dhyāna) is indeed the perception of one's own essential nature by means of the mind;
it is both with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa), and that which is with attributes is remembered as being of many kinds.
And the Vedic twice-born say that among these,
three are considered most excellent, while one alone is devoid of qualities.
Having understood individually the locations of the vital points (marmas), the arrangement of the channels (nāḍīs),
and the positions and functions of the vital airs (vāyus), one should perform self-examination.
A single, pure, and luminous form, with all its limbs as firm as space.
It is unmanifest, stainless, eternal, and indeed devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
It is beyond place, subtle, formless, untouched by space, invisible to the eye, devoid of sound,
and not rich in fragrance; it is immeasurable, incomparable, blissful, undecaying, eternal, both being and non-being, and the cause of all.
The support of all, the form of the world, yet formless, unborn, and undecaying;
invisible and visible, situated within and without, facing every direction.
"Seeing all, with feet everywhere; touching all, with a head everywhere—Brahman am I, composed of Brahman. Thus is the realization of reality.
The knowers of Yoga understand this to be meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa);
or else, it is the embodiment of supreme bliss belonging to the Supreme Selves.
Having understood the Person, who is dark and tawny, through the instruction of the Guru,
as Brahman within this city of Brahman, in the center of the small ether;
The wise perceive with their minds that the medicine for cyclic existence arises from the center of the bulb,
situated within the eight-petaled lotus of the heart.
In this [vessel] with a twelve-finger-long tube and a four-finger-wide opening,
When the pericarp, adorned with filaments, has been opened by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
one should mentally contemplate the chosen deity who grants all desires.
The cognition "I am He" is called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna),
performed within this lotus of the heart, which is the source of Prakṛti and the rest.
It is endowed with the eight petals of the eightfold sovereignty, joined with the filaments of knowledge,
possessing the stalk of wisdom and the great bulb, awakened by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
[He saw] Vaiśvānara, the Lord, the source of the universe, blazing with universal radiance, the great fire with faces on all sides,
emitting flames from his crest.
"His own body was blazing from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head;
within it, the sacrificial fire was kindled like a lamp in a windless place."
Having seen the imperishable Supreme Self within the center of his crest-lock,
radiant like a streak of lightning situated in the midst of a dark rain cloud.
Having known the god Vaiśvānara— who has the appearance of a wild-rice awn, who shines like a lamp, and who is the cause of all— one possesses that mental state which thinks, "I am indeed He."
Those who know yoga recognize that among meditations on the qualities (saguṇa-dhyāna), this is the supreme meditation;
having attained the state of Vaiśvānara, one goes to liberation by that very means.
Alternatively, one should behold within the mandala the Self, the cause of the world, the Person (Puruṣa) in the form of gold, belonging to the Sun of great splendor.
He has golden beard and hair, golden nails, and is dark-complexioned; he is endowed with a beautiful form and countenance, the cause of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the world;
he sits upon a lotus throne, is gentle, and possesses a face like a full-blown lotus.

Having seen him—the sole witness of the world—who illumines the entire universe; whose lips have the luster of the petals of a blooming lotus; who bestows fearlessness upon all the worlds; who always knows everything; who gladdens the righteous; and who is the unique eye of light.
The realization "I am that" is praised in meditation;
O lady rich in austerity, this alone is the great path to liberation.
By means of this solar meditation, the wise shall attain liberation,
[perceiving] the inner self between the eyebrows, whose form is light and who is the cause of all.
Arising from the middle of his body, it reached up to the top of his head like a pillar—
the unmanifest cause of the universe, blazing with immeasurable splendor.
"Having perceived with the mind, 'I shall slay,' this is the supreme method of meditation (dhvayāna). Alternatively, having assumed the bound lotus posture (paryaṅka) and relaxed the body,
becoming Śiva himself, one fixes the gaze upon the tip of the nose."
O fair-faced one, one should meditate in the space between the eyebrows upon the Supreme Self— changeless, auspicious, peaceful, imperishable, consisting of light, and immortal.
The realization that "I am indeed He" is what is praised in meditation;
or else, [one may meditate] upon [the Self] as situated within a lotus of eight petals, complete with pericarp and filaments.
Within the lotus of his heart, which is fully blossomed, in the center of the lunar orb,
he beholds himself as the Lord in the form of the enjoyer,
appearing as a child and surrounded by the rays of the moon that discharge the essence of nectar.
From the downward-facing head-lotus, which is joined with sixteen petals,
thousands of streams of nectar flow forth in every direction.
Having meditated upon that person there, being composed in mind, one should bathe one's own body, along with its limbs and minor members, with that very nectar-like essence:
"I alone am the Supreme Brahman; I am the immutable Supreme Self."
Thus, that feeling which is present therein is called meditation with attributes (saguṇadhyāna).
By thus practicing the nectar of meditation for six months, one becomes a conqueror of death.
He shall be liberated after a year while still alive; of this there is no doubt. For one who is liberated while living, there is no acquisition of suffering whatsoever, in any way.
How much more so for one who is eternally liberated—for whom liberation itself is indeed difficult to attain! And it is said in the Śruti:
"The lotus of the heart is stainless and pure..."
It is to be contemplated within as luminous and free from sorrow;
it is inconceivable, unmanifest, and of infinite forms; it is auspicious, tranquil, immortal, and the source of Brahman.
For instance: "It is one, devoid of middle and end,
all-pervading, consisting of consciousness and bliss, formless, and wonderful."
The Supreme Lord and Master, accompanied by Umā,
the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil one.
Having meditated, the sage goes to the source of all beings,
the witness of all, beyond darkness; then, meditating upon it, he beholds that partless reality.
"It is seen by those of subtle vision through the highest, subtle intellect";
"This is to be attained by the mind alone," and so forth.
Dattātreya says:
"Then one should practice meditation for sixty *ghaṭikās*,
having restrained the vital breath (*vāyu*), upon whichever deity one desires who bestows the desired fruit."
"This indeed is the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa-dhyāna), which bestows qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest;
having meditated upon the attributeless as being like space, one attains the path of liberation."
Yogiyājñavalkya says: "There is no purifier of evil deeds equal to meditation. Even while eating among outcaste dog-cookers, the meditator is never defiled."
Meditation alone is the supreme Brahman; meditation alone is the highest austerity;
meditation alone is the supreme purity; that meditation is the highest state.
Even if one is addicted to every kind of sin, if one meditates for even a moment upon the Imperishable (Acyuta),
he then becomes an ascetic, a purifier of the assembly, and a sanctifier.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Even one who is devoid of all proper conduct, or even one joined with all sins..."
One destroys all that evil by meditating upon auspiciousness within oneself.
In another treatise: "In all sins, even in great sins,
having entered [the house] at night for one quarter [of the time], one should practice meditation on Brahman."
In the Bāśiṣṭha,
in the section on the worship of the Self, following the description of the nature of meditation,
the Lord said:
In meditation, his very self is the supreme object; meditation is his great worship.
Without that [meditation], this Self is indeed not attained by anyone.
O wise one, by performing this meditation for thirteen moments,
even a fool, having worshipped the Lord, shall obtain the fruit of gifting a cow.
Having worshipped the Lord for one hundred moments without blinking,
a person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
He who, by means of the offering of the garland of meditation, worships his own self with his own self for even a single ghaṭikā, shall obtain the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having thus performed the midday worship and so forth, which constitutes a single hundred thousand-fold Rājasūya sacrifice,
and having worshipped in this manner for the entire day, the person shall dwell in the Abode on the following day.
"This is that supreme yoga; this indeed is the supreme practice," as stated in the *Ātmagītā*.
Even if one is unable to realize Me directly, one should contemplate Me without hesitation;
in time, having ascended to direct experience, one will certainly become fully integrated with Me.
Just as a treasure of great depth cannot be obtained by means other than digging,
so too, even when free from greed, there is no other way [to attain the goal] except through reflection on one's own self.
For by drawing away the body with the spade of the intellect and digging further into the ground of the mind,
a person may again seize me, the hidden treasure.
And in another scripture:
"Even if [Brahman] were not experienced, one should simply contemplate 'I am Brahman.
Even that which is non-existent is attained through meditation; how much more so Brahman, which is eternally attained?"
The fruit of meditation day by day is the weakening of the notion of self;
if one does not meditate even while perceiving this, who else indeed could speak otherwise?
If one disregards that [duty] and performs only pilgrimages, recitations, and so forth,
the maxim "having cast away the rice-ball, he licks his own hand" will apply.
Now, regarding meditative absorption (*samādhi*):
Patañjali states therein—
“That very [cognitive state] which appears as the object alone, as if devoid of its own form, is meditative absorption (*samādhi*).”
That very object which has been made the focal point of meditation appears as the ultimate alone; it is free from doubt, complete in its entire nature through its own essential form.
Therefore, because it is devoid of all [external] objects, in that state it is, as it were, empty of its own [apparent] form.
That which shines forth during cultivation—that specific cultivation—is called "concentration" (samādhi).
This is the general characteristic of the two types of concentration. The specific characteristic [is discussed] in the first [chapter], page 242.

The detailed explanation regarding its cessation should be understood as previously stated. Others, however, say that *samādhi* is that wherein the mind is concentrated—that is, made one-pointed—by abandoning distractions.
Yājñavalkya says:
"I shall now describe *samādhi*, which destroys the bonds of worldly existence."
You ought to hear, exactly as it is, [the teaching] for one who is bound by the fetters of existence.
Samādhi, however, is the state of equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
that which is the abiding of the inner self (pratyagātman) in Brahman alone is samādhi.
To the extent that one meditates upon the Self, to that same extent does samādhi arise.
Having meditated thus, one should remain established in the Self, for the Self cannot exist otherwise.
"In this very way, wherever a man exerts effort,
his self becomes distinct therein and attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*). — *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
"Concentration would be of a single form, devoid of direction and objective support; for it is through the mere object as a condition that this supreme means of Yoga is accomplished. — Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
That very [object], for the purpose of grasping its true nature free from conceptual construction, is accomplished by the mind through meditation; that is designated as *samādhi*.
Nor should it be suspected that there is no difference between meditation (dhyāna) and cognitive absorption (saṃprajñāta-samādhi);

for even in meditation—which is accomplished through great effort—there may still be the occurrence of other mental states, whereas in cognitive absorption there is absolutely no room for other mental states at all. This is the distinction between the two.
Sureśvarācārya says:
"The contemplation and meditation upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others shall now be explained."
The non-fluctuation of the intellect arising from meditative absorption is designated as "samādhi."
In the Śaiva dharma,
samādhi is the state of equilibrium between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
it is the attainment of the waveless state, which consists of supreme bliss.
One who is devoid of inhalation and exhalation, motionless yet with eyes still flickering,
meditating on Śiva and perfectly absorbed, is said to be established in samādhi.
Just as water that has entered a river flows undividedly toward its dissolution,
so too the self, remaining undivided, attains absorption (samādhi) here.
"When one hears nothing, sees nothing, smells nothing, and does not perceive any touch, one is said to be established in samādhi. — *Skanda Purāṇa*...
That state of equality between these two— the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—
in which all mental constructions have perished, is designated as samādhi.
The lord of yogis, absorbed in samādhi, knows neither self nor other, neither cold nor heat, neither pleasure nor that which is other than pleasure.
The yogi who is disciplined in meditative absorption is not affected by time, nor is he stained by karma; he is not pierced by weapons or other such means.
"Just as water poured into water becomes that very water, and milk [poured] into milk likewise, so the yogi attains identity with that. (P.
Dattātreya said:
Having perfected the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), one should then practice samādhi;
in exactly twelve days, one shall attain samādhi.
Having restrained the vital breath, the wise man will certainly become liberated while living;
samādhi is the state of equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
If he should desire to cast off this body, he may himself relinquish it;
having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, he would merge into the supreme Brahman.
Now, if he does not wish to cast off his own body,
he may wander through all the worlds, endowed with the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.

And thus, for the yogi who practices yoga with its constituent limbs (*sāṅga-yoga*) in the manner described above, there arise obstacles (*antarāya*) that are *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. Considering that all of these are trivial, the yogi should simply disregard them. Accordingly, Dattātreya says:
"O Sage, even at the time of initial practice, various obstacles indeed arise."
Laziness is the first obstacle; the second is now declared.
Those who know yoga understand that the first is the assembly of rogues, the third is the accomplishment of mantras,
and the fourth is alchemy.
Just as is the form of Kandarpa, so too is that of this very yogin;
women, captivated by his form, long for union with him.
"For in this way, O Sage, many obstacles arise for one who is firm, which are like a mirage; having recognized them, the wise man should abandon them.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Obstacles indeed arise when the yogin perceives the Self;
those [obstacles] I shall fully explain—learn them from me in brief."
Desiring desirable rites, he likewise longs for human pleasures:
women, the fruit of charity, knowledge, magic, base metals, wealth, and riches.
Divinity, lordship over the immortals, the elixir of rejuvenation, the practice of longevity,
the blazing atop Mount Meru, the performance of sacrifice, and likewise immersion in water and fire— these [he taught].
The fruits of ancestral rites (śrāddha) and the giving of power (śakti), as well as the rules of conduct,
likewise the results of fasting, works of public utility (pūrta), and the worship of the deities.
Afflicted by various actions, he longs for wealth;
the yogi should diligently turn away from that which has been set in motion.
By making his mind attached to Brahman, he is liberated from the obstacles that cause him to wander.
When these [internal] afflictions have been conquered by means of [external] afflictions, then, conversely,
the sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic afflictions of the yogin no longer arise.
The intuitive, the auditory, the divine, the delusive, and the whirlpool-like—
these five arise with a bitter onset as obstacles to the yoga of practitioners.
They encompass the meanings of the Vedas, the meanings of poetry and treatises, and all forms of arts and crafts without exception.
That which appears to him is his *prātibha* [intuition]; thus he is called a *prātibha-yogin*.
He knows all words and their meanings, and he grasps the word itself;
he is designated as one who hears from thousands of *yojanas* away.
When eight celestial beings are seen on all sides,
the wise call even that a divine affliction, like madness.
When the mind of a yogin wanders without support due to mental defect,
that wandering is proclaimed as "bhrama" (delusion), arising from the loss of all foundational supports.
Just as there is an eddy in water that is in motion, so too is the eddy of knowledge when it is agitated.
Wherever the mind is destroyed, that is called an obstacle.
All the divine beings whose yoga has been destroyed by these most terrible calamities revolve again and again.

"Having set aside the purely pure yoga consisting of the mind, one should contemplate the Supreme Brahman, making the mind inclined toward That. Thus it is said. Furthermore, those obstacles designated as distractions of the mind—such as lack of fitness for practice, doubt regarding the fruit of yoga, lethargy, indolence, absence of detachment from sense objects, delusion, failure to attain the stages of samādhi, and instability of the mind—are all removed by the very contemplation of Brahman.
This has been stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtra]:

following the definition of Yoga by the sūtras beginning with "Or through devotion to Īśvara," [it continues with] "The designator of that [Īśvara] is the syllable *praṇava*," "The repetition of that and meditation upon its meaning," and "From that comes the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles.

Now, since meditation upon that meaning also takes the form of *saṃyama*, one might ask if there is room for obstacles even there; however, because the worship of the Blessed One—which is like a fire to the scales of all sins—leaves no room for obstacles.
And so it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Just as fire with its flames kindled and fanned by the wind burns dry wood,
so does Viṣṇu, abiding in the mind, burn away all the sins of yogis."

Thus, it has been stated that for the sake of removing all previously mentioned obstacles known as distractions (*vikṣepa*), as well as those born together with distraction—namely pain, mental unease, trembling of the limbs, labored breathing, sleep, and so forth—one should practice meditation upon a single chosen object; this is for the purpose of prohibiting those [obstacles] by means of the sūtra: "The practice of concentration on a single principle" (*eka-tattvābhyāsa*).
Vasiṣṭha says:
"These, O Brahmā, are the defects of pride, which are the causes of the disease of saṃsāra."
They do not disturb even slightly the mind that is one-pointedly concentrated.
Those whose hearts have been mastered and who are free from the transformations born of desire and anger—
no anxieties can afflict the mind that is concentrated in one-pointedness.
Those things which are ill-conceived, poorly undertaken, characterized by bad qualities, wrongly expressed,
and followed by faulty methods— these do not cut through a mind that is single-pointedly concentrated.
"The guardians of the directions protect that within whom the wonder of Truth eternally vibrates— a whole [reality] like one's own non-fragmented universe."
In the Ādipurāṇa:
"One endowed with right vision is not overcome by karmas;
the knower of yoga, whose self is united with yoga, attains supreme liberation."
And scripture says:

"Therefore, he who knows thus—'I am Brahman'—becomes this entire universe; for him, even the gods do not have power to cause failure, since he becomes their very Self," and so forth. Furthermore, those supernatural powers (*siddhis*) that arise prior to liberation must be regarded as obstacles themselves, because for a yogi whose mind is attached to such powers, liberation is difficult to attain.
And so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In this world, obstacles arise for the yogin which cause the loss of yoga;
news from afar is heard, and that which is far away is seen again."
One would have the power to travel a hundred yojanas in half a moment.
Indeed, even scriptures that were previously inconceivable become committed to memory by rote.
The power of retention becomes exceedingly fierce; a great burden becomes light;
in one moment he is emaciated, in another moment he is stout, in one moment he is small, and in another moment he is great.
He enters the bodies of others, understands the speech of animals,
assumes a divine fragrance, and utters divine words.
He is sought after by celestial maidens; he desires a divine body.
These and other such obstacles may arise as indicators of the perfection of yoga;
provided that his mind is not diminished by these obstacles.
Then one attains a body before that [state] and reaches the station difficult even for Brahmā and others to obtain;
having reached it, one does not return, and having reached it, one does not grieve.
"O Kalasodbhava! This is attained through the six-limbed yoga. Thus it is said in the Yogabhāskara:
"For the yogi who has conquered the senses, who is self-controlled, and who has mastered his breath..."
Successes attend upon one who maintains the mind fixed on Hari.
"Though many powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest may be cultivated through various forms of concentration (*dhāraṇā*),
one should abandon them all because they are useless, since they create obstacles [to liberation]."
Bound by latent impressions (vāsanā) such as the desire for supernatural powers (siddhi) and attached to various enjoyments,
he generally perceives [the Self] in its place [as the body] and remains within primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having taken hold of the fortitude born of the Self, the excellent yogi,
remaining well-steadfast and meditating on the attributeless with his mind, is liberated from all obstacles.
Thus practicing yoga, free from desire for status and the like,
and having abandoned the latent impressions of supernatural powers and such, the sage becomes liberated while living.
For fear of prolixity, they have not been stated here, though they are indeed recorded in many places;
for by means of meditation, the [distractions] of Hari, Hara, and others must be warded off by the yogin.
Such is the established conclusion of all the scriptures.

And thus, for the sake of inspiring confidence and for the sake of testing the yogin who, favored by the Supreme Lord, practices the complete yoga without obstacle, the supernatural powers (*siddhis*), which are intermediate fruits of liberation, manifest in due order. There are five kinds of *siddhis* in the world.
Accordingly, Patañjali says:

Regarding the statement, "Perfections (siddhis) are born from herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative concentration," there is the perfection born of birth (*janmasiddhi*), characterized by the power of traveling through the air as seen among the Yakṣas and others, and characterized by knowledge and other qualities arising immediately upon birth as seen among Kapila and others.

The attainment of medicinal herbs characterized by the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and so forth in Pātāla and other realms; (1) the attainment of *kalā* and *mantra* powers such as the ability to travel through the sky for some; the attainment of ascetic power (*tapas-siddhi*) for Viśvāmitra and others; and the attainment of meditative absorption (*samādhi-siddhi*) for yogins such as Yājñavalkya. Among these, it should be understood that the cause for all attainments, beginning with those pertaining to birth, is exclusively the attainment of meditative absorption practiced in previous lives. Mantras and the like are merely instrumental conditions (*nimitta-mātra*). For example:

The transformation of birth and so forth that occurs for Nandīśvara and others in this very life is due to the filling of the *prakṛtis*. For it is the subsequent *prakṛtis* themselves that fill the modifications—characterized by the gross elements, the self, the body, and the senses—in this life by means of a change of species and the like. While the performance of merit (*dharma*) and so forth serves as the impelling cause for the filling of the *prakṛtis*, it actually results in the destruction of the demerit (*adharma*) that constitutes their veil.

Just as the activity of a farmer consists merely in breaking a dam, while the flow of water occurs by itself, so too there is no consequence of destroying the previously mentioned cause of meditative absorption practiced in other births.
And thus Patañjali said in two sūtras:

"The transformation into another species occurs through the filling of the primal nature (prakṛti)," and "An external cause is not the motivator of the primal natures; rather, it is the removal of their covering, as in the case of the farmer. [This is stated] in the *Yogabhāskara*.
Whatever supernatural powers are attained here through birth, herbs, austerities, or mantras—all those are obtained through yoga; one should pursue the path of yoga by no other means.
In the *Yogabīja*: "O Goddess, I shall now tell you the fruit of practice:
first diseases perish, and afterwards the dullness born of the body."
Then, having become engaged in battle, Candra rained [the mercury] incessantly;
Vahni, together with Pavana, seized the metallic essence (dhāturasa) from all sides.
Various sounds arise and the body becomes supple;
having conquered the inertia of the earth element and the others, the man becomes a sky-walker and may move about freely.
He shall become omniscient, able to assume any form at will, and possess the speed of the wind;
he sports in the three worlds, and all supernatural powers (siddhis) arise for him.
When camphor is being rubbed, what hardness can be found there?
In the same way, when the ego is conquered, whence could there be any solidity in the body?
"He becomes omniscient, the creator of all, independent, and possessed of universal form;
he is liberated while living, a great yogi—of this there is no doubt."
The Goddess said:
"O Śaṅkara, whatever web of conceptualization there may be, it serves for liberation;
for what will the supernatural powers do to the non-conceptualizing self of consciousness?"
"O Lord, O Purifier, you ought to sever this doubt of mine! The Lord said:
"What you have spoken is true; I shall tell it to you, so listen, O beautiful one!"
O Śivā, the two kinds of accomplishments in this world are the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized.
Those accomplishments (siddhis) which are achieved through the application of medicinal elixirs, the proper time for action, mantras, yantras, and other such means,
are proclaimed as "imagined" (kalpitā).
Those supernatural powers arising from spiritual practices are of little potency;
indeed, these very powers arise spontaneously even without such practice.

But for those who are solely devoted to the yoga of their own Self, the accomplishments (siddhis) that arise from that state of sovereignty by the Lords are known to be free from conceptual construction.
Pure, eternal, and of great vigor, possessing forms according to their will and self-possessed through yoga,
they are born after a long time even among those free from latent impressions (vāsanā).
The great yoga, which is to be cultivated within the imperishable state of the Supreme Self, is characterized by perpetual radiance even without the sun; this is the mark of one perfected in yoga.
Just as various sacred fords (tīrtha) are seen along the way by travelers journeying toward Kāśī, so too are the supernatural powers (siddhis) encountered on the path to liberation.
They arise spontaneously, free from gain and loss;
the perfected one should recognize them through the signs of accomplishment, as well as liberation while living.
His supramundane qualities are certainly seen at some time or other;
this, O Goddess, has been declared as the characteristic of one perfected in yoga.
One should recognize that man as being bound, for he is deprived of the attainments (siddhis).
He who is indeed ageless, immortal, and a mass of consciousness is truly one who is liberated while living.
O beautiful lady, for those such as chickens and insects who meet with death, can there be liberation through the offering of funeral cakes?
The vital breath does not go outside; it causes the falling of the body. That liberation which occurs through the falling of the body is not called liberation.
The body attains the state of Brahman, just as rock salt attains the state of water.
When that which is mindless arrives, then he is said to be liberated.
As stated in the *Mānasollāsa*:
"When the mind has attained immobility and the vital breath has dissolved into the center..."
These signs arise individually from the conquest of the five elements.
Scantiness of feces and urine, freedom from phlegm, health, lightness of the body,
a pleasant fragrance, and a golden complexion are the first signs of yoga.
Not being caught even on the tip of a thorn is the first sign of yoga.
Non-attachment even upon the tip of a thorn, non-sinking even in water or mud,
and endurance of hunger, thirst, and so forth— this is the second characteristic of yoga.
A great capacity for consuming food and drink, endurance of heat and fire,
and seeing and hearing from a distance— this is the third characteristic of yoga.
Leaping upon the ground like a frog, leaping upon a tree like a monkey,
and traveling through the sky— this is the fourth characteristic of yoga.
Knowledge whose object is the three periods of time, sovereignty consisting of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth,
and the possession of infinite power— this is the fifth characteristic of yoga.
Likewise, the characteristics of *aṇimā* and so forth are as follows:
"Aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, and likewise garimā;
prāpti, prākāmya, aiśitva, and vaśitva—these are the eight siddhis.
Prāpti is the attainment of the infinite and minute, [and] entry into them as one's own self.
The sovereignty known as aṇimā belongs to the Supreme Self who is all-pervading.
The sovereignty known as "Greatness" (Mahimā) consists of the pervasive presence outside of the aggregate of thirty-six principles, from the Egg of Brahmā up to the Egg of Śiva;
it is the capacity for the act of uplifting one whose limbs are equal to the great Mount Meru.
The wise know "levity" (laghimā) to be the state of being as light as a tiny tuft of cotton,
in the act of lifting up one whose body is equal to an atom.
The wise know that the weight of respectability is equal to Mount Meru;
for a man dwelling in the netherworld, it is the beholding of the realm of Brahmā.
That which is called attainment (*prāpti*) is great sovereignty, extremely difficult for non-yogins to achieve,
consisting of the perfection of other supernatural powers such as traveling through the sky and so forth.

The attainment of perfection through mere will is called *prākāmya* (the power of irresistible will). Some declare this sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) to be *prākāmya*, wherein all objects are illuminated by the light of one's own body.
The agency in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds through mere purity,
as well as the power of directing the sun and other luminaries, is designated as "lordship" (īśitva).
All the world-protectors and all the worlds are under their control;
that sovereignty known as "mastery" (vaśitva) is easily attained by the yogins of Śiva.
What indeed cannot be accomplished for those whose minds are fully matured and accompanied by skillful means, once they have attained the uninterrupted sovereignty over all states of being?
The gods themselves abide under the command of that brāhmaṇa who knows this;
how much more so, O tiger among kings, [the command of] serpents, women, men, and the like?
One should abandon the desire for inferior fruits that result in rebirth in heaven and the like;
for a wise man does not consider a kingdom in heaven to be equal to universal sovereignty.
That alone is his true sovereignty which is sovereignty over the self;
for the abundance of sons, grandsons, houses, fields, wealth, and grain, as well as the attainments within this world,
in heaven, in the netherworld, and on earth, are all secondary.
Just as for those engaged in cooking, there is the avoidance of cold and other such things.
Through the constant practice of yoga, the incidental powers and the state of lordship are accomplished; for him, there is no separate existence from that [state].
Even while the person runs, the shadow follows him;
so too do infinite power, sovereignty, and the supernormal faculties such as atomization (aṇimā) follow.
When one's own lordship is doubted, it indeed becomes established by itself.
While bringing a flower, its fragrance is experienced even before the desire to see it has arisen.
The manifestations of those whose sovereignty— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— are limited by the lightning-flashes of His power, even though they are endowed with a full sense of selfhood.
"Those possessed of sovereignty speak thus: 'That very Self is Sadāśiva.
All supernatural powers (siddhis) serve him who possesses the realization of being within all things.
Therefore, one whose mind is disciplined should exercise sovereign rule over the Self. Thus [it is said].

In the Layakhanda as well, following the description of the practice of meditative absorption (samādhi), the sequence of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) is taught precisely through that same sequence of its practice.
For it is said:
"Seated comfortably in a secluded place,
having first assumed a proper posture for a short while..."
With arms extended to the length of a yoke, with a steady gaze and relaxed limbs,
free from anxiety, perform the practice.
Seated comfortably on a pleasant seat, one should practice the cultivation of reality;
through constant practice, one should effect the manifestation of the supreme reality.

The cosmic egg resides within the five elements, the body is composed of the five elements, and all things consist of every element; having abandoned these notions, one should contemplate that "it does not exist."
One who does not meditate on anything with the mind and is free from all thought becomes a yogi, both internally and externally, facing reality itself.
When one is born face-to-face with reality, the mindless state arises;
when the mindless state has arisen, the dissolution of the vital breath occurs.
Through the nose, one releases the mind and breath toward the objects of the senses.
When one is released from the objects of the senses, external cognition does not arise;
and when external cognition has perished, one then becomes equal to all.
When he has become entirely equanimous and free from activity,
the yogi, united with the supreme Brahman, then attains dissolution therein.
I shall describe the characteristics of that supreme dissolution which arises for those whose minds are liberated and who are constantly devoted to practice.
Having reached dissolution, he knows neither pleasure nor pain, nor does he perceive cold or heat; he is unaware of the deliberation upon the objects of the senses,
and being neither living nor dead, he neither sees nor closes his eyes.
Devoid of life, he remains like a piece of wood and is said to be in a state of dissolution;
yet, like a lamp placed in a windless spot, he speaks while remaining motionless.
Just as a lake that is free from wind remains motionless and pure, so too the yogi who has attained absorption (laya) is liberated from all worldly activity.
Likewise, one who has abandoned objects such as sound and remains in a state of dissolution is seen to be like salt thrown into water, which gradually dissolves away.
Through the yoga of practice, even the mind dissolves into that Brahman,
just as salt, through contact with water, becomes identical with the water.
The mind also, through contact with Brahman, becomes composed of Brahman;
just as salt is certainly obtained by means of alkaline matter.
The knowledge of Brahman brings about the effortless liberation of the mind;
it is distinct from mental modifications and devoid of them, just as clarified butter is absorbed within clarified butter.
Likewise, the yogi who has merged into reality does not perceive any separate existence [through the divisions of] moments,
breaths, instants, channels, watches, or days.
Through months, years, and times, he who remains in dissolution shall go to that which is supreme.
Six breaths, consisting of inhalations and exhalations, are known as one *pala*;
sixty *palas* constitute what is traditionally called a *ghaṭikā*.
By means of absorption (*laya*), the yogi certainly dissolves [the mind] in a mere moment.
There occurs contact with the supreme reality and its repeated emergence;
the cooling of the fever arises, along with sound sleep and fainting.
By the dissolution of merely six eye-winks, the yogi becomes established within;
and by the dissolution of even two breaths, the kūrma-vāta and other vital airs [are stilled].
And they turn back, forming a bond within the elements;
by that very dissolution of the three breaths, the vital winds such as Prāṇa and the rest [are restrained].
Through connection with the flow of the breath, they strike their respective locations;
even by the dissolution of four breaths, the essences residing in the seven dhātus [are struck].
The balanced states of the bodily constituents (dhātus) bring about perfect nourishment;
by means of dissolution (laya), even while seated, one does not suffer from fatigue for even a single pala.
The yogi shall have very slight breath and likewise very slight opening of the eyes;
even with the passing of two palas, there shall be no movement of the heart-beat.
The unstruck sound (anāhata) is to be perceived; one should not fix the mind upon that very place.
Through an absorption lasting four palas, an experience arises;
suddenly, an auspicious or inauspicious sound falls upon the ear.
Even by means of a mere eighteenth part [of a moment], his desire ceases;
nevertheless, it may indeed arise again for one embraced by a passionate woman.
Flowing through the path of the Suṣumṇā even by means of the rhythmic cadence (kalāpāda),
she proceeds by her very nature through the western path of that [Suṣumṇā].
Even within half a ghaṭikā, the power (śakti) certainly begins to move;
by obstructing the vital breath (vāta), it awakens along the upward and western path.
"Even by a dissolution of a mere fraction (kalā), the power (śakti) certainly vibrates.
By the dissolution of two fractions and by the vibration of the power,
a trembling of that mind arises instantly."
Even by means of the abode of the four kalās, the state of sleep ceases;
the yogi perceives the reflection of light like a spark within the heart.
Even by taking food at the fourth part of the day, a man becomes one who eats little;
there is scantiness of urine and feces, lightness of the body, and unctuousness.
Even through dissolution in half a day, the light of one's own self shines forth;
radiant like the rays of the sun, the yogi shines throughout the universe.
Even by dissolution for a mere day, one's own essential reality shines forth;
thereafter, the expansion of sensory cognition proceeds within the cosmic egg.
Even with two days and nights, or even with dissolution at the end,
the yogi remains established on his own path through dissolution during the day and night as well.
By the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, one perceives fragrance from afar.
The consciousness that perceives the distant exists by its very own nature.
Even after three days and nights, the bliss of dissolution arises;
free from conceptual construction, the yogi perceives the essence even from afar.
By the power of the dissolution occurring within four days and nights, the lord of yogis perceives touch even from afar; of this there is no doubt.
Even by practicing for five nights,
the certain knowledge of hearing from afar arises for him as well— a wondrous power that functions from a great distance.
This knowledge of the five senses is of the nature of great self-experience;
by means of this, the lords of yogis traverse the entire course of the universe.
Even by dissolving [the mind] for six nights, a great growth sprouts forth;
thus, the inconceivable and transcendent universal knowledge proceeds.
"Even after seven nights of dissolution,

the yogi who has dissolved [into the state] is not afflicted by conditions such as hunger and thirst while abiding in the innate (sahaja). Even after nine nights of dissolution, there is no weariness for one who remains in his own experience."
The state of knowing all things up to Brahmā and the knowledge of the Vedas (Śruti) arise;
even through dissolution after eight nights, the yogi becomes free from all affliction.
The perfection of his speech shall become capable of both cursing and bestowing grace;
even after ten nights have passed, that lord of yogis remains established in his own self.
Whatever very well-guarded and magnificent wonders he beholds,
then, after ten days, through the arising of momentum while remaining in a state of absorption (laya), [he perceives them].
Even with the mind, the body desires to go;
for by dissolving [the self] even in twelve days, the state of moving through the earth is indeed accomplished.
In the measure of half a blink of an eye, he indeed wanders over the surface of the earth.
Then, within eleven days or even through absorption,
the lord of yogis attains the siddhi of Khecarī, even by means of contemplation alone.
If he remains established in dissolution until the end of fourteen days,
the perfection called *aṇimā* shall arise for him, by which the state of atomicity is attained.
Absorbed in himself by means of his own self for sixteen days,
the yogi attains the perfection of greatness, assuming a form like that of Mahādeva.
If one remains established in dissolution until the end of eighteen days,
one attains the siddhi known as Garima, by which one becomes capable of supporting the weight of the earth.
For one whose dissolution remains motionless for twenty days,
the perfection known as "lightness" arises, by which one becomes a bearer of the weight of Mount Meru while possessing atomicity.
He who has attained dissolution in the *svalakṣa* [state] shall have success within twenty-two days;
he who causes the world that exists to reach [that state] shall likewise attain it.
The yogi who has gone to dissolution in the *para* [state] [attains it] in twenty-four days.
By that [practice], the perfection of irresistible will (*prākāmyasiddhi*) is attained, through which one obtains whatever is desired; indeed,
for whomsoever the mind has set for twenty-six days,
he attains lordship over the world by means of which he becomes a teacher of the universe.
If one remains steady in the firm posture for twenty-eight days, his dissolution [of the breath] shall endure.
The attainment of mastery is *prāpti*, by which those who desire to go to dissolution in the state of the Supreme Brahman may indeed proceed as if the world were under their control.
All accomplishments become destroyers for those whose absorption lasts for one month without interruption.
The lord of the yogis does not wake until he attains liberation;
even by means of absorption for nine months, he enters the earth-element.
When the earth element is fully mastered, the lord of yogis becomes like a diamond;
even for a yogi who remains in dissolution, this occurs within one and a half years.
Even for a yogin who has dissolved [the previous elements], the perfection of the water-element (toyatattva) shall be attained within three years,
and then it becomes composed of the wind-element (vāyutattva).
The accomplishment of the fire principle (tejas-tattva) shall occur, and the yogi becomes composed of the fire principle;
established in the state of undivided dissolution, he remains so for six years.
The perfection of the wind-principle (vāyutattva) shall occur, and one becomes composed of the wind-principle;
likewise, for one who remains in dissolution continuously for twelve years.
The perfection of the space-principle (vyomatattva) shall be attained; one becomes composed of the space-principle after twenty-four years of remaining in dissolution (laya) without interruption.
Through the attainment of the perfection of the principle of Śakti, he indeed becomes composed of the principle of Śakti;
he beholds the entire cosmic egg as if it were a pearl situated within his own vital breath.
Having established the true nature of one's own body exactly as it exists,
one should practice the conduct of reality, for it is seen in the world that [the self] resides within the body.
One should indeed practice the conduct of reality for the sake of the power-principle (śakti-tattva) and forbearance;
thus, through the practice of dissolution increased by this gradual progression, the yogin [attains his goal].
Even during the dissolutions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, the yogis enjoy supreme bliss like great souls, partaking of the earth, wine, and other delights.
"The great-souled ones, such as Bhuśuṇḍa and others, enjoy supreme bliss.
Here, following the description of the bliss of yoga (*yogānanda*), the venerable Patañjali states the sequence of accomplishments (*siddhikrama*):

Having designated the term *saṃyama* for the concentration, meditation, and absorption directed toward the objects that are—according to the Vaiśeṣika system—the substances, qualities, and actions, as well as for those objects corresponding to the conventional designations of things, [the author] shall demonstrate the fruit and the application of that *saṃyama* by means of two sūtras.

For example: "From its mastery, the light of wisdom [arises]" and "its application to the stages. The meaning of this is as follows: from the mastery of that *saṃyama*—that is, through practice leading to its becoming one's own nature—the light of wisdom, which consists in the discernment (*viveka*) of the knower, spreads forth. The meaning is that when it is not overwhelmed by other forms of wisdom, there occurs a state characterized by a stainless flow; this is what is meant by "light."

The application of that *saṃyama* should be made to the fluctuations of the mind (*citta-vṛtti*) as they abide in the stages (*bhūmi*), distinguished by their support of either gross or subtle objects. Having mastered each lower stage of the mind, one should practice *saṃyama* on each successive higher stage of the mind. For one who practices *saṃyama* on a higher stage without having brought the lower stage under his own control will not partake in the fruit [of that practice]. To effect the purification of the object of the aforementioned *saṃyama*, he shows the threefold transformation by means of a Sūtra.

"The suppression of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of those of cessation, occurring in the mind at the moment of cessation, is the transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*). Emergence refers to the three stages known as the distracted, the infatuated, and the scattered; cessation is the transformation of the mind through its association with the highest degree of *sattva*.

The first is the transformation involving cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*). This refers to the subsistence of the two latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those two states of emergence and cessation, respectively, in a state where they have been overcome by the other and are thus incapable of producing their respective effects; and it refers to the manifestation of the mind (*citta*), which is the substratum (*dharmin*) existing at the moment of cessation, as it abides in its own essential nature during the two states known as emergence and cessation while on the path of the present.
This is the intended meaning.

When the *dharma* characterized by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of emergence disappears and the *dharma* characterized by the latent impression of cessation appears, while the substratum (*dharmī*) remains established as the underlying continuity of both, it is designated by the term "cessation-modification" (*nirodha-pariṇāma*).

Although there is no absolute immobility of the mind due to its fluctuating nature consisting of the *guṇas*, nevertheless, such a state of modification is called "stability. The fruit of this modification, however, is that the mind—having abandoned distraction—attains a modification consisting of a continuous flow of similar states.

Likewise: "The transformation of concentration (*samādhi*) is the destruction of all-objectedness and the emergence of one-pointedness within the multiform mind. (Regarding the term *artha*: The destruction (*kṣaya*) of distraction, which has the nature of having all things as its object, consists in its absolute suppression and non-arising—characterized by its entry into the past time—and is not merely its subordination. The emergence (*udaya*) of one-pointedness, characterized by a transformation similar to a single object of focus, is its manifestation. This is the persistence of the mind, whose essence is predominantly *sattva*, in its continuity; that is to say, it is most manifest in the present time. This is the second transformation of concentration.

The ultimate limit of this very process is the transformation of one-pointedness (*ekāgratā-pariṇāma*). As it is said: "The transformation of one-pointedness consists of two cognitions, one subsided and the other arisen, which are equal for the concentrated mind. For the concentrated mind alone, there is a specific modification consisting of a single cognition. One is subsided, having entered the past time-path; the other is arisen, manifesting in the present time-path. Both are equal by virtue of being a concentrated state of mind, and similar by virtue of having the same object of focus.

In both cases, the persistence of the variegated [mind] in a state of being concentrated alone is what is called "concentration" (samādhi), which is a transformation into one-pointedness. This very threefold classification is extended to other cases by the following aphorism:

"By this, the transformations of property (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*) regarding the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) have been explained. By this threefold aforementioned manifold transformation, it should be understood that a threefold transformation—distinguished by property, characteristic, and state—is explained with respect to the gross and subtle elements and the sense organs, which exist as distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is defined as the assumption of another property by a persisting substratum (*dharmī*) upon the cessation of its previous property.
Regarding this, the transformation of property (*dharma-pariṇāma*) is as follows: [P.263]...

Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is characterized by the substratum (*dharmin*), such as clay and so forth, relinquishing one attribute (*dharma*)—such as the form of a lump—and assuming another attribute, such as the form of a jar.

Likewise, it is the transformation of that very jar characterized by the relinquishing of its future state and the assumption of its present state, or the relinquishing of that [present state] and the grasping of its past state. Transformation regarding state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) is, for example, the change occurring in the state of that very jar through its persistence across the first and second moments; for it is said: "The activity of the qualities (*guṇa*) does not remain even for a moment without undergoing transformation."

Now, he demonstrates the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) that arise through the power of *saṃyama*: "From *saṃyama* upon the three-fold transformation comes knowledge of the past and the future. Regarding these three transformations—of essence (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*)—which have been described, when one practices *saṃyama* with a mind free from distraction, thinking, "In this essence, this is the essence; this is the characteristic; this is the state," and observing how [an object] moves from the future path into the present path, performs its own function, and then enters the past path, one knows everything of the past and the future.

When the obstacles to concentration caused by such distractions as hunger and the like have been destroyed through *saṃyama*, there occurs the manifestation of the object for the mind’s innate apprehension of all things. Likewise, there is a mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the distinct word, object, and cognition. For when asked, "What is the word?", "What is the object?", or "What is the cognition?", the answer given in the form "It is a cow" shows that from the well-known word "cow," there arises a single uniform appearance of the word, object, and cognition as "cow."

Because he has established a single unified form [of the word, object, and cognition], there is a distinction between the mixed [entities] as follows: "The word 'cow' is the denoter; the individual possessing a dewlap and so forth is the denoted; and the cognition is that which illuminates it. By means of the restraint (*saṃyama*) upon that [unified form], having attained knowledge of the sounds of all beings, one then attains knowledge of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) characterized by merit and demerit arising from attachment to pleasant sounds, of the minds of others, and of the form of the body—such as when one meditates, "There is no form in this body"—and of the characteristics of its maturation as being either swift or long-term.

Through *saṃyama* on friendliness and the other [immeasurables], on the strength of elephants and so forth, on the sun, and likewise on its color, and on the pole star (*dhruva*), there arise—respectively—knowledge of former births, knowledge of the objects of another’s mind, certainty regarding specific qualities, the power to arrest the capacity for grasping, the power of disappearance, knowledge of the union of the body and internal organ as delimited by fixed place and time, knowledge of omnipresence and so forth, the attainment of powers such as becoming minute, knowledge of the worlds, knowledge of the arrangement of the stars known as the stellar wheel (*jyotiścakra*), and knowledge of the movement of the stars; thus it has been described.

Likewise: by the statement, "Through the application of the light of *pravṛtti*, there is knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote," it is meant that when the previously mentioned *pravṛtti*—characterized as being directed toward objects (*viṣayavatī*) and characterized as luminous (*jyotiṣmatī*)—is applied through its sattvic expansion to stable objects, then, by means of the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of those respective types, the internal organs and senses attain a state of superior power; thereby, there arises knowledge of the subtle, such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), and of the concealed, such as treasures hidden within the earth.

O Queen, having thus demonstrated the external perfections (*siddhis*)—such as the knowledge of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like existing on the slopes of Mount Meru—the [text] now sets forth the internal perfections. Through mastery (*saṃyama*) over the hollow at the base of the mark of the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), the channel of the tortoise (*kūrmanāḍī*) situated below that, and the light at the crown of the head in the form of the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), there are established in due order the perfections characterized by the knowledge of the bodily constitution (*vyūha*), the cessation of hunger and thirst, and the vision of perfected beings (*siddhas*).
