Likewise, [it is said]: "Experience is the non-distinction of the cognition of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which are absolutely unmixed; from *saṃyama* upon one's own nature as distinct from that which exists for another, there arises knowledge of the *puruṣa*. By this, it is meant that between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*—which consist respectively of luminosity and bliss, and whose natures are that of the experiencer and the substrate, and which are absolutely distinct by virtue of being insentient and sentient—the "non-distinction of cognition" occurs because they appear undifferentiated through experience. The experience is the consciousness of pleasure and pain, which, though belonging to the *sattva*, is attributed to the *puruṣa* as its agent; and since this experience is independent of its own purpose, it exists for the sake of another (*parārtha*).

The purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is distinct from that [purpose of the intellect]; it is the self-interest (*svārtha*) which rests solely upon the essential nature of the person (*puruṣasvarūpa*). When the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) has transferred onto the existence of the intellect (*sattva*), one who practices *saṃyama* upon that [reflection] gains knowledge of the person. When that knowledge has arisen, the person knows that very form—the knowledge of the object—as residing in the *sattva*. However, the person, as the knower, does not itself become an object of that knowledge.

Having stated that the fruit of the direct realization of the *puruṣa* is the attainment of freedom from dullness (*jāḍya*), [the text] then says: "Intuition (*prātibha*), hearing (*śrāvaṇa*), sensation (*vedanā*), sight (*ādarśa*), taste (*svāda*), and awareness of events (*vārttā*) arise. By this, it is shown that intuition (*prātibha-jñāna*) has subtle objects and so forth as its fruit; that which is called "hearing" (*śrāvaṇa-saṃjñam*) has the knowledge of divine sounds as its fruit; that called "sensation" (*vedanā-saṃjñam*) is tactile knowledge having the knowledge of divine touches as its fruit; that called "sight" (*ādarśa-saṃjñam*) is visual knowledge having the knowledge of divine forms as its fruit; and [that called "taste"] has the knowledge of divine tastes as its fruit.

Having described the knowledge produced by the sense of taste as being called *āsvādana* (tasting) and *kalā* (art), the knowledge produced by the sense of smell as being called *divyagandhajñāna* (knowledge of divine fragrance) and *bhūti* (prosperity), and the knowledge produced by the sense of hearing as being of the nature of the *vārttā* (news) consisting in the perception of sounds located at an extreme distance; and having stated the division of the specific results with the words, "By that, in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is the removal of obstacles and the accomplishment of supernormal powers (*siddhi*"); [he then states] by means of the sūtra: "Entry into another's body occurs through the loosening of the cause of bondage and the awareness of the movement of the mind."

Due solely to the force of determined karma, the all-pervading self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*), being confined within the body, give rise to the experience of "I" and "this" as the enjoyer and the enjoyed—such as "this is mine"—in the form of pleasure, pain, and the nature of the body and mind. This is called the bondage of the body.

For instance, through the power of *samādhi*, the karma known as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which is the cause of bondage, becomes slackened; the mind then attains those very states. That movement of the mind—which is its outward flow from the region of the heart toward the objects of the senses by way of the doors of the sense organs—is thus suspended.

His perception is as follows: the channel through which the mind flows (cittavahā-nāḍī) carries the mind in this manner, and it is distinct from the channels that carry the vital breaths (prāṇa), fluids, and so forth. When he knows the movement of the body within both his own and another's bodies, he then enters another's body—whether dead or a living body—by means of the movement of the mind. (P.266) As the mind enters the other's body, the senses follow it, just as bees follow the queen bee. Consequently, the yogi who has entered another's body conducts himself as if it were his own body.

Having stated another accomplishment—namely, that for the all-pervading *citta-puruṣa*, the production of all enjoyments occurs through its sovereignty because karma, which is the cause for the contraction of enjoyment, has been neutralized by *samādhi* [the Yoga Sūtra states]: "From mastery over *udāna*, there is non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and so forth"; "from mastery over *samāna*, there is radiance," characterized by the relationship between the locus and the located; "from *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, the attainment of divine hearing, which perceives subtle, obstructed, and distant sounds"; and "from *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, [the power of] weighing like a scale."

Having described the attainment of powers through *māyā* and the ability to travel through space, [the text states]: "The external, non-imagined functioning is the *videhā*," and "From that, there is the destruction of the veil of light. By this, it is meant that when the mental function (*manovṛtti*) is associated with the ego-sense of the body, it is called "imagined" (*kalpitā*). However, when the mental function operates independently, having abandoned the state of bodily ego-sense, it is called the "great *videhā*" (*mahāvidehā*), which is non-imagined. Through *saṃyama* upon that, the destruction of various impurities occurs; thus another perfection (*siddhi*) has been stated.

Thus, the various means for the attainment of *sābīja* (with seed) and *nirbīja* (seedless) samādhi—consisting of the mastery of the vital airs (*prāṇa*) and so forth arising from the internal and external organs (*indriya*), which are conducive to concentration (*samādhi*), and those arising from the greatness of the yogi’s mind intended to produce confidence—have been presented with their respective rules. These, along with their commentaries, are now set forth as follows:
As it is said: [text continues]

"From *saṃyama* upon the gross form, the subtle, and the inherence of the objects, there is mastery over the elements. The gross elements consist of the five perceptible elements possessing specific forms: earth, water, fire, air, and ether. Their respective essential natures (*svarūpa*) are characterized by cohesion, solidity, heat, mobility, and the provision of space. Their subtle causes are the *tanmātras*. Their inherent qualities (*anvayitaḥ*) are the three *guṇas*: illumination, activity, and inertia. Furthermore, their "objectivity" (*arthavattva*) is the power residing within those *guṇas* known as the accomplishment of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). (P. 267)

Thus, by performing *saṃyama* sequentially upon each of the five states of the elements as they are differentiated, one becomes a conqueror of the elements (*bhūtajayin*). For example: first, having performed *saṃyama* on the gross form, then on the subtle form, and so on in this order; for one who has thus performed *saṃyama*, the elemental natures become compliant with his will, just as a cow follows its calf. He now states the fruit of that very conquest of the elements:

"From that, there arises the manifestation of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, the perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by its properties. *Aṇimā* is the attainment of an atomic form; because of it, one enters even into diamonds and other such hard substances. *Mahimā* is the attainment of greatness, whereby one becomes large. *Laghimā* is the attainment of lightness like a tuft of cotton. *Garimā* is the attainment of the state of Mount Meru. *Prāpti* is the attainment of the capacity to touch the moon and other distant objects with the tip of a finger. *Prākāmya* is the non-obstruction of desire for both the body and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Īśitva is sovereignty everywhere; it is the state of being all-powerful. Vaśitva is the power of subjugation—because all beings are influenced by it, they do not transgress what has been commanded. Kāmāvaśāyitva is the mastery over desire: in whatever object the yogin’s will (avasāya) is directed, he conquers that object through the process of appropriation, up to the limit of his longing. These eight qualities, beginning with aṇimā, which are conducive to samādhi, are called the great siddhis. (1)
And he states the characteristic of the perfection of the body in a sutra:
"The perfection of the body consists of beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine compactness. (2) "Adamantine compactness" means that his body possesses a firm cohesion like a diamond (*vajra*).
The remainder is clear. The properties (*dharma*) of that wheel (*valaya*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, do not undergo destruction by fire, wind, or other elements.
Now, having described the conquest of the elements (*bhūtajaya*), he speaks of the conquest of the senses (*indriyajaya*) for one who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*).
"From *saṃyama* on grasping, essential nature, egoism, continuity, and purposefulness, mastery over the senses is attained.

Grasping (*grahaṇa*) is the activity directed toward the objects of the senses; essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the state of luminosity in general; egoism (*asmitā*) is the accompaniment of the sense of "I"; and continuity (*anvaya*) and purposefulness (*arthavattva*) have been explained previously. By performing *saṃyama*, as before, upon these five states of the senses, one becomes a master of the senses.
He states the fruit of that:
"Then there is swiftness like the mind (*manojavitva*), the state of being without organs (*vikaraṇabhāva*), and mastery over primordial matter (*pradhānajaya*).

The triad consisting of the body's attainment of movement as swift as the mind, the functioning of the senses independent of the body, and universal sovereignty—these perfections (*siddhis*) manifest for one who has conquered the senses. These are called 'Honey-like' (*madhupratīka*), because just as one feels joy even at a single drop of honey, so too does one feel joy in each of these individually.
Now, he speaks of the conquest of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*):

"By means of the mere discriminative discernment (*anyathākhyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa, there arises for the yogi who has practiced restraint over this pure, *sāttvika* transformation the state of being the presider over all existents and omniscience. In this pure *sāttvika* transformation, for one who has performed *saṃyama*, there arises the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) consisting in the loosening of the egoistic conceit of agency regarding the *guṇas*. By virtue of its greatness, for the yogi established therein, there occurs through *samādhi* the state of being the presider over all existents and omniscience—the act of entering into all existents, which are transformations of the *guṇas*, like a master.

Omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is the knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) regarding those very [guṇas] as they exist in their true nature, characterized by the states of being quiescent (*śānta*), emergent (*udita*), or indeterminable (*avyapadeśya*). And when this state of mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*) has been attained in this quiescence, it is called the perfection (*siddhi*) named "freedom from sorrow" (*viśoka*).
He describes the next stage in sequence:
"From that dispassion (*vairāgya*), upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). (YS 3.50)

When detachment arises for the yogin even toward the state of sorrowlessness (viśoka), then, upon the destruction— that is, the uprooting— of the seed of those defects such as passion and the like, which is ignorance and so forth,
there is isolation (kaivalya), the absolute cessation of suffering.
The completion of the Puruṣa’s authority over the guṇas is its establishment in its own nature.

Regarding this very samādhi, he states the means for remaining therein: "Upon being invited by a stationary being (sthāṇu), one should avoid attachment and pride, lest there be the recurrence of undesirable consequences. (2)
There are four stages for the yogin.
Among them, the first is the one who possesses practice, whose light consists of mere activity;
he is also called "one of the first eon" (*prathamakalpika*).

The second [stage] is called "Honeyed" (madhubhūmika), characterized by truth-bearing insight (ṛtambharā prajñā). The third is the "Luminous" (jyotis) stage, characterized by mastery over the elements and the senses.

The fourth is that which has transcended cultivation (atikrāntabhāvana). For this fourth [practitioner], whose insight has manifested as the sevenfold attainment of the stages of samādhi and who is realizing the final stage known as the "Honeyed" (madhumatī), the gods dwelling in those realms become his inviters.

They offer celestial women, elixirs, and the like. One must not form an attachment to such an invitation, nor should one feel pride regarding it. For if one forms an attachment, one will inevitably experience pride upon enjoying sense objects; then, imagining oneself to have achieved all that was to be done, one will no longer exert oneself toward meditative absorption (samādhi). Therefore, he must avoid both attachment and pride.

Regarding this very discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which is the fruit [of yoga], he states another means distinct from the previously mentioned *saṃyama*: "From *saṃyama* on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discernment arises. (YS 3.52)

A *kṣaṇa* is the ultimate unit of time, whose constituent parts (*kalā*) cannot be further divided. The sequence of such temporal moments is their successive transformation in a temporal order. Through *saṃyama* upon that, the previously mentioned knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arises.
This is the meaning:

When, through the practice of *saṃyama* regarding such a sequence as "this moment is posterior to that moment" or "this is prior to that," there arises direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) even of the internal, subtle gradations of time, then one also directly perceives other subtle things, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth; thus, discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) arises.
Regarding this very *saṃyama*, he states the means for the discernment of its objects:
"From the differentiation of two similar things by means of genus, characteristic, and location, there arises [discriminative] cognition. (YS 3.52)
When the causes of distinction among objects consist of genus (*jāti*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and location (*deśa*)— as for example,
"cow" [is distinguished] by genus and characteristic, such as "spotted" or "red," and the locations of a balance-beam and its pans are the distinguishers [of their respective weights]—
but where a distinction cannot be determined, as in the case of two white, earthy atoms situated in the same place.

When discriminative knowledge (*bhedajñāna*) arises for one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon such an object, then through its cultivation even subtle principles such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth are understood in their distinction. To declare the scope of the aforementioned discriminative knowledge and its ethereal nature (*khebhāva*), it is said: "Discriminative knowledge is saving (*tāraka*), has all things as its object, has all modes as its object, and is non-sequential. (1) Knowledge that has arisen on the stage established by the power of the aforementioned *saṃyama* "saves" the yogi from the unfathomable limitation of *saṃsāra*; thus, it is "saving" (*tāraka*).
He states its object: "It has all principles as its object"—that is, *sarvaviṣaya* (all-objected)—meaning that all principles beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) are its object.
He states another internal state [of the mind]:—

"And non-sequential" (*akrama*) means that by grasping two, three, or one state [of an object] simultaneously, its sequence is transcended; thus, he sees everything all at once, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. He then states what results from this discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) called "the star":
"When there is equality of purity between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa, there is isolation (*kaivalya*)" (Sūtra 3.56).

"Equality" refers to the *sattva*'s complete cessation of the conceit of agency and its re-absorption into its own cause, which is its "purity"; the "purity" of the Puruṣa is the absence of even attributed experience. When both have attained this same purity, liberation occurs.
And thus, as the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arising from the sequence of practice— beginning with sovereignty and ending with liberation—
come into being, the yogi must not reveal them anywhere, nor should he feel wonder or pride; for if he does so, his attainment will be lost.
And furthermore, Dattātreya says:
"Because of the explanation of the characteristics of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), the consciousness of the yogi likewise dissolves; therefore, worldly activities must be concealed."
In the *Yogatattvaprakāśa*:
"One should never display one's own supernatural power (*sāmarthya*) before ordinary people;
however, at times one may display it out of affection, or again, toward one who is endowed with devotion."
Just like one who is mute, just like one who is deluded, or just like one who is deaf,
so does he conduct himself in the worlds for the sake of concealing his own power.
Many disciples will arise for you, of this there is no doubt;
however, while preoccupied with performing those rituals, your practice may be forgotten. Deprived of that practice, one should then perform worldly actions.
If one becomes attached to worldly things, one will undoubtedly fall away.
Likewise, even this practice (karma) should not be made public; if it is revealed, it becomes fruitless.
Thus it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"The science of Haṭha should be kept secret by the yogi who desires perfection;
it becomes potent when guarded, but powerless when revealed."
Now, by means of perfected yoga (*siddhayoga*), all the signs of time (*kālacihna*) must necessarily be observed; these are now being written down.

Here, for one who desires liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) by means of perfected yoga, it is for the purpose of deceiving time (*kālavañcana*). But for one whose yoga is not yet perfected (*asiddhayoga*), at the time of death there is a connection with yoga (*yogasamspr̥ti*) so that yoga may be attained in another birth.

And so it is said in the Gītā: "O son of Kuntī, whatever state of being one remembers when they abandon the body at the end, to that very state they go, for their thought is constantly fixed on that."
"This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha! Having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding in this even at the time of death, one attains the liberation of Brahman.
(1) The method for cheating death has already been explained previously in passing.
The signs of that [death] are as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"If one's wind flows through the left nostril day and night without interruption,
his entire lifespan perishes indeed within three years."
The sun flows continuously for two days and nights, or three days and nights;
this is said here to be the limit of one's lifespan in the first year.
It should flow continuously through the pair of nostrils for ten days.
If the breath returns [to its course], then one shall live for three seasons.
Having abandoned the threefold path of the nostrils, Mātariśvan (the breath) moves through the mouth;
for by means of the intellect (dhī), he then effects his departure back toward the path of the ether.
When the Sun is situated in the seventh sign and the Moon is in the natal asterism,
that time is not to be desired as the Pauṣṇa [lagna], provided that the Sun moves in the southern course.
At that time, death may suddenly befall him.
One who fears death should diligently reflect upon that time [of death].
He who gazes upon the man who is dark-brown (Kṛṣṇapiṅgala) without cause—
In this very moment, one may live for two years, provided that his semen,
feces, urine, sneeze, or even his excrement,
should at any time here on earth, strive toward [the divine]; such a person's life is considered to last for those two years.
He who sees a multitude of serpents resembling sapphires moving here and there in the sky shall live for six months.
Arundhatī is the tongue; Dhruva is released at the tip of the nose.
Viṣṇu’s steps are the space between the eyebrows; the eye is Glau; and the circle of the Mothers is the forehead.
One whose death is imminent will not behold Arundhatī, Dhruva, the three steps of Viṣṇu, nor the fourth, the circle of the stars in the mother’s constellation.

If the complexion of the body suddenly changes from its natural state— such as becoming pale, blue, or otherwise— and the taste of the mouth similarly alters from its natural state— such as becoming bitter or sour— then that person will meet death within six months.
For one destined to die within six months, the throat, lips, tongue, and teeth,
as well as the tongue and the palate as the fifth, become constantly parched.
If semen, fingernails, or the corners of the eyes possess a dark blue tint,
then that man shall go to the city of Yama in the sixth month.
If one quickly mounts a three-colored lizard whose head is moving forward and then proceeds,
his life will come to an end within six months.
Even for one who has bathed well, if his heart, feet, and hands quickly become parched, his life remains for only three months.
The messengers of Death bind that man in the fourth month whose wife trembles even when his own body is motionless.
If one's intellect falters, or if two Indras' bows are seen,
or if two moons appear at night and two suns at the beginning of the day;
By day, the sky was filled with stars and the moon; by night, it was devoid of stars.
Simultaneously, in the four directions, the clearly visible circle of Indra’s bow appeared.
A tree upon a mountain peak, a city of Gandharvas in the sky,
and the dancing of Piśācas by day— these are indeed the causes of death.
If even one of all these signs is observed,
then one should expect death within the limit of one month, and not beyond that.
For he is carried off and devoured by piśācas, asuras, and crows;
by bhūtas, pretas, dogs, vultures, jackals, donkeys, and pigs.
At the end of the year, having abandoned his life in the Khapla hell, he beholds Yama along with śarabhas, young elephants, kīras, hawks, mules, and vultures.
The man who sees his own body adorned with red perfumes, flowers,
and unbroken grains (akṣata) during the time of sleep, lives for eight months.
He who, in a dream, climbs a heap of dust, an anthill, or even a sacrificial post, perishes in the sixth month; likewise,
one who sees himself mounted on a donkey, smeared with oil, and shaven.
Whoever should see one being led toward the direction of Yama shall [be purified] as before.
That man who sees grass or dry wood upon his own head or his own body shall perish in the sixth month.
If one sees a black man dressed in black garments holding an iron staff standing at the head of one's bed in a dream, one shall not violate the three-month period.
If a maiden named Kālī binds one with arm-nooses in a dream,
he shall behold within a month the city inhabited by Yama.
Or, if a man travels toward the eastern direction while dreaming that he is mounted upon a monkey;
In exactly fifty days, he shall behold the city of Saṃyamanī.
If even a sword were generous, or if a generous person were miserly,
then nature would become its opposite, and one would meet with death.
These are the signs of the time; there are many others as well.
Having recognized them, a person should practice yoga, or else take refuge in Kāśī.
"O Sage, I do not see any other means than the acquisition of untimely gold.
Thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"One whose bonds of karma are undiminished, having realized that death is uncertain..."
By recollecting this at the time of departure from the body, one attains the state of a yogin once again.
Therefore, whether by means of non-attainment or again by means of attainment,
one should always recognize the signs of death (ariṣṭas), so that one does not falter at the time of the soul's departure (utkrānti).
O Great King! Listen, for I shall tell you of those omens of death, by the sight of which the knower of yoga recognizes his own approaching end.
Having seen his own reflection, the sun,
and the radiant fire for eleven months, a man lives for one year.
He who vomits urine and feces, or likewise gold and silver—
whether in waking reality or in a dream— has but ten months of life remaining.
Having seen ghosts, piśācas, and the like, as well as cities of the gandharvas and trees of golden hue, he lives for nine months;
he who suddenly becomes stout and then thin, or thin and then stout, [will not survive].
And he shall turn away from Prakṛti; his lifespan shall be eight months.
If a person's foot becomes mangled at the heel or at the tip of the toe while standing between dust and mud,
he shall live for seven months.
If a pigeon, a vulture, a crow, an owl, or a raven should perch upon the head of a person,
or if a carnivorous bird should stand there, it indicates a lifespan of six months.
The crow is killed by handfuls of earth, and the monkey by a shower of dust;
likewise, one whose vital organs are parched may die from bathing in cold water.
If he sees his own shadow in a different way, death will approach him with obstacles after five months; however, if it is otherwise, he shall live for four months.
Having seen lightning in a cloudless sky appearing in the southern direction,
or even a rainbow in the north, one's life remains for only two or three months.
He who sees his own body in ghee, oil,
or in a mirror as headless, does not live beyond a month.
If a yogin possesses a fragrance like that of sandalwood or even like the scent of a lion on his body,
his lifespan, O King, should be known to be half a month.
He whose brain and heart-lotus dry up to the size of a thumb,
yet whose lips remain moist as he drinks water, even he lives for ten days.

He whose vital breath is suppressed, whose limbs become rigid, who does not shiver despite contact with water, and in whom the clouds do not fall from their places— for him, death stands present in bodily form.
He who wanders toward the southern direction in a dream while mounted on a vehicle drawn by bears or monkeys,
for him death does not wait for its appointed time.
If Gāyatrī, wearing red and black garments,
laughs at a man and leads that woman toward the southern quarter in a dream, he too shall not live.
If a young woman sees in a dream a powerful, naked mendicant laughing in this manner,
she should know that death has approached.
But that man who, submerged in an ocean of mud,
sees himself in a dream reaching down to the very bottom of the earth, dies immediately.
If one sees hair, a forest fire, ashes, a serpent, or a river without water in a dream,
death will occur after ten days on the eleventh day.
If one is crushed by stones in a dream by terrifying, hideous, black men with uplifted weapons, one shall meet death immediately.
If at sunrise a jackal comes howling toward a person,
whether by circling them clockwise or counter-clockwise, that person immediately meets with death.
He whose heart is indeed afflicted by hunger immediately after eating, and who experiences pain in his teeth and gums, will undoubtedly depart from this life;
he does not perceive the scent of lamps and the like, and likewise trembles at the sight of water at night.
He who does not see his own self reflected in the eyes of others does not live.
Having seen Indra’s weapon at midnight, or likewise an eclipse of the sun or moon,
the knower of the self should consider his own life to be nearly exhausted.
If the nose becomes crooked, if there is depression or elevation of the ears,
and if the left eye weeps, the life of that person has reached its end; likewise,
if the face turns reddish and the tongue becomes black.
Then the wise man should recognize that death is near for himself.
O lord of men, one who is seen traveling toward the southern direction in a dream by means of a camel or a donkey vehicle should know that death awaits him in his sleep.
One whose ears are blocked by wax does not hear the faultless sound produced within himself;
and he whose light of sight perishes likewise does not live.
And for one who has fallen into the Vaigarta hell, whose door is closed,
and who does not rise from his sleep— that is the end of his life.
The gaze was directed upward and remained fixed; moreover,
it was bloodshot and rolling about.
The heat of the face and the coolness of the navel indicate that the body of a man belongs both to himself and to another.
He who enters fire in a dream and does not emerge again,
or likewise enters water, his life ends there.
Furthermore, the man who is struck by spirits during his vision or while awake will undoubtedly meet his death at the end of seven nights.
Furthermore, the man who sees his own garment— which was previously stainless and white— become black,
should indeed recognize that death is near for him.
The reversal of one's natural disposition and the inversion of one's innate character—
these they say indicate that death is near for men.
Those whom he has constantly disciplined and who are considered by him to be most worthy of worship— those very people he disregards and those very people he reviles.
The learned man does not worship the gods, he reviles his gurus and the Brahmins,
and he displays arrogance toward his parents and his sons-in-law.
The wise man should discern the birth of yogis, of the learned, and of other great souls when the time has arrived;
for through the constant effort of yogis, the omens of death (ariṣṭas) are warded off.

The wise one should always observe these [omens] until the end of the year, for they yield results day and night; O timid one, the lord of men, having understood the matter in his mind, should act at the proper time when they are joined with their results.
Having correctly understood that time and having taken refuge in the state of fearlessness,
the yogi should apply himself to practice so that this time may not be fruitless for him.
Having thus perceived the omen of death, the yogi,
casting off the fear born of dying and contemplating that very nature, remains until the appointed time has arrived.
During that period, the knower of yoga should likewise practice yoga at the appointed time—
either in the forenoon, the afternoon, or at midday— day after day.
Or rather, during that portion of the night when the omen was observed,
he should remain engaged [in yoga] for as long as it takes until the auspicious day arrives.
Then, having abandoned all fear and conquered that time,
the knower of the Self remained right there in his dwelling, wherever he found stability for himself.
Having conquered the three qualities, the yogi should unite himself with the Supreme Self;
becoming absorbed in That by means of his own self, he should even abandon the fluctuations of consciousness.
Beyond that is the supreme Nirvāṇa, which is beyond the range of the senses;
that which cannot be grasped by the intellect or described by speech is what one hears from the Teacher.
In the *Brahmayāmala*:
"In a cloudless sky at night during the bright fortnight, or again every day,
with the mind fixed one-pointedly and steady upon the navel, the feet, or the surface of the forehead."
First covering one eye with the shadow of the hand, one should look at the sky;
immediately thereafter, one sees there the Kāla-puruṣa, who resembles the ocean of milk and the jasmine flower.
By the mere sight of him, one is liberated from all sins.
And when one perceives it as complete, then whence can there be fear of death?
When one beholds that stainless [reality] endowed with all perfect characteristics, then no time exists, certainly not even for as long as a year.
If the head is missing, death will occur within six months; of this there is no doubt.
If the arms are missing, disease will arise, or there may be the wasting away of the body.
If there is a crack in the tree (or in the black portion), there will be loss of wealth; if there is a crack in the vulva, death of the wife;
and if there is a crack in the middle, there will be the falling of a weapon or a famine.
In the case of a departure, there will be abundance; in the case of a neck-bend (grīvābhaṅga), there is the destruction of the king.
In the yellow color, there will be gain; in the black color, it causes untimely death.
If it is red in color, there will be sovereignty; if yellow, long life.
Merely by the sight of it, rebirth no longer exists.
Devoid of colors such as white and the like, and free from the form of sound,
they make known the supreme reality, which is beyond the reach of mind and speech.
"For if [the mantra] is hidden, it steals away death; one should not show it even to a guru.
If shown, there is no fruit; if kept secret, he who sees it is wasting time.
This is the general direction.
This very practice of profound meditation (nididhyāsana), together with its means of accomplishment,
has been described by me in brief, according to the scriptures and according to my own understanding.
Hearing and reflection, along with their specific details and full extent, are to be sought in the Vedāntas alone; they have not been stated here for fear of excessive prolixity.
Whatever secret of Rājayoga and Haṭhayoga exists has been revealed by me here for the delight of those devoted to yoga.
Indeed, that haṭhayoga which was practiced by Uddālaka, Bhuśuṇḍa, and others, has not been written down by me, because it is impossible to accomplish through such concordant means.
As for the ritual procedures and other such matters composed by the Kāpālikas,
I have not written them down, for they are in contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti.
He who has propitiated Mahādeva on a mountain, or Brahmā, or Hari,
or Lambodara, or even Ravi, shall attain perfection through yoga.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Yogacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrīmacchivānandasarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya Śrī Rāmacandrasadānandasarasvatī; and this work is now complete.
